sections.results:
Psoriasis is a chronic, recurrent, and inflammatory skin disease that affects about 2–3% of the global population, making it one of the most common chronic skin diseases in the world []. The disease is characterized by erythema, scales, and itching, which seriously affects the quality of life of patients, including skin symptoms, mental health, and social interaction. According to its clinical features, psoriasis can be classified as the common, arthropathy, pustule, or erythroderma type. Psoriasis vulgaris is the most common, accounting for more than 99% of cases. Its main pathological features include epidermal hyperproliferation, inflammatory cell infiltration, and dermal vasodilation. These pathological changes are mainly caused by immune abnormalities induced by genetic and environmental factors, involving keratinocytes and various immune cells, such as T cells, plasma-like dendritic cells, myeloid dendritic cells, neutrophils, and macrophages, which together form an inflammatory circuit and promote the onset and development of psoriasis [,,]. These cells secrete a large number of proinflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), interferon γ (IFN-γ), and interleukin-17 (IL-17), which leads to abnormal proliferation and persistent inflammatory reaction of keratinocytes [,]. Although remarkable progress has been made in the treatment of psoriasis in recent years, the understanding of its pathogenesis is still limited. At present, the treatment methods for psoriasis mainly include local medication, phototherapy, and systematic treatment. Topical medication, such as glucocorticoids and vitamin D analogs, is the first choice of treatment for mild psoriasis. Phototherapy, such as ultraviolet B (UVB) and narrow-band ultraviolet B (NB-UVB), is effective for moderate and severe psoriasis. Systematic therapy includes traditional drugs, such as methotrexate, cyclosporine, and avia, as well as biological agents, such as anti-TNF-α antibodies and IL-17 inhibitors [,]. However, these treatments have some limitations. Therefore, it is of great significance to study the pathogenesis of psoriasis and find new therapeutic targets.

Protein geranylgeranylation is a kind of lipoprotein modification that plays a key role in regulating the membrane localization and activation of coenzyme A reductase. PGGT1B, also known as BGGI or GGT, is an enzyme involved in the acylation of protein amino acid geranyl geranium. Under normal circumstances, the acylation of protein geranyl geranium helps to maintain the normal function of immune cells. However, when PGGT1B is defective, it may affect this modification process, resulting in abnormal immune cell function []. Studies have shown that myeloid PGGT1B deficiency results in the abnormal function of immune cells []. For example, the deletion of PGGT1B in mouse intestinal epithelial cells leads to cytoskeleton rearrangement and tight junction redistribution, thus preventing cell detachment, further attracting neutrophils and CD4+ T cells, and finally inducing chronic intestinal inflammation []. In addition, the defect of PGGT1B in T cells damages the function of RhoA, increases the expression of α4β7, and leads to an increase in CD4+ T cells in the colon, which leads to the over-expression of Th17-related inflammatory cytokines and mediates the development of colitis []. Knocking out PGGT1B in vascular smooth muscle cells can reduce Rac1 activity and ERK1/2 and JNK phosphorylation levels; inhibit vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, NADPH oxidase activity, and oxidative damage; and effectively inhibit the accelerated atherosclerosis process of diabetes in mice []. On the other hand, the conditional deletion of PGGT1B in mouse macrophages increases Rac1 activity; the phosphorylation level of p38, IKK, Src, and STAT3; and the expression of proinflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-α after LPS stimulation, which leads to the development of chronic erosive rheumatoid arthritis in mice []. These inflammatory factors also play an important role in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. They can stimulate the proliferation and inflammatory reaction of keratinocytes, thus aggravating the condition of psoriasis [].

The purpose of this study is to explore the role and molecular mechanism of PGGT1B in the development of psoriasis. We established a mouse model of psoriasis induced by imiquimod by constructing myeloid cell-specific PGGT1B gene knockout mice and combined it with RNA-seq analysis to study the role of macrophage activation induced by PGGT1B gene downregulation in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. The results showed that PGGT1B deficiency in myeloid cells aggravates imiquimod-induced psoriasis-like lesions, accompanied by excessive secretion of inflammatory factors. The results of this study help reveal the pathophysiological process of psoriasis and provide a new target for treatment.

In order to study the relationship between PGGT1B deficiency and rash in psoriasis, we used myeloid cell-specific PGGT1B knockout mice as the conditional knockout (cko) group, and wild Pggt1b fl/fl Lyz2 wt/wt mice as the control group (wt group). The acute psoriasis model was established by applying IMQ to the back of mice for 5 days after depilation, and the control group was given the same dose of Vaseline (VAS) ointment. When the skin injury reached its highest severity, samples were photographed and examined using histopathology, IHC, mRNA analysis, and skin homogenate (A). The results show that compared to the VAS group, erythema and a small amount of scales and wrinkles appeared around the coated area on the wt mice one day after modeling. When the drug was used continuously for 4–5 days, erythema and scale thickening were the most obvious. On the other hand, compared to the wt mice, the cko mice displayed an earlier appearance of rash, more obvious erythema, more scales, and a thicker rash appearance (B). At the same time, the psoriasis area and severity index (PASI) score (evaluating erythema, scales, and hypertrophy) of the cko mice was significantly higher (C, p < 0.05). Compared to the wt group, after IMQ treatment, the cko group had more obvious hyperkeratosis, significantly increased epidermal thickness, enlarged epidermal processes, and proliferated inflammatory infiltrating cells in the dermal papilla (D, p < 0.05). After the IMQ model was established, compared to the wt group, the rate of Ki67-positive cells in the cko group increased (E, p < 0.05). In addition, loricrin in the cuticle of the two genotypes of mice decreased, and the decreasing trend in the cko group was more significant than that in the wt group (F, p < 0.05), which indicates that in the IMQ-induced psoriasis model, myeloid PGGT1B deficiency promoted the proliferation of keratinocytes and inhibited their differentiation.

In order to explore the relationship between PGGT1B deficiency and inflammation in psoriasis, we measured the mRNA and cytokine expressions of inflammatory factors IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-17A, and IL-10 in the most serious stage of skin injury in mice using Luminex and qRT-PCR. The results show that the levels of IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-17A in the IMQ group were higher than those in the VAS group, while the level of IL-10 in the IMQ group was lower than that in the VAS group. In addition, in the psoriasis group induced by IMQ, the levels of IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-17A were higher in the cko group than those in the wt group, especially IL-1β and IL-6 (A,B,D–G,I,J, p < 0.05). The mRNA level of IL-10 decreased, but there was no significant difference (C,H, p > 0.05). The main sign of NF-κB activation is the transfer of NF-κB from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, where it combines with a specific DNA sequence to start the transcription of related genes. In this study, the IHC staining results of skin sections of the four groups of mice show that NF-κB staining was positive in the cytoplasm of the two groups of VAS mice. Nuclear translocation was observed in epidermal cells, infiltrating inflammatory cells, and some epidermal cells of the IMQ mice in both groups. The number of NF-κB nuclear translocations in the cko group was significantly higher than that in the wt group (K, p < 0.05), indicating that the lack of myeloid PGGT1B aggravated the psoriasis-like inflammation induced by IMQ. In order to clarify the role of myeloid cells in this process, IHC staining of Ly6G (neutrophil marker) and F4/80 (macrophage marker) was performed on the skin lesions of each group of mice. The results show that there was no statistical difference in the number of Ly6G-positive stained cells between the two genotypes (L, p > 0.05). After 5 days of IMQ coating, the positive rate of F4/80 in the mouse dermis and dermal papilla increased significantly, and a small number of positively stained cells was also observed in the epidermis (M, p < 0.05). These results show that PGGT1B regulated the activation of macrophages, affecting the intensity of the inflammatory response in psoriasis.

To investigate the effects of myeloid-specific PGGT1B knockout on the development of psoriasis, we stimulated BMDMs with R848 to mimic the immune microenvironment of psoriatic macrophages in mice. Then, transcriptome sequencing was employed to identify the alterations in biological processes induced by PGGT1B knockout (A). Gene analyses of four binary comparison groups (wtcon, wtR848, ckocon, and ckoR848) were performed. To identify the DEGs resulting from PGGT1B deficiency in response to R848 stimulation, we compared three sets of differentially expressed genes: wtR848 vs. wtcon, ckoR848 vs. ckocon, and ckoR848 vs. wtR848. The results reveal 226 DEGs (B–D). Next, the differentially expressed gene–protein interaction network was analyzed. For the species within the database, the interaction relationships of the target genome were directly extracted to construct the network (E). The MCODE plug-in was used to identify subnet clusters. All the genes with the highest score in the network were considered the central gene (cluster1), and the results are listed in (F). Central genes promote the biological process of cytokine binding to cytokine receptors by affecting the molecular function of mediated signaling pathways. In addition, the concentrations of proinflammatory factors IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-17A in the cko group were significantly higher than those in the wild-type group 12 h after R848 stimulation of bone marrow stromal cells. The IL-10 in the ckoR848 group was significantly lower than that in the wtR848 group (G–K, p < 0.05). The mRNA expression of the hub gene was verified using qPCR (L–P, ). This suggests that PGGT1B deficiency promotes the secretion of proinflammatory factors and inhibits the secretion of anti-inflammatory factors in BMDMs.

In order to explore the effect of bone marrow-specific PGGT1B knockout on the NF-κB signaling pathway, we found the top 10 pathways related to cytokine secretion through KEGG enrichment analysis of hub genes. These pathways include cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction, the chemokine signaling pathway, the toll-like receptor signaling pathway, the NF-κB signaling pathway, and the TNF signaling pathway (A). In addition, a protein blot was used to detect the expression of p65 in BMDM whole cell lysate at different time points after R848 stimulation. The results show that after 5 min, the expression of p-p65 in both groups began to increase and, after 15 min, the expression of PGGT1B-deficient BMDM was higher than that in the wild-type group (B, p < 0.05). At the same time, after 24 h of R848 stimulation, the expressions of NLRP3, ASC, caspase-1, p-p65, IL-1β, and cleaved-caspase-1 in the whole cell lysate and the activation of NLRP3 inflammatory vesicles in the supernatant were analyzed. There was no significant difference in ASC expression between the two groups. The expression of NLRP3 increased in both groups, especially in PGGT1B-deficient cells. Compared with the wild-type BMDM, the expressions of cleaved-caspase-1 and IL-1β were significantly higher in the PGGT1B-deficient BMDM cells and culture supernatant (C). Next, we pretreated BMDMs with or without the NF-κB pathway inhibitor JSH-23. In addition, we used MCC950, an inhibitor of NLRP3, to further clarify whether PGGT1B affects the expression of IL-β through the activation of NLRP3 inflammatory corpuscles. The results show that compared to the R848 group, the expressions of p-p65, NLRP3, and IL-1β in the supernatant of the JSH+R848 group were significantly decreased. Compared to the R848 group, cleaved-caspase-1 in the MCC950+R848 group decreased significantly in the supernatant, while the intracellular expressions of IL-1β, p-p65, NLRP3, and cleaved-caspase-1 decreased slightly (D). These results indicate that JSH-23 directly inhibits the production and secretion of IL-1β in cells, while MCC950 inhibits the secretion of IL-1β by inhibiting the production of cleaved-caspase-1 and reducing the maturation of IL-1β. This suggests that PGGT1B deficiency promotes the activation of inflammatory corpuscles and the secretion of IL-1β in NLRP3 by activating the NF-κB signaling pathway.

In order to study the effect of PGGT1B-deficient macrophages on the proliferation and differentiation of keratinocytes, we established a co-culture system of macrophages and keratinocytes in vitro. EDU analysis, Ki-67 immunofluorescence analysis, and RT-QCPR analysis were used to observe the effect of PGGT1B on the proliferation and differentiation of HaCaT (A). We generated PGGT1B knockout THP-1 cell lines (B). We used R848 at concentrations of 0, 0.5, 1, and 2 μg/mL to stimulate HaCaT cells. After 48 h, the cell proliferation rate was determined using the EDU test. The results show that 0.5 μg/mL R848 had no significant effect on the growth of HaCaT cells, while 1 μg/mL R848 led to a significant increase in the proliferation rate of HaCaT cells. Therefore, the concentration of R848 was selected as 0.5 μg/mL in the subsequent experiments (see ). The expressions of inflammatory factors after R848 stimulation were detected through qRT-PCR, and their levels were consistent with those in the PGGT1B-deficient BMDMs (see ). In addition, we found that when these two types of cells were in direct contact, the cell proliferation and K17 mRNA level of HaCat cells co-cultured with PGGT1B knockout macrophages were significantly higher than those of wild-type macrophages (G–H). At the same time, the expression of K14 mRNA in HaCaT cells co-cultured with wild-type macrophages increased slightly, but there was no statistically significant difference. However, with PGGT1B knockout, the expression of K14 mRNA in HaCaT cells increased significantly. This suggests that macrophages with PGGT1B gene knockout can promote the proliferation of HaCaT, which may be achieved through intercellular anchoring connection and communication connection.

In order to study how the acylation of geranium protein regulates NF-κB activity, we used small interfering RNA (siRNA) to inhibit the expression of Cdc42, Kras, or Rhoa in BMDMs with PGGT1B deficiency (A), followed by stimulation with R848. The results show that the phosphorylation level of p65 decreased significantly in BMDMs with PGGT1B deficiency after downregulating Cdc42. The inhibition of Kras and RhoA had no effect on p65 phosphorylation (B). This suggests that Cdc42 is more easily activated in PGGT1B-deficient cells, which leads to the overactivation of the NF-κB signaling pathway stimulated by R848. This, in turn, increases the production of inflammatory cytokines in macrophages. C presents a diagram of this mechanism.

In this study, it was found that PGGT1B deficiency in myeloid cells aggravates imiquimod-induced psoriasis-like lesions, accompanied by excessive secretion of inflammatory factors. These results suggest that PGGT1B may play a role in inhibiting the inflammatory response in myeloid cells, and its absence leads to an uncontrolled inflammatory response, thus aggravating the condition of psoriasis.

Previous studies have found that the expression of PGGT1B in peripheral blood mononuclear cells of patients with psoriasis decreased significantly, suggesting that this enzyme may be involved in the pathogenesis of psoriasis []. However, the specific method and mechanism of action are still unclear. In this study, bone marrow cell-specific PGGT1B knockout mice were constructed using gene knockout technology, which further confirmed the key role of PGGT1B in psoriasis. By comparing the performance of wild-type and PGGT1B knockout mice in the psoriasis model, we found that the lack of PGGT1B in bone marrow significantly aggravated the psoriasis-like lesions induced by imiquimod in mice. This result preliminarily confirmed our hypothesis that PGGT1B plays a protective role in the pathogenesis of psoriasis.

The level of inflammatory factors is closely related to the onset and severity of psoriasis. Among them, IL-17 mainly comes from proinflammatory cells in diseased skin, such as mast cells, T cells, and innate lymphoid cells. These cells can stimulate the production of various antimicrobial peptides, chemokines, and factors that promote inflammation and cell proliferation, thus aggravating the inflammatory reaction in tissues [,]. In addition, IL-17 can also promote the production of IL-6, which can not only activate and attract more inflammatory cells to the damaged area but also lead to abnormal skin desquamation and hyperkeratosis, which further promotes the formation and development of psoriasis plaques [,]. TNF-α also plays an important role in psoriasis. It can induce more proinflammatory cytokines by activating macrophages and T cells. The inhibition of TNF-α has been proven to have a significant effect on relieving psoriasis symptoms [,]. In this study, in order to explore the relationship between PGGT1B deficiency and inflammation in psoriasis, we also detected the mRNA and cytokine expressions of inflammatory factors IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-17A, and IL-10 in the most serious stage of skin injury in mice. Our experimental results show that the expressions of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1B, IL-6, and TNF-α were significantly increased. The overexpression of these inflammatory factors is one of the important characteristics in the pathogenesis of psoriasis, which is consistent with previous research results showing that the loss of PGGT1B may lead to an imbalance of the immune system, thus aggravating the inflammatory response. Then, BMDMs were stimulated by R848 to simulate the immune microenvironment of psoriasis. R848 is a synthetic TLR7/8 agonist, similar to IMQ, which can activate the TLR7/8 signaling pathway and induce immune cells to produce an inflammatory reaction. During in vitro experiments, R848 is often used as a stimulator of BMDMS (bone marrow-derived macrophages) to simulate the immune activation state in the psoriasis microenvironment. Compared with IMQ, R848 is more convenient to operate and has its role in vitro experiments. We found that the NF-κB signaling pathway was overactivated in BMDMs with PGGT1B deficiency. These results indicate that PGGT1B may affect the development of psoriasis by regulating the NF-κB signaling pathway.

NF-κB is a widely studied signal transduction pathway that plays a central role in regulating the inflammatory response, immune response, cell proliferation, and apoptosis. P65 is a member of the NF-κB family, which usually forms a heterodimer with p50. In unstimulated cells, this dimer is bound to the cytoplasm by the inhibitory protein IκB. When cells are stimulated by external stimuli (such as TNF-α, IL-1β, LPS, etc.), IκB kinase (IKK) is activated, which leads to phosphorylation and the subsequent degradation of IκB protein, releasing p65/p50 dimer. The released p65/p50 complex can enter the nucleus and start the transcription of downstream genes [,]. In order to further explore the possible biological process of PGGT1B regulation, we conducted RNA-seg analysis and found differentially expressed genes induced by PGGT1B knockout. Through bioinformatics analysis, we found that these differentially expressed genes are closely related to biological processes, such as the NF-KB signaling pathway, cell proliferation, and differentiation. At the same time, we detected the expression of p65 in BMDM whole cell lysates at different time points after R848 stimulation. The results show that 5 min after R848 stimulation, p-p65 in both groups began to increase, indicating that the NF-κB signaling pathway was activated rapidly. However, after 15 min, the expression of p-p65 in PGGT1B-deficient BMDMs was significantly higher than that in the wild-type group. This result indicates that the loss of PGGT1B may aggravate the inflammatory reaction by promoting or prolonging the activation of the NF-κB signaling pathway. After 24 h of R848 stimulation, the expressions of NLRP3, ASC, caspase-1, p-p65, IL-1β, and cleaved-caspase-1 in whole-cell lysates and the activation of NLRP3 inflammatory vesicles in the supernatant were further analyzed. These results indicate that the loss of PGGT1B not only affects the NF-κB signaling pathway but also promotes the activation of NLRP3 inflammatory corpuscles. The NLRP3 inflammatory corpuscle is an important inflammatory regulator that can promote the maturation and release of proinflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1β, after activation, thus aggravating the inflammatory state of psoriasis. These results suggest that PGGT1B plays an important role in maintaining macrophage homeostasis and preventing excessive inflammatory reaction.

In the process of exploring the regulatory mechanism of PGGT1B, we also found that the activation of cell division cycle 42 (Cdc42) may mediate the activation of the NF-κB pathway in PGGT1B-deficient BMDMs. CDC42 is an important cytoskeleton protein involved in regulating biological processes, such as cell morphology, polarity, and migration []. Previous studies have found that increased serum Cdc42 levels in psoriasis patients reflect disease severity []. In this study, in BMDMs with PGGT1B deficiency, the phosphorylation level of p65 decreased significantly after downregulating Cdc42. This suggests that the activation of Cdc42 may be one of the key links that PGGT1B deletion leads to overactivation of the NF-κB signaling pathway and an increase in inflammatory factor expression. However, at present, it is not clear whether PGGT1B’s influence on Cdc42 is direct or indirect. Cdc42 belongs to the small G protein family, and many members of this family (such as Ras and Rac) are known to undergo isopentenylation modification. This modification usually occurs on the C-terminal cysteine residue. By adding isoprene groups (such as farnesyl or geranyl geranyl), the combination of protein and cell membrane is promoted, thus affecting its localization and function. PGGT1B may indirectly regulate the activity of Cdc42 by influencing geranyl geranyl acylation of other small G proteins. Importantly, it is crucial to acknowledge that direct evidence of Cdc42 isopentenylation remains lacking, and further investigation is required to determine whether Cdc42 itself is a direct substrate of PGGT1B. In addition, PGGT1B may indirectly participate in the pathogenesis of psoriasis by affecting the proliferation and differentiation of keratinocytes. Our results show that PGGT1B deletion can promote the proliferation and inhibit the differentiation of HaCaT cells, which may be closely related to the pathological characteristics of excessive proliferation and abnormal differentiation of keratinocytes in psoriasis lesions. This discovery further emphasizes the important role of PGGT1B in maintaining skin homeostasis.

The advantage of this study is that we use a knockout mouse model, which can specifically study the role of PGGT1B in myeloid cells and avoid other interference factors that may be caused by systemic knockout. At the same time, the mouse model of psoriasis induced by imiquimod can simulate the pathological process of human psoriasis well and provide a powerful tool for studying the pathogenesis of psoriasis. In addition, we combined RNA-seq analysis to fully understand the effect of PGGT1B deficiency on the gene expression of myeloid cells, which provided clues for further study of its mechanism. However, this study also has some limitations. First of all, this study is mainly based on animal models, and whether the results are applicable to humans needs further verification. Although the mouse model of psoriasis induced by imiquimod can simulate some characteristics of human psoriasis, there are still differences between it and human psoriasis in etiology and pathology. Therefore, future research needs to include human psoriasis skin or PBMC datasets and verify the expression level and function of PGGT1B in patients with psoriasis in clinical samples. Secondly, this study mainly focuses on the role of PGGT1B in myeloid cells while ignoring the possible role of other cell types (such as keratinocytes, T cells, etc.). Psoriasis is a complex disease, involving the interaction of many cell types. Therefore, future research needs to explore the role of PGGT1B in different cell types and its overall role in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. Furthermore, a key limitation is the lack of direct evidence demonstrating Cdc42 as a direct target of PGGT1B. Future studies should focus on elucidating whether Cdc42 undergoes geranylgeranylation by PGGT1B and the functional consequences of this modification. In addition, the specific molecular mechanism of PGGT1B regulating the inflammatory response of myeloid cells has not been explored in this study. Future research can further explore how PGGT1B affects the signal pathway, transcription factor activity, and inflammatory factor secretion of myeloid cells, thus providing a theoretical basis for developing therapeutic strategies for PGGT1B.

Pggt1b em1Cflox /Gpt mice were obtained from GemPharmatech Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China) Pggt1b fl/fl Lyz2 iCre/wt and littermate control Pggt1b fl/fl Lyz2 wt/wt mice were generated by first crossing the Pggt1b em1Cflox /Gpt with B6/JGpt-Lyz2 em1Cin(iCre) /Gpt mice and then intercrossing the resultant Pggt1b fl/fl Lyz2-Cre mice. Littermate controls were used in the experiments. The mouse strains were maintained in specific pathogen-free conditions in the Experimental Animal Center, Institute of Dermatology, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, and Peking Union Medical College, and the animal study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Dermatology Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences (22-DW-007).

This study used a recognized mouse model of IMQ-induced psoriasis []. Briefly, healthy C57/B6 mice aged 6–8 weeks were selected for back shaving 1 day before the experiment. The shaving area was 2.5 cm × 3 cm, and hair removal cream was used to remove hair. IMQ was applied to the shaved back skin of mice at a dose of 62.5 mg per day for 5 consecutive days to establish a psoriasis mouse model, while the control group was given the same dose of VAS ointment. The PASI score and pathological changes were evaluated to confirm the success of the model and to evaluate the severity of psoriasis.

The immortalized human keratinocyte cell line HaCaT was obtained from the China Center for Type Culture Collection (Wuhan, China) and maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM, Welgene, Daegu, Republic of Korea) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and 1% antibiotics (100 U/mL of penicillin, 100 μg/mL of streptomycin). THP-1 cells, the human monocytic cell line, were purchased from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) and maintained in RPMI-1640 (Welgene, Gyeongsan-si, Republic of Korea) supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% antibiotics. THP-1 cells were induced to differentiate into macrophages using 50 ng/mL of phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) in basal medium for 24 h.

THP-1 cells cultured in 24-well plates at a density of 2.5 × 10 5 cell/mL or 0.5 mL/well were induced with PMA (50 ng/mL) for 48 h, and then the medium was replaced with PMA-free culture medium. Logarithmically grown HaCaT cells were added to the PMA-THP-1 cells at a concentration of 5 × 10 4 cells/mL or 0.5 mL/well. The next day, the medium in each well was replaced with a complete culture medium containing R848 (0.5 µg/mL) for 48 h.

THP-1 cells were cultured in 24-well Transwell plates at a density of 5 × 10 5 cell/mL, with 0.25 mL/well, and induced with PMA (50 ng/mL) for 48 h. Then, the medium was replaced with PMA-free complete culture medium, and logarithmically grown HaCaT cells were added to the wells below the Transwell inserts at a concentration of 5 × 10 4 cells/mL, with 0.5 mL/well. The next day, the medium in both the upper and lower chambers of each well was replaced with a complete culture medium containing R848 (0.5 µg/mL) for 48 h.

Bone marrow cells were harvested from 6–8-week-old wild-type and conditional knockout mice by flushing the femurs and tibias with PBS, and the cells were cultured in DMEM (C11995500BT; Gibco, Waltham, MA, USA) with 10% FBS (10270106, Gibco) and 20% L929 supernatants for 7 days. BMDMs were stimulated with 1 μg/mL of resiquimod (R848) (S28463; MedChemExpress, Monmouth Junction, NJ, USA) or DMSO (D2650; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). The experiment comprised the following four groups: wild-type BMDMs stimulated with DMSO (wtcon), wild-type BMDMs stimulated with R848 (wtR848), Pggt1b-deficient BMDMs stimulated with DMSO (ckocon), and Pggt1b-deficient BMDMs stimulated with R848 (ckoR848). After 5 h, the cells were collected for quantitative real-time analysis. BMDMs were collected at 0, 5, 15, 30, 60, and 120 min after stimulation for signaling pathway validation using Western blot analysis.

The details of qRT-PCR are described in the and Methods Section. The gene-specific primers used in this study are listed in and .

The details of immunohistochemistry, HE staining experiment procedure, Luminex detection technology, bioinformatics analysis, and Western blot analysis are described in the and Methods Section.

Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 22.0 software and Prism7.0 software. The data are presented as the mean and SD of at least three independent experiments. A two-sided t -test was used for two groups, and one-way ANOVA was used to compare three groups. Statistical significance was observed at p < 0.05.

In summary, this study explored the role and molecular mechanism of PGGT1B in the pathogenesis of psoriasis by establishing myeloid cell-specific PGGT1B gene knockout mice and imiquimod-induced psoriasis mice models. It was found that the deletion of PGGT1B significantly aggravated the psoriasis-like lesions in mice, which was mainly due to the fact that macrophages with PGGT1B deletion were more likely to migrate to the epidermis during psoriasis, leading to the activation of Cdc42, NF-κB signaling pathway, and NLRP3 inflammatory bodies. These findings indicate that the myeloid cell PGGT1B plays an important protective role in the pathogenesis of psoriasis, and its absence leads to an out-of-control inflammatory response, thus aggravating the condition of psoriasis. This study not only provides a new perspective and thinking for the study of the pathogenesis of psoriasis but also provides a theoretical basis for developing new treatment strategies.

title: A Chronic Psoriasis Model Using Long-Term Imiquimod Application in IL-10-Deficient Mice: Recapitulating Skin Inflammation, Comorbidities, and Gut-Skin Axis Alterations.
abstract: Background Psoriasis is a persistent systemic inflammatory condition mediated by the interleukin (IL)-23/IL-17 signaling pathway. Existing murine models, including imiquimod (IMQ)-applied wild-type (WT) mice, may not reflect chronicity and systemic comorbidities of psoriasis, particularly gut-related manifestations linked to the gut-skin axis. Objective To establish a murine model that more accurately reflects chronic psoriasis, its systemic comorbidities, and associated gut environment alterations. Methods C57BL/6 IL-10-deficient (IL-10 knockout [KO]) and WT mice received topical IMQ or vehicle for 6 weeks. Subsequently, tissue samples from skin, colon, joints, kidneys, liver, abdominal aortas, lymph nodes, and spleens, as well as fecal and blood samples, were collected for histopathologic, immunologic, gut environment analysis. Results IMQ-treated IL-10 KO mice developed prolonged psoriatic inflammatory responses with increased epidermal thickness and higher infiltration of CD45+, myeloperoxidase+, and IL-17+ cells. They also exhibited early-onset, severe colitis with marked weight loss, shortened colon length, and elevated colitis severity scores. While IMQ induced systemic inflammation in multiple organs, IL-10 KO mice did not show more severe joint, liver, or kidney involvement than WT mice. Elevated serum tumor necrosis factor alpha and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 levels, increased heart/body weight ratio, enhanced gut permeability, and distinct gut microbiota profiles were observed in IL-10 KO mice. Conclusion The 6-week IMQ-applied IL-10 KO model may better reflect chronic and severe psoriasis with gut-related comorbidities, offering a valuable platform to investigate the gut-skin axis.

sections.other:
Psoriasis is an immune-mediated, chronic inflammatory skin disease. However, it is not skin deep and it has systemic pathogenic implications. Psoriasis is associated with several comorbidities, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome, which can negatively impact quality of life and shorten life expectancy.

IBD is a well-known psoriasis comorbidity—a chronic relapsing inflammatory disease of the gastrointestinal tract requiring long-term management. Previous studies have identified common genotypes, clinical course, and immunological features shared between psoriasis and IBD. Genetic correlation between psoriasis and IBD, including the interleukin (IL)-23 receptor and IL-12 subunit beta genes, has been identified. Regarding shared immunological features, increased levels of IL-17 are found in both IBD and psoriasis. However, the mechanism underlying association between psoriasis and IBD is largely unclear.

Recently, studies suggest that the gut microbiota is important in food digestion, host immunity, drug metabolism, and the regulation of gut neuroendocrine function. It is well-known that gut microbiome has a critical role in IBD. Additionally, gut microbiota composition and related gut environment changes are increasingly recognized to have a role in various immune-mediated inflammatory skin diseases, including psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, and alopecia areata. Therefore, gut microbiota may be another shared factor between IBD and psoriasis, explaining their association. This is supported by the “gut–skin axis” theory, which suggests that intestinal bacterial composition strongly influences dermatological health.

Topical imiquimod (IMQ) application is a popular model for studying psoriasis-like inflammation in mice. It is widely used because it is inexpensive, straightforward, and resembles human psoriasis through its dependence on the IL-23/IL-17 axis.

Nonetheless, this model lacks fundamental characteristics of long-term psoriatic disease and fails to adequately represent its related comorbid conditions. We previously reported that an IL-10 deficient mouse with short-term (3 to 14 days) IMQ treatment could more accurately reflect chronic psoriasis accompanied by systemic inflammatory responses, compared to conventional models. However, short-term application of IMQ did not induce psoriasis-associated comorbidities in this model. Therefore, we aimed to establish the psoriasis animal model that can reflect chronic psoriasis, its comorbidities, and altered gut environment with the long-term (6-week) application of IMQ in IL-10 deficient mice.
sections.methods:
All experimental procedures involving mice were approved by the Seoul Metropolitan Government-Seoul National University Boramae Medical Center Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees (IACUC No. 2018-0005). The experiments were performed in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals published by the National Institute of Health. This study is reported in accordance with Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments guidelines.

Wild-type (WT) mice were purchased from Oriental Bio (Seongnam, Korea), and IL-10-deficient mice (IL-10 knockout [KO] mice of C57BL/6 background) were obtained from the Center for Animal Resource and Development (Seoul, Korea) and bred in house under specific pathogen-free conditions. All subjects, male mice, were concurrently raised in identical environments to minimize external variable influences.

The experimental procedures are summarized here; detailed methods are provided in and .

WT and IL-10 KO mice, aged 7–8 weeks, were utilized for the experimental procedures. These mice were allocated into 2 groups: one receiving long-term treatment with IMQ (n=5–6) and the other serving as the control group receiving vehicle treatment (vaseline [VAS]) (n=3–5). For the IMQ treatment group, a dose of 62.5 mg of 5% IMQ cream (Aldara ® ; 3M Pharmaceuticals, St. Paul, MN, USA) was administered topically to the depilated dorsal surface and ears of the mice daily for 5 consecutive days, followed by a 2-day interval for one week (induction period), and subsequently thrice weekly for 5 weeks (maintenance period). Conversely, the control group received an application of petroleum jelly (Vaseline ® ; Unilever, Rotterdam, Netherlands). On day 39, euthanasia was performed for further analysis.

The assessment of skin inflammation on the dorsal surfaces of the mice was performed using a modified PASI scoring system described previously.

Skin samples were used for histological examination according to the protocol described previously.

The colon, heart, abdominal aorta, joints, kidney and liver specimens were obtained on day 39, samples were fixed in 10% buffered formalin, paraffinized and stained with hematoxylin and eosin. The severity of inflammation in organs was assessed according to previously established methods.

We extracted LPMCs from each group of mice to assess the mucosal cytokine response. Colonic LPMCs were isolated as previously described.

RT-qPCR was conducted in accordance with methods previously established.

Blood samples were taken on day 39 to measure serum levels of cytokines (IL-17A, and tumor necrosis factor alpha [TNF-α]) and markers of activated endothelium (plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), pro-matrix metallopeptidase 9 (proMMP-9), soluble E-selectin (sE-selectin), soluble P-selectin (sP-selectin), and soluble intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (sICAM-1).

16S rRNA gene sequencing was performed by Macrogen (Seoul, Korea). The V3–V4 variable regions of the bacteria 16S rRNA gene were used for the analysis and also Metagenome Amplicon sequencing was application. Fecal specimens were obtained at the beginning of the experiment and at the time of sacrifice, subsequently stored in −80 deep freezer. Differential abundance testing was performed using Random Forest, Linear Discriminant Analysis Effect Size (LEfSe), and Analysis of Composition of Microbiomes with Bias Correction (ANCOM-BC).

To assess gut permeability, FITC-dextran was administered orally after overnight fasting. Serum FITC levels were measured 1 hour later, as described in the .

All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 20 (IBM Co., Chicago, IL, USA). Data were presented as the mean and standard error of the mean. The Mann-Whitney U test was performed to identify the differences between groups, and permutational multivariate analysis of variance was used to analyze the microbiome. All multiple comparisons were adjusted using Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction.
sections.results:
From day 8, IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice exhibited more severe psoriatic inflammation (, and ). Erythema and desquamation persisted throughout the study duration in the IL-10 KO cohort alone. IMQ-treated IL-10 KO mice demonstrated higher PASI scores compared to those of WT mice from day 8 onwards (). The cumulative score difference between the 2 groups reached statistical significance by day 39 ( p =0.018). In comparison to short-term (3 or 14 days) IMQ application in IL-10 KO mice, long-term IMQ application resulted in mild erythema, but increased epidermal thickness and more prominent scale, giving the appearance of a chronic psoriasiform lesion.

IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice exhibited more pronounced acanthosis, hypogranulosis, and parakeratosis, than those observed in WT mice (). Image analysis revealed that IMQ-treated IL-10 KO demonstrated significantly increased epidermal thickness compared to WT mice ( p =0.006; ). IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice also showed markedly elevated CD45+ ( p =0.006; , ) and MPO+ cell counts ( p =0.006; , ) than those of WT mice. Additionally, IL-17+ cell counts were significantly greater in IL-10 KO mice relative to WT mice ( p = 0.025; , ).

During the induction period, the IMQ-treated cohort exhibited weight loss beginning on day 3 relative to control subjects. During the maintenance period, despite IMQ treatment, WT mice continued to gain weight and there was no difference in body weight between WT and control group mice. On day 39, IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice demonstrated significantly greater body weight reduction than that of IMQ-applied WT mice ( p =0.012; ). Additionally, colon length in the IL-10 KO-IMQ group was significantly shorter than that in the WT-IMQ group (). Histologically, IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice showed more severe colonic inflammation than that in WT mice (, ). The colons of IL-10 KO-IMQ mice exhibited diffuse transmural inflammation, ulceration and submucosal inflammation. However, there was no notable colonic inflammation in IMQ-applied WT mice. The IL-10 KO-VAS group exhibited mild multifocal inflammation and epithelial hyperplasia. Similarly, histological scores were higher in IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice than WT mice. These results suggest IMQ application in IL-10 KO mice accelerated colitis development and persistence. The IL-10 KO-IMQ group also showed substantially elevated CD45+ cell populations compared to WT-IMQ mice ( p =0.014; , ).

In WT mice, IMQ treatment did not affect heart weight (). However, IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice showed increased heart weight and heart weight/body weight ratio (a cardiac hypertrophy index) compared to WT mice. However, histopathological assessment revealed no appreciable inflammatory cell infiltration in any group (). This suggests IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice had relatively greater cardiovascular burden.

Of the 5 endothelial cell dysfunction markers investigated (PAI-1, proMMP-9, sE-selectin, sP-selectin, and sICAM-1), IMQ treatment significantly increased PAI-1 levels in IL-10 KO mice ( p =0.024; ). However, the levels of proMMP-9, sE-selectin, and sP-selectin were not specifically induced by IMQ treatment. Also, histopathological assessment and image analysis of CD45+ cell counts with the abdominal aortas revealed no significant inflammatory cell infiltration ().

With regard to the synovitis score, IMQ application induced slight inflammatory changes in joints. However, there were no significant differences between IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice and those of WT mice ( p =0.638; ).

Similarly, although long-term IMQ application induced slight kidney inflammation, there were no significant differences between IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice and those of WT mice ( p =0.247). Most of inflammatory cells were located in the tubulointerstitial areas, but scarce in glomeruli ().

Hepatic lobular activity demonstrated elevation in IL-10 KO mice relative to WT mice, though these changes did not achieve statistical significance ( p =0.247). Furthermore, portoperiportal activity scores showed no meaningful differences between the 2 groups ().

We measured the expression levels of genes encoding the inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-17α, interferon gamma, and IL-1β in LPMCs, inguinal lymph nodes, and the spleen using RT-PCR. Gene expression of Il17a tended to be higher in LPMCs from IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice than WT mice, though not significantly (). Tnfa expression also showed a downward trend in IL-10 KO mice after IMQ treatment, but was not statistically significant. In inguinal lymph nodes, Il17a expression was elevated in IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice compared to WT mice, but did not reach significance (). Tnfa expression levels also tended to be elevated in the IL-10 KO-IMQ group; however, the difference was not significant. In the spleen, the gene expression levels of Tnfa and Il1b were significantly increased in IMQ-applied IL-10 KO mice compared with those in WT mice ().

To assess the extent of systemic inflammation in the mouse models, we measured serum IL-17 and TNF-α levels using ELISA. Serum TNF-α levels were significantly higher in IMQ-treated KO mice than in WT mice ( p =0.03; ). IL-17α levels also tended to be elevated in the IL-10 KO-IMQ group; however, the difference was not significant.

To assess gut microbiome dysregulation in WT and IL-10 KO mice, stool samples were analyzed for alpha and beta diversity. Initial analysis revealed marked baseline beta-diversity differences between WT and IL-10 KO mice. Post-IMQ treatment analysis indicated significant microbiome alterations in WT mice, while IL-10 KO mice remained largely unchanged (, unweighted and weighted plots; p =0.000). Notably, the weighted principal coordinates analysis plot demonstrated that post-treatment, the microbial strain abundance in the WT group closely resembled that of the IL-10 KO group following IMQ treatment. Alpha-diversity is shown in . WT mice exhibited greater baseline diversity compared to IL-10 KO mice. Following IMQ treatment, a significant reduction in diversity was observed in WT mice ( p <0.01), with only a marginal decline in IL-10 KO mice.

Taxonomy plots showed baseline microbiome differences between WT and IL-10 KO mice. Prior to IMQ treatment, the IL-10 KO group showed a decrease in Bacteroidaceae ;_ Phocaeicola and Lactobacilaceae ; _Ligilactobacillus , and an increase in Muribaculaceae ;_ Duncaniella and Muribaculum compared to the WT group. Following IMQ treatment, the WT group exhibited an increase in Muribaculaceae ; _Sangeribacter ; Heminiphilus , and a decrease in Bacteroidaceae ;_ Phocaeicola and Lactobacilaceae ; _Ligilactobacillus . Conversely, the IL-10 KO group showed an increase in Bifidobacteriaceae ; _Bifidobacterium and Bacteroidaceae ; _Phocaeicola , and a decrease in Muribaculaceae ; _Duncaniella and Bacteroidaceae ; _Bacteroides following IMQ treatment.

Following IMQ treatment, both WT and IL-10 KO groups showed similar microbiome compositions, as confirmed by taxonomy plot analysis. While baseline microbiomes significantly diverged between IL-10 KO and WT mice, this disparity was reduced after IMQ treatment due to pronounced IMQ-induced alterations in the microbiome of WT mice.

Differential abundance analysis (Random Forest, LEfSe, and ANCOM-BC) revealed consistent microbial shifts across groups (). Inflammatory conditions (IL-10 deficiency and IMQ treatment) enriched genera including Duncaniella , Muribaculum , Faecalibaculum , and Paramuribaculum , while beneficial commensals ( Ruminococcus , Akkermansia , Roseburia ) were more abundant in WT mice. These differential abundance patterns suggest a distinct microbial signature shaped by the combined effects of IL-10 deficiency and IMQ-induced inflammation on gut microbiota composition.

In this study, we evaluated gut permeability at baseline in both WT and IL-10 KO groups using FITC-dextran (4 kDa). The fluorescence levels were markedly higher in the IL-10 KO group compared to WT, indicating that gut permeability is elevated in the absence of IL-10 ( p =0.047; ).
sections.discussion:
Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory systemic disease that has been linked to arthritis, IBD, and cardiovascular diseases. However, the lack of chronicity and comorbidities in the IMQ-applied WT mice model represents a major limitation for studies on psoriasis comorbidities. Recent research increasingly demonstrated that psoriasis exhibits significant associations with intestinal microbiota through the so-called “gut–skin axis”, which could be common factors between psoriasis and its comorbidities. At present, an animal model of psoriasis reflecting chronic skin lesion as well as its comorbidities has not yet been established.

In the present study, long-term 6-week IMQ treatment in IL-10 KO mice showed persistent psoriatic skin inflammation with leukocytes, MPO+ neutrophils, and IL-17+ cells than WT mice and early onset of more severe colitis compared to vehicle-applied IL-10 KO mice. In addition, this model had more severe cardiovascular burden and systemic inflammatory response than those observed in WT mice. Moreover, it demonstrated moderate inflammation of hindfoot joint, kidney and liver, although the difference was not statistically different between groups. These findings support the utility of this model for investigating the pathophysiology of psoriasis and its comorbidities, thereby providing valuable insights for therapeutic strategies.

Psoriasis and IBD share immunological features and genetic susceptibility, with IBD being a well-known comorbidity in psoriasis patients. Notably, the prevalence of IBD among psoriasis patients is approximately 4 times higher than in the general population. Notably, IL-10 deficiency is a shared pathogenic mechanism in psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, and IBD, where reduced levels fail to suppress proinflammatory Th1/Th17 cytokines and antigen-presenting cell activation. In psoriatic tissues and IBD-affected intestinal mucosa, impaired IL-10 production and responsiveness compromise anti-inflammatory checkpoints, enabling uncontrolled immune activation and chronic inflammation. However, no mouse model fully reflects this association. In this study, IL-10 KO mice treated with IMQ developed consistent and severe colitis, compared to vehicle-treated IL-10 KO mice or IMQ-treated WT mice. While IL-10 KO mice develop spontaneous colitis, IMQ application further amplified inflammation, suggesting that IMQ acts as an external trigger that synergizes with IL-10 deficiency to promote inflammatory state. Thus, this model may serve as a representative model of psoriasis with concurrent IBD.

IL-17 expression is elevated in the gut mucosa and serum of IBD patients compared to healthy controls, suggesting its role in IBD pathogenesis. Macrophage-specific IL-10Rα deficiency has been shown to enhance IL-1β production-driven Th17 responses and colitis severity. In our study, Il17 mRNA levels in LPMCs of IMQ-treated IL-10 KO mice were elevated, though not significantly. Paradoxically, TNF-α expression was significantly lower in IL-10 KO mice than in WT mice, suggesting a potentially greater role for IL-17 in IMQ-induced colitis and possible post-translational regulation of TNF-α, warranting further investigation.

Psoriasis is associated with cardiovascular diseases such as myocardial infarction and stroke, potentially through systemic inflammation involving Th1/Th17 activation and cytokines like TNF-α and IL-17, as well as endothelial cell activation with upregulation of adhesion molecules. In this study, IMQ-treated IL-10 KO mice showed cardiac hypertrophy and significantly elevated levels of PAI-1, an endothelial marker. PAI-1, a serine protease inhibitor, is known to be elevated in psoriasis and correlate with increased angiogenesis. Similarly, increased plasma PAI-1 levels have been observed in patients with psoriasis, which decreases during therapy. Its levels also rise in patients with abdominal obesity, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular disease—common comorbidities of psoriasis. However, no histological signs of vasculitis or vascular occlusion were observed in the colon, heart, or abdominal aorta, the elevated PAI-1 levels may merely reflect an IMQ-induced hyperinflammatory state.

Long-term IMQ application also induced inflammation in the liver, kidneys, and joints in the present study. Yokogawa et al. reported that WT mice developed hepatitis, glomerulonephritis, carditis, and photosensitivity following 4 weeks of IMQ application suggesting its use as a model for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, in our study, characteristic lupus nephritis—glomerulonephritis with or without tubulointerstitial nephritis, was not prominent following prolonged IMQ exposure. Instead, IMQ-treated IL-10 KO mice developed persistent psoriasiform skin lesions and colitis, better reflecting chronic psoriasis and its comorbidities. While SLE and psoriasis have traditionally been viewed as distinct, they may coexist. Given the complexity of SLE and the emerging role of the IL-23/Th17 axis in SLE, further studies are needed to determine whether the systemic inflammatory state of the current model better represents psoriasis, SLE, or overlapping features of both.

The connection between immune regulation and gut microbiota has opened new avenues for understanding chronic multifactorial diseases, from gastrointestinal inflammatory and metabolic conditions to neurological, cardiovascular, cutaneous, and respiratory illnesses. Recently, research involving humans and animal models has highlighted the role of the “gut–skin axis” in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. For example, mice with a gut microbiome depleted by broad-spectrum antibiotics exhibit less severe psoriasiform lesions and show diminished local and systemic Th17 activation following IMQ treatment. Similarly, recovery from gut dysbiosis may alleviate the erythema of psoriatic lesions in mice. Additionally, increased gut permeability during active psoriatic episodes may facilitate bacterial DNA translocation into systemic circulation, initiating widespread inflammatory responses.

In our investigation into the gut microbiomes, we observed marked differences between IL-10 KO and WT mice even before IMQ administration. This aligns with previous reports showing that IL-10 KO mice fail to develop the diverse and rich microbial communities seen in WT mice. Specifically, IL-10 KO mice showed reduced levels of Bacteroidaceae ; _Phocaeicola and Lactobacilaceae ; _Ligilactobacillus , known for their anti-inflammatory properties. The observed gut microbial shifts were primarily driven by IL-10 deficiency rather than IMQ treatment, suggesting that while the model demonstrates gut dysbiosis, it does not fully establish a causal gut–skin axis mechanism. Conversely, the previous literatures demonstrated that IMQ-induced psoriatic inflammation primed the gut for more severe colitis with dextran sulfate sodium challenge by altering immune cells, metabolites, and gut microbiome. Future studies using fecal microbiota transplantation or antibiotic modulation may help clarify this relationship.

In this study, IL-10 KO mice demonstrated increased gut permeability, facilitating pathogen translocation and potentially triggering immune activation and chronic inflammation. This disrupted state may alter gut microbiome diversity, promoting pathogenic bacteria while reducing beneficial microbes. The elevated baseline permeability in IL-10 KO mice likely drives distinct microbiome changes linked to IL-10 deficiency. These results support the hypothesis that a leaky gut may promote microbial dysbiosis, which can exacerbate inflammation and further damage the gut barrier. Overall, our results highlight the interplay between IL-10 deficiency, gut barrier integrity, and microbiome composition, suggesting a valuable model to study gut homeostasis, psoriasis, and related comorbidities, particularly IBD.

Our model has limitations, as psoriatic arthritis and vascular lesions were not consistently induced, limiting studies of these specific comorbidities. However, long-term IMQ application in IL-10 KO mice induced persistent psoriasis-like dermatitis, systemic inflammation, and earlier, more severe colitis compared to spontaneous colitis in untreated IL-10 KO mice. Overall, our findings provide experimental evidence that long-term IMQ-treated IL-10 deficient mice represent a useful model for severe, persistent psoriasis with associated comorbidities and gut changes. Multidisciplinary approaches will further advance understanding of systemic inflammation and multi-organ involvement in psoriasis. IL-10 deficiency and related gut alterations may underlie severe psoriasis and its systemic comorbidities, including IBD.

title: G-CSF Mediates Increased Renal Neutrophils and Kidney Damage in a Psoriasis Mouse Model.
abstract: Background Psoriasis is an autoimmune skin disease associated with increased incidence and severity of chronic kidney disease and hypertension. The mechanisms linking psoriasis skin inflammation with these comorbidities remain unclear. Methods We used flow cytometry, radiotelemetric blood pressure measurements, and histological and ELISA-based assessments of renal damage in mice with experimental psoriasis induced by keratinocyte-specific Tie2 overexpressing (KC-Tie2) and their littermate controls. Results Compared with littermate controls, KC-Tie2 mice with chronic skin inflammation developed albuminuria, histological evidence of glomerulosclerosis, and elevated blood pressure. KC-Tie2 mice had a selective and marked increase in circulating and renal neutrophils, along with increased neutrophil extracellular trap formation in the kidneys by flow cytometry. KC-Tie2 mice also exhibited increased bone marrow granulopoiesis along with increases in cutaneous and systemic G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor), the primary mediator of granulopoiesis. Finally, neutralization of G-CSF decreased renal neutrophils and kidney damage in KC-Tie2 mice. Conclusions Our findings demonstrate G-CSF-dependent increases in renal neutrophil accumulation and renal damage in a mouse model of psoriasis. Results suggest a novel link between chronic psoriasiform skin inflammation and renal damage via G-CSF-mediated granulopoiesis, providing new insight into interorgan communication in psoriasis and a potential new therapeutic target for the treatment of psoriasis-related renal dysfunction.

sections.other:
NOVELTY AND RELEVANCE What Is New? We provide novel evidence that chronic psoriasiform skin inflammation promotes kidney injury by increasing systemic and renal neutrophilia through G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) dependent granulopoiesis. What Is Relevant? Psoriasis is associated with enhanced kidney dysfunction, but mechanisms linking skin inflammation and kidney disease are poorly understood. Our findings suggest G-CSF as a mediator of interorgan cross-talk in psoriasis, leading to kidney injury. Clinical/Pathophysiological Implications? We validated increases in G-CSF in keratinocytes and endothelial cells in lesional skin from psoriasis patients, adding translational relevance. Results suggest that G-CSF or enhanced granulopoiesis may be novel therapeutic targets for mitigating kidney disease in psoriasis.

Multiple autoimmune diseases increase cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, primarily through increased incidence and severity of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease affecting 2% to 5% of the global population, with rising incidence. , Chronic plaque psoriasis, the most common form, causes symmetrically distributed pruritic, erythematous, and scaly plaques with well-demarcated borders, typically distributed across the skin. Although these cutaneous psoriatic lesions have significant negative physical and psychosocial impacts, increased mortality in psoriasis occurs primarily through extracutaneous manifestations, such as enhanced atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. – Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease is driven by key risk factors including hypertension and kidney disease. , Indeed, individuals with psoriasis have a 2-fold increase in the incidence of hypertension and require more medications to achieve blood pressure (BP) control compared with patients with hypertension without psoriasis. – Likewise, chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease are ≈2- to 3-fold more common in individuals with psoriasis. ,, These conditions are interrelated, as kidney disease contributes to increases in BP, and increased BP worsens kidney disease, resulting in a vicious self-sustaining cycle. Together, epidemiological evidence demonstrates that psoriasis is strongly associated with increased incidence and severity of both hypertension and kidney disease; however, the mechanisms linking psoriasis to these conditions are not defined.

Chronic plaque psoriasis, the most common form of psoriasis, is marked by cutaneous infiltration of innate and adaptive immune cells with increased production of inflammatory cytokines, including IL (interleukin)-17A, IL-23, TNFα (tumor necrosis factor α), and IL-1β. IL-17A and IL-23 (which induce T-cell IL-17A production) are important mediators of psoriasis, as inhibition of these cytokines results in near-complete resolution of skin lesions. , Despite the efficacy of these cytokine inhibitors on skin disease, mechanisms mediating extracutaneous manifestations of psoriasis, including increased risk of kidney disease and hypertension, remain unclear. In a recent meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, cardiovascular event rates were not significantly different in those treated with IL-17, IL-23, or TNFα inhibitors despite reductions in psoriasis severity. In addition, in a smaller study of 34 patients with psoriasis and chronic kidney disease, treatment with these cytokine inhibitors did not significantly alter glomerular filtration rate at 3 years. Larger studies of existing therapies are still needed, but these findings suggest that alternate mechanisms may mediate the extracutaneous manifestations of psoriasis.

We sought to identify the immunologic mechanisms underlying kidney disease and BP elevations in psoriasis. Using a well-established mouse model of psoriasis, we examined circulating and renal immune cell populations and observed selective increases in neutrophils and neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation in the kidneys of psoriasis mice. These changes were associated with increased levels of cutaneous and circulating G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor). Critically, we demonstrate that blocking G-CSF decreases renal neutrophils and improves the renal damage associated with chronic psoriasiform skin inflammation. These findings demonstrate a novel role for G-CSF as a mediator of interorgan communication linking psoriasis skin inflammation with kidney damage.

This study identifies a novel link between psoriasiform skin inflammation and renal damage, characterized by selective increases in circulating and renal neutrophils in a mouse model of psoriasis. These changes occur alongside elevated G-CSF production and enhanced granulopoiesis in the bone marrow. Our findings establish a role for G-CSF-dependent granulopoiesis in promoting renal neutrophil accumulation and renal damage, highlighting a new axis of interorgan communication in psoriasis. These results also position G-CSF and enhanced granulopoiesis as potential therapeutic targets for psoriasis-associated renal dysfunction.
