sections.methods:
Recombinant poly (I:C), CpG, imiquimod, CL307, and loxoribine were purchased from Invivogen. Pentoxifylline was purchased from Cayman Chemical. Antibodies against the following proteins were used in this study: c-Rel (D4Y6M and D38BS, Cell Signalling Technology), c-Rel (G7 and B6, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), p65 (F6 and C20, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), p65 (L8F6, Cell Signalling Technology), p50 (D4P4D, Cell Signalling Technology), Sp1 (E3, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), hnRNPA1 (9H10, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), tubulin (H300, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), actin (C4, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), TLR7 (3269, ProSci), PLCy1 (1249, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), lamin A/C (H-110, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), HDAC2 (680104, BioLegend), vinculin (938402, BioLegend), RelB (C19, Santa Cruz Biotechnology), p52 (4882, Cell Signalling Technology). Further details, including catalogue numbers and RRIDs can be found in the supplementary reagent list document. Antibodies used were validated with Western blot analysis using knockout cell lines. Cell suspensions were stained with antibodies against one or more of the following proteins for flow cytometric analysis: CD11c (N418, BioLegend), IL-6 (MP5-20F3, BioLegend), IL-1β (17-7114-80, Thermo Fisher Scientific), CD80 (16-10A1, BioLegend), CD86 (Gl-1, BioLegend), CD4 (GK1.5, BioLegend), IL17A (TC11-18H10.1, BioLegend), Zombie NIR Fixable Viability Kit (BioLegend). Lipofectamine 3000 was purchased from Thermo Fisher and used according to manufacturer’s protocol.

DC2.4 cells (RRID:CVCL_J409) were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium containing 10% SCS, 1% HEPES, 1% nonessential amino acids, 1% sodium pyruvate, 100 U/mL penicillin/streptomycin, 1% L-glutamine. HaCaT cells (RRID:CVCL_0038) were grown in RPMI 1640 medium containing 10% FBS, 100 U/mL penicillin/streptomycin, and 1% L-glutamine. J558L cells (RRID:CVCL_3949) were grown in DMEM medium containing 10% FBS, 100 U/mL penicillin/streptomycin, 1% L-glutamine for generation of J558L cultured supernatants. Primary bone marrow derived dendritic cells were cultured with 10 mL of RPMI 1640 medium containing 10% FBS, 1% HEPES, 1% nonessential amino acids, 1% sodium pyruvate, 100 U/mL penicillin/streptomycin, 1% L-glutamine, 0.05 mM β-mercaptoethanol with the addition of 1:15 J558L supernatant. All cells were incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 . Cells were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination and only mycoplasma negative cells were used in all the experiments.

The CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown of c-Rel, p65, and p50 in DC2.4 cells and HaCaT cells was performed as previously described. , Wild-type DC2.4 cells or HaCaT cells were incubated with lentiviral supernatants expressing vector control or gene specific guide RNA with 8 μg/mL polybrene transfection reagent for 24 h. Cells were selected with 350 μg/mL of hygromycin or 1 μg/mL of puromycin and single cell clone populations were generated, expanded, and tested by Western blotting for expression of the protein of interest. Three or more individual clones of control vector or specific guide RNA infected cells with undetectable amounts of specified protein were pooled and used as controls (designated as WT) or stable knockout (c-Rel KO, p65 KO and p50 KO) cell lines. Guide RNA for c-Rel was used as described previously. Other guide RNAs used were as follows: p65 - For: CACCGAGCGCCCCTCGCATTTATAG, Rev: AAACCTATAAATGCGAGGGGCGCTC; p50 – For: CACCGACGATGATCCCTACGGAACT, Rev: AAACAGTTCCGTAGGGATCATCGTC.

All mice were handled in accordance with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) guidelines under protocol (#2013-0134) approved by the Case Western Reserve University’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. All the experiments were performed in compliance with animal use guidelines (including the ARRIVE guidelines) and the above ethical approval.

The c-Rel knockout mouse line in the C57BL6/J background were kindly provided by H.C. Liou (Weill Medical College of Cornell University, New York). The C57BL6/J mice were purchased from Jackson Laboratories and maintained in-house. c-Rel KO mice will be available at Jackson Laboratory (Stock No. 039712). Animals were housed in specific-pathogen-free conditions in the animal facility room. Mice had free access to autoclaved food and water. Bedding and nesting materials were provided as standard enrichments to reduce animal distress, and no unexpected adverse events occurred throughout this study. At designated end points, mice were humanely sacrificed in accordance with institutional guidelines using controlled CO 2 asphyxiation followed by cervical dislocation.

For the imiquimod-induced psoriasis, the dorsal skin of mice was shaved, and 62.5 mg of Aldara cream (5% IMQ, 3M Pharmaceuticals) was applied daily on the shaved skin for 5 consecutive days. Mice were weighed daily, photographed, and sacrificed on day 6. Disease severity was assessed daily based on a scoring system based on a modified clinical Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) as previously described. Briefly, erythema and scaling were scored in a blinded manner by a dermatologist on a scale from 0 to 4: 0, none; 1, slight; 2, moderate; 3, marked; 4, very marked.

For DC2.4 cells and BMDCs, total RNA was isolated from cells using EZ10 DNAaway RNA miniprep kit (BioBasic). For skin samples, RNA was purified using TRIzol (Invitrogen). RNA yields were quantified by NanoDrop spectrophotometer, and 1 μg of total RNA was used for cDNA synthesis using High Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems). Quantitative real-time PCR was performed using PowerUP SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) following manufacturer’s protocol. Primers used to amplify IFNβ were: For: AGATGTCCTCAACTGCTCTC, Rev: AGATTCACTACCAGTCCCAG. Other primer sequences used were previously described. Samples were normalised to the housekeeping gene L32. Gene expression was quantified using the ΔΔCt method.

HaCaT cells (1 × 10 5 /well) were seeded in a 96 well plate 24 h before stimulation. Cell proliferation was measured by Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK8) (APEx BIO) following manufacturer’s protocol.

For haematoxylin and eosin staining, skin samples were processed at the CWRU Skin Diseases Research Center (SDRC) core facility for dermatopathology. Tissue samples were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and embedded in paraffin. Deparaffinised 5-μm sections were stained with H&E. Epidermal thickening was assessed by measurements of four representative images from each slide, for each mouse. For immunohistochemistry, 7 μm cryosections were brought to room temperature and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 30 min. Endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked in 0.3% peroxide for 10 min. Sections were blocked and permeabilised in 5% FBS in PBS with 0.5% saponin. Sections were incubated with anti-c-Rel antibody (B6, 1:100, Santa Cruz Biotechnology) overnight at 4 °C. Slides were counterstained with haematoxylin and visualised using an Olympus IX73 microscope.

Cells were lysed in hypotonic cytoplasmic lysis buffer (10 mM HEPES pH 7.6, 10 mM KCl, 0.1 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM EGTA, 1X protease inhibitor cocktail in dH 2 O) for 15 min on ice. A final concentration of 0.625% NP40 was added to each sample and vortexed to disrupt cellular membranes. Lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 g for 30 s and supernatants were collected as cytoplasmic lysates. Remaining nuclear pellets were washed with hypotonic cytoplasmic lysis buffer 1X. Nuclear pellets were then lysed with hypertonic nuclear lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES pH 7.6, 400 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM EGTA, 1X protease inhibitor cocktail in dH 2 O) for 30 min on ice. Lysates were cleared at 12,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C and supernatants were collected following centrifugation. Protein levels were normalised using BCA assay (ThermoFisher Scientific). For immunoprecipitation, cytoplasmic lysates were supplemented with NaCl, and nuclear lysates were diluted with salt free lysis buffer to obtain a final salt concentration of 150 mM in each sample. Lysates were rotated at 4 °C with protein G or protein A beads (Invitrogen) and antibodies against p65, c-Rel or p50 for 3 h. To assess p50 homodimer, samples were subjected to formaldehyde crosslinking with slight modifications. Following immunoprecipitation, beads were incubated with 4% formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature. The crosslinking reaction was quenched with the addition of 750 mM Tris (pH 7.5) for 5 min at room temperature. Beads were washed with lysis buffer and heated at 85 °C for 5 min with nonreducing 1X Laemmli sample buffer. For Western blot analysis, lysates were resolved through 9% SDS–PAGE gels. Proteins from the gel were transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes, probed using the indicated antibodies, and visualised by enhanced chemiluminescence assay.

Oligonucleotide pulldown assay using biotinylated promoter sequences were performed as previously described. Briefly, nuclear lysates were normalised to 100 μg of total protein and NaCl concentration in the buffer was adjusted to 150 mM. Lysates were incubated with 1 μg of biotinylated oligonucleotides and 6 μg of sheared salmon sperm DNA for 1 h at 4 °C with constant rotation. After 1 h, neutravidin agarose beads (Thermo Scientific) were added and samples were incubated for an additional 2 h. To assess NF-κB complexes bound to the oligonucleotide, beads were incubated with 4% formaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature, and quenched with 750 mM Tris (pH 7.5). Beads were washed with lysis buffer and heated at 85 °C for 5 min with nonreducing 1X Laemmli sample buffer. Samples were analysed by Western blotting. Oligonucleotides containing NF-κB binding sequences were as follows: IL-1β oligonucleotide sequences: forward: CTAACCCAGGAAAACCCAATATT, reverse: AAATATTGGGTTTTCCTGGGTTAG; IL-6 oligonucleotide sequences: forward: CAAATGTGGGATTTTCCCATGAGT, reverse: ACTCATGGGAAAATCCCACATTTG.

Mouse bone marrow cells were isolated by flushing femurs and tibias with sterile PBS, and strained through a 40 μM filter. All cell suspensions were resuspended in red blood cell lysis buffer (155 mM NH 4 Cl, 12 mM NaCHO 3 , 0.1 mM EDTA in H 2 O) for 5 min. Cells were then plated at 2 × 10 6 /10 cm plate in BMDC RPMI media with added 1:15 J558L conditioned media for GM-CSF supplementation for DC differentiation. Loosely adherent cells were harvested on day 6 and DC differentiation was confirmed by CD11c + flow cytometry. BMDCs (1 × 10 6 /mL) were stimulated with 6 μg/mL of IMQ for 20 h, collected with PBS with 10 mM EDTA, and washed with PBS. Total naïve CD4 + T cells were collected from freshly harvested spleens of WT C57BL6/J mice by magnetic sorting with MojoSort CD4 T cell Isolation Kit (480033, BioLegend). Purified T cells were cocultured with BMDCs at a 4:1 ratio in a 96 well plate. For Th17 polarisation conditions, cultures were supplemented with plate bound anti-CD3 (5 μg/mL; 145-2C11, BioLegend) and soluble anti-CD28 (5 μg/mL; 37.51, BioLegend), IL-6 (20 ng/mL; BioLegend), IL-1β (10 ng/mL; BioLegend), TGFβ (2 ng/mL; BioLegend) and the following neutralising antibodies: anti-IL-4 (10 μg/mL; 11B11, BioLegend), anti-IFNγ (10 μg/mL; AN-18, BioLegend), anti-IL2 (10 μg/mL; JES6-1A12, BioLegend). For Th0 polarising conditions, cultures were supplemented with plate bound anti-CD3 (2 μg/mL; 145-2C11, BioLegend) and soluble anti-CD28 (1 μg/mL; 37.51, BioLegend). After 3 days, cocultures were stimulated with PMA, ionomycin, and brefeldin A for 5 h. Cells were harvested and stained with surface antibodies and Zombie NIR Viability Kit for 20 min at 4 °C. For intracellular staining, cells were fixed and permeabilised according to manufacturer’s recommendation (True-Nuclear Transcription Factor Buffer Set, BioLegend) and stained with intracellular antibodies overnight at 4 °C. Samples were analysed with CytoFLEX flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter) and FlowJo software (TreeStar).

Data are presented as means with 95% CI. Shapiro–Wilk test and generated Q–Q plots confirmed normality of all variable data (p > 0.05). Homogeneity of variance was confirmed by examining the homoscedasticity of residual plots. Differences between groups were compared by two-way ANOVA, followed by pairwise comparisons via Tukey’s multiple comparisons when all the pairwise comparisons were of interest or Sidak’s multiple comparison when specific pairwise comparisons were of interest. The factors used for two-way ANOVA were mouse genotype (WT or c-Rel KO) and treatment (ctrl or IMQ). Mixed effects model was used to assess the difference in temporal patterns between groups considering the correlation of observations within experimental units. Time, treatment and genotype correspond to fixed effects while mice correspond to the random effects in this model. We assessed the assumption of sphericity with Geisser-Greenhouse epsilon and applied the corresponding correction if the assumption of sphericity was violated. We assessed the assumption of linearity by examining plots of residuals against predicted values. Two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test was performed for unmatched groups. Study design typified a clustered comparison with four clusters per group and four randomly selected observations per cluster. Power analysis for in vivo studies was performed for epidermal acanthosis measurements, which estimated that four animals per group were sufficient to obtain a power of 0.8 with a significance p < 0.05.

The funders had no role in planning the study, in the experimental, data collection, analysis, and interpretation, in the writing of the manuscript, and in the decision to submit the manuscript for publication.
sections.results:
To assess whether NF-κB c-Rel may be functionally relevant in psoriasis, we analysed the expression of NF-κB c-Rel in psoriatic skin biopsies from seven transcriptome datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (). Compared to healthy and nonlesional skin biopsies, we found a marked increase of c-Rel expression in psoriatic lesional skin in all datasets analysed (a–c and )., , , , Interestingly, c-Rel expression was downregulated following treatment with brodalumab ( GSE117468 ), ustekinumab ( GSE117468 ) and etanercept ( GSE11903 ) (b and c). Of note, the downregulation of c-Rel following etanercept treatment was only seen in patients who successfully responded to the biologic and achieved histological disease resolution, while c-Rel levels remained elevated in non-responders (c). Given the amount of structural and functional overlap that can exist between NF-κB subunits, we also checked the expression of NF-κB p65 in these samples. In contrast to c-Rel, there are no substantial changes in the levels of p65 among non-lesional, lesional, and etanercept treated skin biopsies in both non-responder and responder patients (c). Consistent with our transcriptomics analysis, c-Rel levels were increased in the dorsal skin of IMQ-induced psoriasis mouse model, specifically in the dermis (d and ). Taken together, data from both human and mouse models indicate that c-Rel expression is increased in psoriatic lesional skin.

To further confirm that c-Rel is relevant to psoriasis, we utilised an IMQ-induced psoriasis-like mouse model using WT and c-Rel KO (C57BL/6J) mice. WT and c-Rel KO mice were shaved 1 day prior to application of 62.5 mg IMQ cream daily to the dorsal skin for five days (a). Treatment with IMQ induced a psoriasiform skin pathology, which was reduced in c-Rel KO C57BL/6J mice (b). Erythema and scaling were scored daily, with all mice starting with a score of 0. c-Rel KO mice had a lower erythema and scaling score starting at Day 4 as measured by raw score (c) and standard mean difference (). To observe histological changes, dorsal skin biopsies were taken on Day 6 and epidermal thickness was measured. c-Rel KO mice exhibited substantially reduced IMQ-induced acanthosis of their dorsal skin compared to WT mice. However, compared to untreated controls, c-Rel KO mice still showed modestly enhanced epidermal thickness, suggesting residual inflammation in the absence of c-Rel (d and e). We examined expression of inflammatory genes in the dorsal skin of untreated and IMQ-treated WT and c-Rel KO mice and found increased expression of IL-1β, IL-17A, and IL-17F in WT IMQ-treated mice compared to c-Rel KO IMQ-treated mice (f). These findings suggest that the c-Rel is critical in promoting the TLR7-induced psoriasiform skin pathology.

Topical IMQ treatment has been shown to cause systemic effects in mice including loss of body weight and immune activation. , Interestingly, c-Rel deficiency did not prevent overall weight loss, as WT and c-Rel KO mice showed similar systemic body weight loss in response to IMQ-treatment (g). We also found that both WT and c-Rel KO mice showed comparable splenomegaly as an indicator of immune activation (h). This suggests that c-Rel may regulate IMQ-induced localised skin inflammation, and is not critical for the systemic inflammation, which can be caused by IMQ treatment.

The IMQ-mouse model agonises TLR7 to cause a psoriasis-like phenotype and TLR7 has been suggested to be critical for the inflammation which occurs in psoriasis. Our analysis of psoriatic skin biopsies from transcriptome datasets also found the upregulation of NF-κB c-Rel, but not NF-κB p65, in psoriatic lesions. Thus, we hypothesised that the TLR7/c-Rel axis may be a signalling mechanism involved in psoriasis pathogenesis. Immunohistochemistry staining indicated that c-Rel was increased in both the epidermis and the dermis layer of the skin (d), suggesting that c-Rel function in keratinocytes in the epidermis or immune cells that infiltrated into the dermis may contribute to the TLR7-induced inflammation. Psoriasis causes an infiltration of immune cells, primarily T cells and DCs, to the dermis which causes keratinocyte hyperplasia leading to the inflamed psoriatic lesion. c-Rel has been found to be critical in keratinocyte proliferation. , We first evaluated TLR7 signalling on keratinocytes by using the spontaneously transformed human keratinocyte cell line, HaCaT. IMQ was able to induce NF-κB translocation by 1 h in HaCaT cells (), indicating active TLR7 signalling in these cells. We then generated HaCaT cells that lack c-Rel using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing. The expression of TLR7 in keratinocytes is debated., , We found that WT HaCaT cells expressed TLR7 and the deletion of c-Rel did not affect TLR7 expression in these cells (). Next, we studied whether the genetic absence of c-Rel results in altered TLR7-induced inflammatory gene expression. IL-1β and IL-6 are commonly upregulated inflammatory cytokines during psoriasis and stimulation of keratinocytes with TLR agonists have been shown to induce their expression. We found that IMQ stimulation induced similar levels of IL-1β and IL-6 expression in both WT and c-Rel KO HaCaTs (). We also studied IMQ-induced proliferation of WT and c-Rel KO HaCaT cells. We found that IMQ stimulation had no effect on the proliferation of both WT and c-Rel KO HaCaT cells () and the absence of c-Rel did not alter keratinocyte proliferation (). Taken together, these results suggest that TLR7 signalling does not affect keratinocyte proliferation and c-Rel is dispensable for the expression of psoriasis relevant inflammatory cytokines in HaCaT cells. Hence, we hypothesised that the cellular mechanism controlled by TLR7/c-Rel axis in psoriasis pathogenesis was likely not through its cell intrinsic function in keratinocytes.

TLR7 is predominantly expressed in DCs, , and NF-κB c-Rel is also abundantly expressed in DCs. To study the role of c-Rel in TLR7 signalling in dendritic cells, we used CRISPR-Cas9 mediated gene editing to generate c-Rel deficient immortalised dendritic cells (DC2.4s) (a). Our previous work showed that c-Rel can act as a repressor of inflammatory gene expression and can also change the kinetics of gene expression. Hence, we studied TLR7-induced inflammatory gene expression at 30 min and 3 h in DC2.4 cells, to determine whether the genetic absence of c-Rel results in altered inflammatory gene expression. We found that the transcription of IL-1β and IL-6 was induced in WT DC2.4 cells following IMQ stimulation, but not in c-Rel deficient cells (b). We further found that the transcription of other inflammatory genes examined (ICAM1, TNFα, CXCL2, IP10, A20) were also induced at 3 h in WT cells but not in c-Rel deficient cells (b). ICAM1 and TNFα showed a 4-fold reduction in expression while several other genes (IL-1β, IL-6, CXCL2, IP10, and A20) were reduced more than 10-fold in c-Rel deficient cells when compared to WT cells (b). To exclude the possibility that absence of c-Rel compromises general transcription, we checked the expression of an NF-κB independent gene, c-Fos, and found that its expression was not dependent on c-Rel (c). IMQ stimulation was able to induce similar levels of c-Fos expression by 30 min in both WT and c-Rel deficient cells (c). We also assessed the expression of the type 1 interferon, IFNβ, which is induced by TLR7 in DCs but has been reported to be regulated by the noncanonical NF-κB pathway. We found that IMQ-induced expression of IFNβ expression was not affected in c-Rel deficient DCs (d). Together, these findings suggest that c-Rel is required for the induction of select inflammatory cytokine and chemokine genes following TLR7 stimulation in DCs. This is likely due to the role of c-Rel as a transcription factor in TLR7 signalling, and not due to a difference in the expression of TLR7, as WT and c-Rel KO DC2.4s had comparable amounts of TLR7 (a and ). Further confirming that this signalling axis is relevant in DCs during psoriasis in vivo , we found a substantial increase in the colocalisation of TLR7, c-Rel, and CD11c in the dermis of IMQ-treated dorsal skin samples of WT mice (e). The importance of c-Rel and TLR7 have separately been described in DCs, , , however, the TLR7/c-Rel signalling axis has not yet been described. Taken together, these data suggest that c-Rel has a critical transcriptional regulatory role in TLR7-induced inflammatory signalling in DCs during psoriasis.

In addition to the genetic c-Rel KO model, we sought to chemically inhibit c-Rel to further validate the role of c-Rel in TLR7 signalling. We used Pentoxifylline (PTX), a xanthine derivative that has previously been shown to be a potent inhibitor of c-Rel function. , Treatment of DC2.4s with 300 μg/mL of PTX resulted in a slight decrease and 500 μg/mL PTX resulted in a more substantial decrease in the nuclear translocation of NF-κB c-Rel, p65, and p50 (f). Treatment with 500 μg/mL PTX also inhibited the production of IL-6 and IL-1β following stimulation with IMQ (g). Taken together, this suggested that chemical inhibition of NF-κB resulted in the inhibition of TLR7-mediated inflammatory signalling in DCs.

To ensure that the IMQ-induced c-Rel dependent inflammatory signalling was exclusively due to effects of TLR7 stimulation and signalling, and not due to any nonspecific effect of IMQ, we treated our WT and c-Rel deficient DC2.4 cells with two other chemically distinct TLR7 agonists, CL307 and loxoribine. CL307 is an adenine analogue while loxoribine is a guanine derivative that both exclusively signal via TLR7. Stimulation of WT DC2.4 cells with CL307 and loxoribine resulted in a robust increase of IL-1β expression, while IL-6 expression was induced only modestly. Nevertheless, absence of c-Rel compromised both CL307-and loxoribine-induced increase in IL-1β and IL-6 production (a and b). Given the robust effect on DCs, clinical relevance, and similar results as other TLR7 agonists, we chose to use IMQ in subsequent experiments.

TLR7 is located in the endosome and structurally homologous with other TLRs, such as TLR9. To study the specific regulatory role of c-Rel in endosomal TLR signalling, we stimulated WT and c-Rel KO DC2.4s with CpG and poly (I:C) to stimulate TLR9 and TLR3, respectively. We found that CpG was able to induce a substantial increase in the production of IL-1β and IL-6 in wild-type DC2.4s, while poly (I:C) resulted in only a modest induction (c). Notably, c-Rel deficiency did not affect the transcription of inflammatory cytokines after 3 h of TLR9 or TLR3 stimulation (c). This suggests that TLR7 has a distinct signalling mechanism from TLR3 and TLR9, and that c-Rel is uniquely necessary for TLR7-induced proinflammatory signalling in DCs.

NF-κB subunits are structurally similar via a shared Rel-homology domain and display both unique and redundant functional roles. To study the unique and redundant role of c-Rel in TLR7 signalling with NF-κB p65 and NF-κB p50, the other subunits within the canonical pathway of NF-κB signalling, we generated p65 and p50 () deficient DC2.4s using CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene editing. We observed that p65 deficient DC2.4s were also unable to produce high levels of inflammatory cytokines following TLR7 stimulation (d). This confirms previous studies showing that p65 inhibition ameliorates TLR7-induced inflammation., , TLR7 stimulation of p50-deficient DC2.4s resulted in comparable amounts of IL-1β production as WT cells (d). This is in line with previous studies that have found that IL-1β production in activated immune cells is not mediated by p50. In contrast, p50-deficient DC2.4s produced an increased amount of IL-6 compared to WT cells following TLR7 stimulation (d). The inability of both c-Rel KO and p65 KO cells to express IL-1β and IL-6 following TLR7 stimulation suggests that both c-Rel and p65 is required in this signalling pathway. Taken together, this suggests that an activating p65/c-Rel heterodimer is being formed following TLR7 stimulation, which may be the key NF-κB dimer regulating TLR7-induced inflammatory cytokine expression.

NF-κB-dependent gene transcription involves signal induced nuclear translocation of homo- and heterodimers of NF-κB proteins and their binding to cognate promoter sequences. Mechanistic studies of the specific role of c-Rel in TLR7 and how it interacts with other canonical subunits of NF-κB during TLR7-induced inflammation have not been previously described. We assessed IMQ-induced nuclear translocation of NF-κB subunits in WT and c-Rel KO DC2.4s to determine the altered inflammatory cytokine production in c-Rel KO cells as a function of specific NF-κB subunits in the nucleus. We found that c-Rel KO cells had a basal increase of p65, p50, RelB, and p100 in the nucleus, and a basal increase of p50, RelB and p100 in the cytoplasm (). This is likely due to the functional compensation that exists between NF-κB dimers. RelB can act as both a transcriptional activator and participate in inhibitory complexes which repress NF-κB activity. Hence, we investigated the possibility that increased levels of RelB may act as a suppressor of IL-1β and IL-6 transcription in c-Rel deficient cells. We overexpressed RelB in WT DC2.4s () and found that an increase in RelB did not inhibit IMQ-induced IL-1β and IL-6 gene expression (). This suggests that RelB, in spite of the enhanced basal expression level, may not constitute an inhibitory dimer in c-Rel KO DCs.

To further dissect the molecular mechanism of c-Rel in TLR7 signalling, we performed a kinetic analysis by stimulating WT and c-Rel deficient DC2.4s with IMQ at timepoints from 1 h through 6 h and assessed nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions by western blotting. We found a time-dependent translocation into and out of the nucleus of c-Rel, p65, and p50 where their amounts were increased in WT cells starting at 1 h, and decreased by 3 h. Similarly, p65 and p50 translocated into the nucleus of WT and c-Rel KO DC2.4s at 1 h. Interestingly, p50 translocated to the nucleus starting at 1 h and was sustained until 6 h in c-Rel KO DC2.4s (a bottom, ). p65 nuclear translocation at 3 h and 6 h was not enhanced in c-Rel KO DC2.4s as compared to WT cells (a, bottom, ). In the absence of c-Rel, it is possible that the presence of nuclear p50 may contribute to a greater ratio of p65/p50 heterodimers. This suggests that although p65/p50 heterodimers are typically thought of as activating dimers, at least in c-Rel deficient DCs, the sustained translocation of p50 is not involved in forming dimers that activate the transcription of the proinflammatory genes described here.

Next, we investigated whether the sustained nuclear translocation of the p50 subunit seen in our c-Rel-deficient cells exists as homo- or heterodimers. The p65/p50 heterodimer is abundant within the canonical NF-κB pathway and has been described to activate the transcription of inflammatory cytokines., , On the other hand, the p50 homodimer has been described to inhibit the transcription of inflammatory cytokines., , , , In part, this is because p50 lacks a transactivation domain and thus binding to DNA blocks access to other NF-κB dimers. To examine p65/p50 heterodimers, we immunoprecipitated NF-κB p65 from the cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions of wild-type and c-Rel deficient cells after 0 h, 1 h, 3 h, and 6 h of IMQ stimulation. We found similar amounts of p65/c-Rel and p65/p50 heterodimers present in the cytoplasm of WT cells at the time points indicated (b, top). Corresponding to the basal increase in p65 and p50 subunits seen in the cytoplasmic fraction of c-Rel KO DC2.4s, we found a basal increase in the amount of p65/p50 heterodimer found in the cytoplasm of c-Rel KO cells, potentially due to the replacement of p65/c-Rel dimers with p65/p50 dimers in the absence of c-Rel (b, top). Of note, there was also an increase in the basal level of the p65/p50 heterodimer in the nucleus of c-Rel deficient cells at the 0 h time point as compared to the WT cells (a, top). However, when comparing WT and c-Rel deficient DCs after 3 h and 6 h of IMQ stimulation, no enhancement of the p65/p50 dimer in the nucleus was observed, showing that there is an overall decrease of the p65/p50 heterodimer translocated to the nucleus following TLR7 stimulation of c-Rel KO cells (a, top, lane 3, 4, 7, 8). Together, these observations suggest that although there is enhanced translocation of p50 in the c-Rel deficient cells, this subunit is not forming p65/p50 heterodimers at an increased ratio as compared to WT cells. Therefore, we hypothesised that the increased levels of p50 found in the nucleus of c-Rel deficient cells forms an inhibitory p50 homodimer, thereby suppressing the production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.

Effective DNA binding of the translocated NF-κB dimers should accompany nuclear translocation to regulate transcription. To study the specific TLR7-induced DNA binding NF-κB subunits in WT and c-Rel KO cells, we designed biotinylated oligonucleotides of the promoter regions of IL-1β and IL-6 and performed an oligonucleotide pulldown assay. We found that p65 binding to the IL-1β promoter was decreased in the nuclear extracts of c-Rel deficient DC2.4 cells at 3 h compared to the WT cells. In contrast, there was sustained binding of p50 to the IL-1β promoter at 1 and 3 h (c, top), further suggesting that the p50/p50 homodimer may be causing the inhibition of IL-1β transcription in c-Rel deficient cells. Similarly, we found decreased p65 binding to the IL-6 promoter at 1 and 3 h (d, top). Strikingly, there is a substantially increased amount of p50 bound to the IL-6 promoter at 1 and 3 h (d), further suggesting that a p50/p50 homodimer inhibits the transcription of IL-6 in c-Rel deficient cells.

To investigate whether increased levels of p50 in IMQ-stimulated c-Rel deficient cells form dimers, we immunoprecipitated p50 from nuclear fractions after 0 h and 1 h of IMQ stimulation in WT and c-Rel KO DC2.4s and crosslinked samples to preserve native conformations (e). We found an increase of p50 containing high molecular weight complexes present in IMQ-stimulated c-Rel deficient cells as compared to WT cells. To confirm that these complexes indeed contain p50/p50 homodimer, we performed sequential immunoprecipitation to deplete c-Rel and p65 containing complexes from the nuclear lysate (f). We assessed the depleted lysate to determine if the increased formation of the p50/p50 homodimer in stimulated c-Rel KO cells was functional in binding to the IL-6 promoter DNA, which would lead to the inhibition of IL-6 transcription. We found a substantial enrichment of p50, with no signal for p65 or c-Rel, indicating the induction of a p50 homodimer following TLR7 stimulation in the absence of c-Rel (g). Crosslinking samples following the oligonucleotide pulldown, showed an enriched p50 complex bound to IL-6 DNA around 100 kDa, further suggesting the formation of a p50/p50 homodimer in the absence of c-Rel (h).

To further validate the function of TLR7/c-Rel signalling using physiologically relevant primary cells, we generated bone marrow derived dendritic cells (BMDCs) from WT and c-Rel KO C57BL/6J mice. Similar to our in vitro system, we found that WT and c-Rel KO BMDCs had similar levels of TLR7 (a). Like c-Rel KO DC2.4s, c-Rel KO BMDCs also showed compromised IL-1β and IL-6 mRNA expression following IMQ stimulation (b). To confirm that the decrease in IL-1β and IL-6 mRNA was also reflected in their protein expression, we confirmed that protein expression of both IL-1β and IL-6 were decreased in c-Rel KO BMDCs following IMQ stimulation (c). Chemical inhibition of c-Rel using PTX in WT BMDCs also inhibited the production of these cytokines (d). As expected, stimulation with CpG and poly (I:C) to stimulate TLR9 and TLR3 was able to induce similar amounts of IL-1β and IL-6 expression in both WT and c-Rel KO BMDCs (e). Taken together, these data further suggest that c-Rel is required for TLR7-induced inflammation in both immortalised and primary DCs.

Aberrant crosstalk between DCs and T cells is key in psoriasis pathogenesis. T cell differentiation is determined by cytokines secreted from DCs. IL-6 and IL-1β are among the key cytokines that are required for Th17 differentiation. Th17 cells are critical in both human and IMQ-induced psoriasis pathogenesis. , Given that c-Rel deficient DCs are unable to produce inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β and IL-6 (, b and c), we hypothesised that the TLR7/c-Rel signalling axis in DCs regulated the induction of naïve T cells to differentiate into Th17 cells during psoriasis. To investigate the functional consequence of the decrease in IL-1β and IL-6 observed in c-Rel deficient BMDCs, we developed an ex vivo co-culture system using WT and c-Rel KO BMDCs that were pre-stimulated with IMQ for 20 h and naïve WT T cells (a). We cultured cells for 3 d in Th17-polarising conditions and observed that TLR7-activated WT BMDCs had an increased ability to polarise naïve T cells to Th17 cells compared with non-activated WT BMDC (b, top). We also observed that TLR7-activated WT BMDCs more readily polarised naïve WT T cells to Th17 cells than TLR7-activated c-Rel deficient BMDC (b bottom, 7c). Because ex vivo Th17 polarising conditions required the addition of exogenous IL-6 and IL-1β, we repeated our experiments under Th0 polarising conditions to better observe the intrinsic ability of WT and c-Rel deficient BMDCs to induce Th17 differentiation. Similarly, TLR7-activated WT BMDCs had an increased ability to polarise naïve T cells to Th17 cells compared with TLR7-activated c-Rel KO BMDCs under Th0 polarising conditions (d and e).

DCs can influence the differentiation of naïve T cells through secreted cytokines as well as through costimulatory molecules, such as CD80 and CD86, that interact with T cells at the DC:T cell interface. Therefore, we validated that the decreased ability of c-Rel deficient DCs to induce Th17 differentiation was solely due to hindered DC cytokine expression, and not a difference in the ability of c-Rel KO DCs to activate T cells via expression of costimulatory molecules. We found that both WT and c-Rel-deficient BMDCs had similar basal and IMQ-induced levels of the DC activation markers, CD80 (f) and CD86 (g), suggesting that global DC activation is not affected in c-Rel KO cells. These observations suggest that c-Rel is required for inflammatory cytokine expression in DCs, which in turn regulates the ability of DCs to induce Th17 cell differentiation (, schematic model). Taken together, the unique transcriptional regulatory role of c-Rel controls TLR7-induced DC-mediated inflammatory signalling in the skin.
sections.discussion:
In this study, we show that NF-κB c-Rel is a transcriptional regulator of TLR7-induced inflammatory signalling in DCs which is critical in psoriasis-like skin inflammation. c-Rel has been reported to be a psoriasis susceptibility locus and has also been reported to act as both a positive and negative regulator of inflammatory signalling. , Analysis of multiple transcriptomics datasets also showed that c-Rel is upregulated in psoriatic lesions, and c-Rel levels decrease upon treatment with biologics currently used for psoriatic treatment (a–c). In vivo , we confirmed the importance of c-Rel in psoriasis development, as our c-Rel deficient mice were protected from IMQ-mediated psoriasiform skin inflammation (). We identified DCs as a key cell type contributing to this phenomenon, and found that chemical inhibition and genetic knockout of c-Rel led to a drastic inhibition of TLR7-induced inflammatory cytokines (). Our mechanistic studies showed how c-Rel dictates NF-κB dimer compositions and binding of specific NF-κB dimers to specific promoters following TLR7 stimulation. TLR7 induces an activating c-Rel/p65 heterodimer in wild-type cells, while c-Rel deficiency increases the p50/p50 inhibitory homodimer binding to the promoters of IL-6 and IL-1β, thus inhibiting their transcription (). Functionally, this impeded TLR7-activated c-Rel deficient DCs in their ability to induce Th17 differentiation (b–e). TLR7 signalling has been implicated in the uncontrolled inflammation associated with psoriatic disease in humans. In addition, topical IMQ in patients can exacerbate previously controlled psoriasis in both IMQ-treated and uninvolved distant skin sites , further emphasising the role of TLR7 signalling in psoriasis pathogenesis. This study on the role of TLR7/c-Rel signalling axis in DC mediated inflammation during psoriasis provides a comprehensive view of an essential molecular mechanism involved in psoriatic disease pathogenesis.

TLR7 is a receptor for ssRNA and contains two distinct ligand-binding sites: site 1 and site 2. Site 1 recognises nucleoside or base analogues and small molecule agonists including imiquimod while site 2 binds oligoribonucleotides. , In this study, we utilised three chemically distinct TLR7 agonists; IMQ (chemically modified imidazoquinoline small molecule agonist), CL307 (adenine base analogue), and loxoribine (guanine derivative) to stimulate TLR7. All three TLR7 agonists showed a dependence on c-Rel for the production of a subset of proinflammatory genes, suggesting that this observation is not an off-target effect of the compounds used. Moreover, the role of TLR8, a TLR structurally related to TLR7, is debated in mice as some studies have suggested TLR8 to be non-functional in mice while other studies have found stimulation with a combination of select imidazoquinolines and polyT oligonucleotides can enhance murine TLR8 activation. Given the differences in receptor specificity between mouse and human TLR8, it is possible that current ligands that agonise human TLR8 are not recognised by the mouse counterpart, suggesting a current technical limitation in parsing out the differences in the role of c-Rel in TLR7 and TLR8 signalling using murine cells. Our study used only murine DCs for in vitro and ex vivo studies. Future studies including human DCs, with the utilisation of CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to delete TLR7/c-Rel axis proteins, will further help to dissect the mechanism and human relevance of this pathway. , In addition, utilising human samples from patients with psoriasis for similar studies will further validate the clinical application of the TLR7/c-Rel signalling pathway as a potential target for therapeutic development for psoriasis. The REL SNP rs702873 has been identified as a susceptibility locus in psoriasis, however, the mechanism in which this SNP is able to alter c-Rel expression or function is unclear. It has been hypothesised that REL polymorphisms are able to increase c-Rel protein expression, thereby causing overactive c-Rel-dependent pro-inflammatory signalling. , However, further studies are needed to investigate the clinical outcomes of patients with REL SNPs which increase psoriasis susceptibility and c-Rel protein function.

The relevance of the IMQ-induced psoriasis mouse model to human disease has long been discussed., , The translation of the IMQ-induced psoriasis mouse model to human disease, and thus the necessity of TLR7 signalling in psoriasis, has been questioned due to IMQ treatment inducing psoriasis in TLR7 KO mice. However, this can potentially be explained by possible TLR7-independent effects of IMQ through its binding to adenosine receptors to trigger inflammation or to tubulin to inhibit its polymerisation. Mechanistically, phosphorylation of TLR7 may control its aberrant function, as TLR7 dephosphorylation promotes the exacerbation of psoriatic inflammation in mice. This suggests a critical role for TLR7 signalling in psoriasis, and warrants future studies on the link between post-translational modifications of TLR7 and c-Rel activation. We acknowledge that as with any disease, it is difficult for a single animal model to capture the many facets of disease pathogenesis. Case reports have shown that clinical application of IMQ on basal cell carcinoma can worsen previously stable psoriasis leading to localised and disseminated psoriasiform lesions and application of IMQ on nonlesional psoriatic skin has caused the development of psoriasis-like inflammation. However, as these complications do not arise in all patients using IMQ cream, more research is needed to decipher the molecular mechanisms which trigger aberrant TLR7 signalling and contribute to disease pathogenesis. With this in mind, despite the limitations, our study emphasises the potential role for TLR7 signalling in human psoriasis, and highlights the usefulness of the IMQ-induced psoriasis mouse model as a tool to study the TLR7/c-Rel signalling axis in disease development.

TLR7 activation also upregulates proinflammatory cytokine production and thus is implicated in fuelling uncontrolled inflammation in human psoriasis. , , , siRNA targeting of c-Rel has also been shown to ameliorate the severity of IMQ-induced psoriasiform skin modulation, however this study did not delineate the signalling mechanisms, specific role of TLR7, or the cell types mediating inflammation. Elucidating this current gap in mechanistic insight on the TLR7/c-Rel axis is key in developing better therapeutic strategies for treating psoriasis. Clinically, a wide range of viruses, including HIV, HPV, and HCV have been associated with the development of psoriasis. However, the mechanisms in which these viruses are associated with psoriasis are unclear. Our study reveals a c-Rel-dependent molecular mechanism regulating DC function following TLR7 agonism that is critical for T cell-mediated hyperinflammation during psoriasis, which may be a potential link for how viral TLR7 activation is involved in worsening psoriatic disease.

Because imiquimod treatment in mice is known to cause systemic inflammation, we hypothesised that our global c-Rel knockout mice that were protected from IMQ-induced psoriatic skin phenotype would also be protected from a systemic inflammatory response. Interestingly, we found that our IMQ treated c-Rel deficient mice also develop systemic inflammation like WT mice, as evidenced by their comparable weight change and splenomegaly (g–h). Thus, it appears that c-Rel function is not critical for generic inflammatory responses elicited by IMQ, which may act through multiple cell types and other NF-κB subunits. To reduce confounding factors, mice were housed in a pathogen-free facility to eliminate possibility random infections and both male and female mice of age between 8 and 12 weeks were used to avoid sex-biased conclusions.

It is possible that the observed psoriasiform skin protection seen in our c-Rel KO mice could be partially caused by cell types other than DCs. For example, the presence of c-Rel deficient keratinocytes or T cells may have contributed to the decreased IMQ-induced psoriasiform phenotype. Our study highlights strong biochemical mechanism of NF-κB pathway signalling following TLR7 activation, however we acknowledge that future studies should utilise mice with a DC-specific deletion of c-Rel to further investigate the cell type specific role of TLR7/c-Rel axis in psoriasis. Epidermal hyperplasia is a key feature of psoriasis and transcription factor signalling cascades in keratinocytes can trigger psoriasis development. We evaluated the contribution of the TLR7/c-Rel axis to keratinocyte function using the HaCaT cell line and found that both TLR7, as indicated by the response to IMQ stimulation, and c-Rel was not critical for both keratinocyte proliferation and key inflammatory cytokine production. c-Rel has previously been shown to have a role in cell cycle progression, with similar results found in the HaCaT keratinocyte cell line and primary keratinocytes. This suggests that while c-Rel may play a role in other keratinocyte functions, it likely does not play a role in TLR7-induced cell proliferation. However, we acknowledge that our mechanistic studies were only conducted using the HaCaT cell line and in vivo disease mechanisms involve dynamic interactions between primary keratinocytes and multiple other immune and non-immune cell types. Thus, validation of our in vitro data using primary cells is extremely important and future studies using keratinocyte-specific c-Rel deficient mice are necessary to fully understand the contribution of the TLR7/c-Rel signalling axis in keratinocytes to psoriasis.

TLR7 stimulation of naïve T cells has been shown to inhibit Th1 and Th17 differentiation. c-Rel is also required for Th17 cell development in T cells. To parse out the molecular mechanisms of TLR7/c-Rel signalling specific to DCs, we performed in vitro and ex vivo assays with immortalised and primary DCs. Our ex vivo co-culture system using WT and c-Rel deficient DCs cultured with WT T cells helps tease out the DC specific role of c-Rel in TLR7-induced inflammation. We washed out all TLR7 ligand following initial DC activation to prevent any extraneous effect of IMQ stimulating naïve WT T cells. The decreased ability of TLR7-primed c-Rel deficient DCs to induce Th17 differentiation (b–e) appeared to be specific to the transcriptional role of c-Rel in regulating cytokine production (, b and c) as we found similar levels of DC activation following IMQ stimulation between WT and c-Rel KO DCs (f and g). c-Rel-dependent cytokine production from DCs is critical in Th1 and Th2 polarisation following TLR4 stimulation, further supporting the potential regulatory role of c-Rel in TLR7-activated DCs for Th17 differentiation. These data suggest that future utilisation of a DC-specific c-Rel KO mouse will be valuable to further delve into potential DC-T cell cross-talk in vivo during psoriasis. The interplay between the innate and adaptive immunity is critical to develop and sustain psoriasis. Consistent with this, we believe that c-Rel is critical in the production of key inflammatory cytokines in DCs needed for Th17 polarisation, thus delineating this specific arm involved in psoriasis pathogenesis.

A vast number of candidate therapeutics have been designed to inhibit pan-NF-κB in order to ameliorate inflammation. However, as NF-κB is involved in several vital functions, its global inhibition results in more adverse complications than beneficial effects. , Previous studies showed that p65 inhibition in vivo ameliorates TLR7-induced skin inflammation., , Although our biochemical results suggest that TLR7 likely induced an activating c-Rel/p65 heterodimer. p65 inhibition may not be a desirable strategy to adopt in the clinic. Our transcriptomics analysis showed that p65 is not upregulated in human psoriatic lesions (c) and p65 inhibition leads to many unwanted off target effects, likely due to its ubiquitous role in the regulation of essential cellular functions as evidenced by the embryonic lethality of p65 knockout mice. In contrast, c-Rel expression and activity is largely associated with cells from haematopoietic lineages and c-Rel knockout mice show no developmental defects. , c-Rel/p65 heterodimers, as described in this study, are a common activating heterodimer in inflammation. Thus, c-Rel inhibition may be a viable strategy to selectively hinder NF-κB-mediated inflammation without global inhibition of NF-κB function. As c-Rel inhibitors are well tolerated in mice, it is more likely that a c-Rel-specific inhibitor may have a better safety profile than a pan-NF-κB or a p65-specific inhibitor.

From a broad perspective, it would be interesting to further explore the role of c-Rel in other biologically relevant diseases involving TLR7, such as systemic lupus erythematosus , and viral infections. , c-Rel deficiency has been shown to be protective against systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). , Separately, TLR7 agonism has been shown to accelerate SLE while TLR7 neutralisation protects against lupus nephritis. Several TLR7 agonists have also been tested as HIV treatment strategies. Understanding the specifics of the TLR7/c-Rel axis in varying disease contexts is key in obtaining a comprehensive understanding of this relatively less studied pathway, which may aid in developing novel disease-specific therapeutic strategies.

title: Rutin ameliorates imiquimod-induced psoriasis-like skin lesions by inhibiting oxidative stress injury and the inflammatory response in mice via the Keap1/Nrf2 signaling pathway.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease with a high world-wide incidence. Rutin, a natural citrus flavonoid glycoside, has been shown to have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. To investigate the protective effects of rutin in imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasis model mice and its underlying molecular mechanism. IMQ was applied to mice to induce inflammatory skin that phenotypically mimics psoriasis. The Psoriasis Area Severity Index (PASI) score was used to evaluate the degree of erythema, scale and thickening of skin lesions. The inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress factors were measured to evaluate the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects of rutin. Finally, experiments were performed using Nrf2-deficient mice to determine the underlying molecular mechanism of rutin in the treatment of psoriasis. Mice treated with rutin showed reduced erythema, scaling, and epidermal thickening compared to mice without treatment. In skin tissue, topical administration of rutin inhibited the IMQ-induced increases in reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, and malondialdehyde, and significantly increased the IMQ-induced decreases in total antioxidant capacity, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione peroxidase. Additionally, the expression levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-1β, IL-17A, and IL-23A were significantly increased in the IMQ-treated group compared to the control group, but were significantly reduced by rutin. Importantly, Nrf2-deficient mice exhibited aggravated psoriasis-like symptoms and reduced response to rutin treatment. Our data evidence that rutin ameliorated IMQ-induced psoriasis-like skin lesions by inhibiting oxidative stress injury and the inflammatory response via the Keap1/Nrf2 pathway, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for rutin in the psoriasis treatment.

IMQ was applied to mice to induce inflammatory skin that phenotypically mimics psoriasis. The Psoriasis Area Severity Index (PASI) score was used to evaluate the degree of erythema, scale and thickening of skin lesions. The inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress factors were measured to evaluate the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects of rutin. Finally, experiments were performed using Nrf2-deficient mice to determine the underlying molecular mechanism of rutin in the treatment of psoriasis. Mice treated with rutin showed reduced erythema, scaling, and epidermal thickening compared to mice without treatment. In skin tissue, topical administration of rutin inhibited the IMQ-induced increases in reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, and malondialdehyde, and significantly increased the IMQ-induced decreases in total antioxidant capacity, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione peroxidase. Additionally, the expression levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-1β, IL-17A, and IL-23A were significantly increased in the IMQ-treated group compared to the control group, but were significantly reduced by rutin. Importantly, Nrf2-deficient mice exhibited aggravated psoriasis-like symptoms and reduced response to rutin treatment. Our data evidence that rutin ameliorated IMQ-induced psoriasis-like skin lesions by inhibiting oxidative stress injury and the inflammatory response via the Keap1/Nrf2 pathway, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for rutin in the psoriasis treatment.
sections.other:
Psoriasis is a chronic systemic inflammatory and an autoimmune skin disease . The present paradigm of psoriasis pathogenesis revolves around the IL-23/IL-17A axis . IL-23 is mainly expressed by activated dendritic cells and macrophages , which induce the differentiation of naive T cells into Th17 cells and activate γδT cells . Activated γδT cells produce numerous inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), IL-22, IL-6, IL-10, and IL-17 family members . IL-17A and IL-22 induce keratinocyte proliferation and neutrophil infiltration, resulting in epidermal hyperplasia, thickened spinous, and hyperkeratosis, all of which are typical histopathological characteristics of psoriasis . Under chronic inflammatory conditions, the inflammatory cells, in cooperation with keratinocytes, produce IL-23 and other cytokines or chemokines, which generate a positive feedback loop and form a vicious cycle, further exacerbating the chronic inflammatory process of psoriasis , . Psoriasis is also associated with systemic oxidative stress, which occurs when antioxidant defense mechanisms fail to counterbalance reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (ROS/RNS) – . Recently, the role of ROS and oxidative stress in psoriasis was demonstrated . ROS can damage skin wound healing in the inflammatory stages through regulating the local microenvironment , which plays a key role in the pathogenesis and progression of psoriasis by causing inflammation . Meanwhile, as a protective mechanism, antioxidants, such as catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), NADPH quinine oxidoreductase (NQO1), and glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px), act against oxidative agents to maintain the dynamic balance. Studies have shown that the skin is a primary target of oxidative stress, and that disturbances in the oxidant-antioxidant system in skin may play an important role in the pathogenesis of psoriasis . Therefore, antioxidative strategies to decrease the production of ROS and increase the activities of antioxidative enzymes through pharmacological intervention may serve as effective and easy treatment options for psoriasis.

Rutin is a common dietary flavonoid, which is widely found in vegetables and most citrus fruits. Several studies have shown protective effects of rutin in oxidative stress injury, which are mediated by antioxidant mechanisms such as scavenging free radicals and upregulation of antioxidant CAT – . Rutin has also been shown to partially protect skin fibroblasts against UVA- and UVB-mediated inflammatory responses by inhibiting the levels of phosphorylated STAT3 , . In addition, we have previously shown that rutin could ameliorate H 2 O 2 -induced oxidative stress injury in HaCaT cells via the Nrf2-regulated pathway . Taken together, this evidence suggests that rutin has a protective effect against oxidative stress injury in skin and may serve as a therapeutic drug for future clinical studies on psoriasis therapy.

In this study, an imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasis-like mouse model was used to determine the effects of rutin in psoriasis and its potential antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms in vivo.

sections.results:
To determine the effects of rutin treatment on IMQ-induced psoriasis model mice, rutin was formulated into a topical cream and applied after IMQ stimulation for 7 consecutive days. The PASI score was used to evaluate the degree of erythema, as well as the scale and thickening of skin lesions in mice, every day. As shown in Fig. , the cumulative PASI scores (Fig. a) suggested an aggravation of IMQ-induced skin inflammation in the IMQ group and IMQ + Vehicle group, specifically a series of inflammatory skin reactions to elicit redness, scaling, and stiffness of skin patches. Interestingly, these symptoms were alleviated after rutin treatment. The mice were sacrificed after anesthesia on day 8, and skin samples were collected for HE staining. As illustrated in Fig. b, vehicle group demonstrated typical epidermal morphology with no significant alterations in thickness, intact dermal architecture devoid of inflammatory cell infiltration, and absence of pathological abnormalities. In contrast, both the IMQ-treated group and the IMQ + Vehicle co-treatment group exhibited pronounced epidermal hyperplasia, accompanied by robust inflammatory cell accumulation within the dermis, consistent with hallmark psoriasiform pathology. Notably, the IMQ + Rut group displayed a marked attenuation of epidermal hyperplasia and a significant decrease in dermal inflammatory cell density compared to the IMQ group. These findings suggest that rutin mitigates IMQ-induced cutaneous damage, potentially through modulation of inflammatory cascades and immune regulatory pathways.

As psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease, the changes in inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1β, IL-17A, and IL-23A) in IMQ-induced psoriasis-like mice were further examined by qRT-PCR and ELISA. As shown in Fig. a, topical rutin administration significantly inhibited the IMQ-induced increase in the mRNA levels of IL-6 ( p < 0.01), IL-1β ( p < 0.01), IL-17A ( p < 0.01), and IL-23A ( p < 0.05). Similarly, the IMQ-induced increases in IL-6 ( p < 0.001), IL-1β ( p < 0.001), IL-17A ( p < 0.05), and IL-23A ( p < 0.01) expression were significantly reduced by rutin. Subsequently, the levels of ROS, NO, T-AOC, SOD, MDA, and GSH-Px in skin tissues were measured. As shown in Fig. b, the contents of ROS, NO, and MDA in IMQ-treated mice were significantly increased compared to those in untreated mice (i.e., the vehicle group) and were all decreased by topical rutin administration ( p < 0.05). Moreover, IMQ caused a significant reduction in T-AOC ( p < 0.001), SOD ( p < 0.001), and GSH-Px ( p < 0.05), while rutin increased the levels of T-AOC ( p < 0.001) and SOD ( p < 0.01). These data indicated that rutin could inhibit inflammatory responses and oxidative stress in IMQ-induced psoriasis-like mice.

Nrf2, an important factor in the cellular antioxidant defense system, is regulated by Keap1, which sequesters Nrf2 in the cytoplasm . To test whether the protective effects of rutin in psoriasis-like model mice is related to Keap1/Nrf2 signaling, the expression of Keap1 and Nrf2 were detected by western blot. As shown in Fig. , compared to the control group, the expression of Keap1 was significantly increased in the IMQ group ( p < 0.01), while Nrf2 expression showed a downward trend. As expected, rutin treatment significantly decreased the protein expression of Keap1 ( p < 0.05), and exhibited an increased trend of Nrf2 expression.

To further verify whether the ameliorating effect of rutin on IMQ-induced psoriatic lesions is related to the regulation of Nrf2 expression, subsequent experiments were performed using Nrf2-deficient mice. As shown in Fig. , after IMQ stimulation, compared to WT mice, the skin lesions in Nrf2-deficient mice showed an aggravating trend of skin redness, thickening, and stiffness. Rutin does not significantly improve psoriatic lesions caused by Nrf2 knockout.

As shown in Fig. a, compared to the wild-type IMQ treated mice, topical application of IMQ significantly upregulated the expression of IL-6 ( p < 0.001), IL-1β ( p < 0.001), and IL-23A ( p < 0.01) in Nrf2 -/- mice. Following rutin treatment, there was a significant decrease in IL-6 ( p < 0.01) and IL-23A ( p < 0.05) levels in Nrf2 -/- mice. As shown in Fig. b, after IMQ stimulation, the SOD ( p < 0.05) activity and MDA ( p < 0.01) and NO ( p < 0.05) content in the skin lesions of Nrf2 -/- mice were significantly lower than those of wild-type IMQ-treated mice. In Nrf2 -/- mice, rutin showed a tendency to regulate SOD, MDA, NO, GSH-Px, and T-AOC, but there was no significant difference. These results suggest that the inflammatory response and oxidant stress injury in psoriatic lesions can be exacerbated by Nrf2 knockout, and that the therapeutic effect of rutin on IMQ-induced mice is primarily dependent on Nrf2 activation.
sections.discussion:
Psoriasis is one of the most common chronic inflammatory skin diseases worldwide . However, the pathogenesis of psoriasis has not yet been clarified and remains a hot research area worldwide. Currently, there is reasonable consensus that oxidative stress and inflammation play an important role in the pathogenesis of psoriasis . Indeed, previous studies have shown that patients with psoriasis have increased levels of CAT and decreased activity of SOD in the blood , which indicate an imbalanced redox state, facilitate the production of free radicals, and result in skin oxidative damage. Psoriasis is a complicated disease with both autoimmune and autoinflammatory features. The skin epidermis contributes to the recruitment of inflammatory cells, and the cross-talk between epidermal cells and immune cells is likely to be important for the pathogenesis of psoriasis , . Several cytokines, such as IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-23, and IL-17, are implicated in the pathogenesis of psoriasis, with previous studies demonstrating that blockade of TNF-α, IL-17A, and IL-23 downregulated many proinflammatory genes . Moreover, IL-38 can inhibit the expression and secretion of IL-17 from γδT cells, with consequent improvement in the pathological manifestations of psoriasis . Efficient and safe long-term medical therapy and drugs are urgently required for the treatment of psoriasis.

The IMQ-induced psoriasis-like mouse model is one of the most widely used methods to replicate psoriasis in vivo . In the present experiment, we demonstrated that ROS, NO, and MDA were significantly up-regulated, while T-AOC, SOD, and GSH-Px were strongly down-regulated by topical administration of IMQ to the skin of mice. These data indicate that IMQ-exposed mice present with oxidative stress imbalance. The clinical severity of psoriasis in these mice was evaluated by PASI . The results demonstrated that IMQ induced the typical pathological features of psoriasis in mice, such as erythema, scaling, and thickening, as well as an increased PASI score. Furthermore, rutin treatment led to a notable improvement in psoriasis lesions, along with significantly improved oxidative stress injury in mouse back skin, which in turn improved the symptoms of psoriasis.

Keratinocyte hyperproliferation during inflammatory stimulation and the resulting thickening of the epidermis is one of the most important histological features in psoriasis . Previous studies have shown that blocking the IL-36R signaling pathway or knocking out the IL-36R led to a reduction in the number of dermal γδT cells and IL-17 secretory cells in IMQ-induced psoriasis-like mice, resulting in a significant improvement in the manifestations of skin inflammation in mice , . Additionally, it has been shown that the IL-36R signaling pathway promotes the pathological process of psoriasis by promoting the release of IL-17A and accelerating the recruitment of IL-17 secretory cells, such as γδT cells, to the inflammatory site. In this study, we also determined the levels of IL-6, IL-1β, IL-17A, and IL-23A, which are known key regulators in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. The results showed that rutin treatment significantly reduced the expression of these proinflammatory cytokines, indicating that rutin can promote IMQ-induced skin damage under pathological inflammatory conditions.

Nrf2 is a master regulator of the antioxidant response. Keap1 loses its inhibitory function on Nrf2 during oxidative stress, enabling Nrf2 to translocate to the nucleus and activate gene promoters containing antioxidant response elements (ARE) , . Our results showed that the expression of Keap1 protein in the model group was significantly increased, while that of Nrf2 was significantly decreased. However, compared to the model groups, rutin increased the expression levels of Nrf2, and considerably decreased the levels of Keap1. Importantly, Nrf2-deficient mice exhibited aggravated psoriasis-like symptoms and reduced response to rutin treatment. These results indicate that rutin activates pathways downstream of the antioxidant transcription factor Nrf2 and induces the expression of antioxidant proteins, further removing excess ROS and preventing oxidative damage in skin.

In conclusion, the present study confirms that treatment with rutin effectively alleviates IMQ-induced psoriasis lesions by inhibiting oxidative stress injury and the inflammatory response in mice, with the Nrf2/Keap1 signaling pathway thought to be the underlying molecular mechanism.
sections.methods:
Rutin (Solarbio Science & Technology Co., Ltd, Beijing, China) was mixed with Vaseline to prepare the rutin cream, which had a rutin concentration of 1 mg/mL. The vehicle cream was Vaseline alone.

All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Experiment Committee of Zunyi Medical University (Appl. No.: ZMU21-2203-548). Animals enrolled in the experiment were treated in accordance with the standards set forth in the 8th Edition of Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Male C57BL/6 mice (8–12 weeks, obtained from Laboratory Animal Center of Zunyi Medical University) were housed under a 12-h light/dark cycle with free access to food and water in the Laboratory Animal Center of Zunyi Medical University. IMQ (China Meheco Keyi Pharma Co., Ltd, Hubei, China) was administered to the mice to generate a psoriasis-like mouse model as previously reported . Four mice per group were used for the subsequent experiments. Briefly, wild-type mice were shaved on the back skin (2 cm × 3 cm) and randomly sorted into four groups: vehicle (control group), IMQ (model group), IMQ + Vehicle, and IMQ + Rutin groups. In subsequent experiments designed to test whether rutin treats psoriasis through impacting the Nrf2 protein, Nrf2-knockout mice (8–12 weeks, obtained from Laboratory Animal Center of Zunyi Medical University) were added to create seven groups: vehicle (wild-type mice), IMQ (wild-type mice), IMQ + Vehicle (wild-type mice), IMQ + Rutin (wild-type mice), IMQ (Nrf2 -/- mice), IMQ + Vehicle (Nrf2 -/- mice), and IMQ + Rutin (Nrf2 -/- mice) groups. IMQ was applied at a dose of 62.5 mg daily per mouse for 7 consecutive days. Vaseline (0.1 mL/mouse) and rutin cream (0.1 mL/mouse) were administered 4 h after IMQ treatment to vehicle and IMQ-induced psoriatic mice, respectively. Vehicle mice were shaved and treated with Vaseline. After recording the Psoriasis Area Severity Index (PASI) scores on the 7th day, mice were euthanized by intraperitoneal injection with 200 mg/kg sodium pentobarbital, and skin samples were collected. The study is reported in accordance with ARRIVE guidelines. The tissue samples were precisely weighed and homogenized in PBS at a 1:9 (w/v) ratio using a mechanical tissue homogenizer. The homogenate was subsequently centrifuged at 4 °C and 3,000 rpm for 20 min, after which the supernatant was collected and stored at -80 °C for determining oxidative stress factors and inflammatory factors.

In the process of model establishment, the PASI scoring method was used to evaluate the degree of erythema and the scale and thickening of mouse skin lesions. The PASI has an integral score of 0–4 points, which was scored by three scorers who were blinded to the experimental grouping. The PASI scoring criteria were as follows: 0, asymptomatic; 1, mild symptoms; 2, moderate symptoms; 3, severe symptoms; and 4, very severe symptoms. The trend line was drawn after the average value of the integral of mice in each group, and the changes in the skin lesions of mice in each group were observed.

Skin tissues were fixed in 10% formaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and cut into 5-μm sections. Briefly, sections were stained with HE solutions according to the standard method, before observing under a microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) at 200× magnification.

Mice were treated as outlined above. The oxidative stress factors in each group of mice were measured by commercial kits. The kit for reactive oxygen species (ROS) was purchased from Ruifanbioon (for tissue samples, Shanghai, China); and the kits for malondialdehyde (MDA), SOD, GSH-Px, nitric oxide (NO), and total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC) were obtained from Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute (Nanjing, China). The content of these oxidative stress factors in skin tissues was determined following the manufacturer’s instructions.

The concentrations of inflammatory factors in skin tissues were determined by ELISA kits for mouse IL-6, IL-1β, IL-17A, and IL-23A (MEIMIAN Co., Ltd., Jiangsu, China), according to the manufacturer’s protocols.

Total RNA was extracted from mouse skin tissues and reverse transcribed using a total RNA preparation kit (AXYGEN Biosciences, Union City, CA, USA) and PrimeScriptTM RT reagent kit (TaKaRa, Beijing, China), respectively. The mouse-specific primers were designed as follows: IL-6 (forward 5′-TAGTCCTTCCTACCCCAATTTCC-3′ and reverse 5′-TTGGTCCTTAGCCACTCCTTC-3′), IL-1β (forward 5′-GCAACTGTTCCTGAACTCAAC-3′ and reverse 5′-ATCTTTTGGGGTCCGTCAACT-3′), IL-17A (forward 5′-CCACGTCACCCTGGACTCTC-3′ and reverse 5′-CTCCGCATTGACACAGCG-3′), and IL-23A (forward 5′-ATGCTGGATTGCAGAGCAGTA-3′ and reverse 5′-ACGGGGCATTATTTTTAGTCT-3′). The relative mRNA expression levels were analyzed by the 2 –ΔΔCt method and normalized against the expression level of the housekeeping gene glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH; Sangon Biotech, Shanghai, China).

Proteins from the lysates of the back skin of mice were analyzed by western blotting. Total proteins of lesional skin were extracted by RIPA lysis buffer (Solarbio Science & Technology Co., Ltd.) and homogenized using a mechanical tissue homogenizer, centrifuged at 12,000 r/min for 10 min at 4 °C, and quantified by a BCA Kit (Generay Biotech Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). Protein samples were loaded on 8% or 15% SDS-PAGE gel for separation, which was then transferred to 0.45-µm PVDF membranes (4.5 × 9 cm). The membranes were blocked by blocking buffer (Beyotime, Cat# P0252, Shanghai, China) for 10 min, and then incubated with the following primary antibodies: Nrf2 (1:1000), Keap1 (1:2000), and β-actin (1:2000) at 4 °C overnight. Subsequently, the membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibody (goat anti-mouse IgG, Cat# A0216, 1:2000, Beyotime; goat anti-rabbit IgG, Cat# A0208, 1:2000, Beyotime) for 1 h at room temperature. Finally, protein bands were visualized with ECL substrate and quantified with FujiFilm Multi Gauge Ver. 3.0 software (Fuji Photo Film Co., Tokyo, Japan). The quantification of protein band intensity was divided by the normalized intensity of the loading control.

All data were analyzed with GraphPad Prism software v5.01 (GraphPad Software Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) and are shown as the mean ± SEM. Comparisons between groups were performed by one-way analysis of variance followed by Tukey’s multiple comparison test. p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

title: Aloesin alleviates imiquimod-induced psoriasis in dermal layers through inhibition of interleukins and NF-κB signaling pathways.
abstract: Aloesin is an aromatic chromone found in Aloe vera. Aloesin exhibits medicinal properties, including anti-inflammatory, anticancer, antioxidative, and antibacterial properties. Nonetheless, the possible therapeutic effects of aloesin on psoriasis have not yet been explored. The present study evaluated the impact of aloesin on psoriasis using an imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasis model in mice. A standard drug group receiving methotrexate (MTX) was included to benchmark the efficacy of aloesin. The effects of aloesin on body weight, PASI, oxidative/anti-oxidative indexes, and histological alterations in skin tissue were estimated. Additionally, the inflammatory modulators interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22, IL-23, tumor necrosis factor, nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), and transforming growth factor (TGF-β) were evaluated. Furthermore, oxidative stress parameters, including malondialdehyde (MDA), reactive oxygen species (ROS), superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione (GSH), and catalase (CAT), were assessed. Our findings revealed that both aloesin and MTX effectively reduced psoriasis area severity index (PASI) scores without any significant changes in the body weight of mice and ameliorated psoriatic lesions. Moreover, aloesin demonstrated effects comparable to those of MTX in several parameters and significantly downregulated the levels of immunomodulatory molecules, while increasing the levels of TGF-β. It efficiently up-regulated the levels of antioxidants (SOD, GSH, and CAT) and suppressed MDA as well as ROS activity. Our study demonstrated that aloesin had a significant effect on IMQ-induced psoriasis in mice, and the underlying mechanism may be the improvement of antioxidant and anti-inflammatory status, as well as the inhibition of NF-κB expression. MTX, as a standard comparator, allowed for direct benchmarking of aloesin anti-psoriatic effects. Psoriasis treatment could benefit from this approach in the future.

sections.other:
Psoriasis is a severe, immune-mediated dermatological condition characterized by dry, scaly patches of skin. Several etiological factors, such as genetic and environmental causes, are responsible for the development of psoriasis – . Reportedly, psoriasis affects around 2% of the world population and is more frequent in adults than in children , . Recent studies have revealed the contribution of gut bacteria to psoriasis pathophysiology . Various comorbidities are associated with psoriasis, such as psoriatic arthritis (PsA), cardiovascular disorders, and type 2 diabetes mellitus , .

Previously reported, psoriasis development has been linked to an abnormal infiltration of immune cells, including effector T cells, dendritic cells, neutrophils, and macrophages. After activation, these infiltrated cells secrete higher levels of cytokines . Importantly, Th1 cells trigger the production of proinflammatory mediators, including interleukin (IL) IL-23, IL-17, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), which contribute to inflammation , . Additionally, inflammasome development is crucial in psoriasis development by promoting caspase 1, IL-1β, and IL-18, thereby causing pyroptosis . Inflammatory responses in psoriasis are triggered through a network formed by the cytokines IL-17, IL-22, and IL-23. These cytokines are crucial for promoting the production of antimicrobial proteins, chemokines, and pro-inflammatory cytokines, causing damage to the skin and joints , . Research has revealed that IL-22 mRNA is overexpressed in characteristic skin lesions of psoriasis. Furthermore, IL-22 has been found to affect keratinocyte differentiation and contribute to epidermal alterations , . IL-23 and IL-17 play a central function in the pathophysiology of psoriasis, triggering innate and adaptive immune responses , .

Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) is a key regulator of several immune pathways, cell apoptosis, and cellular proliferation. It plays a central role in the progression of psoriasis; therefore, it could be a potential target for drug development in psoriasis. Elevated levels of phosphorylated NF-κB have been reported in psoriasis. Moreover, previous genomic studies have demonstrated a link between psoriasis and NF-κB expression. Furthermore, NF-κB has been postulated to alter the behavior of immune cells and keratinocytes, which is prominent in the psoriatic milieu ,, . TNF-α contributes to the initiation of psoriatic lesions by promoting the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and triggering immune cells. It is also involved in navigating inflammatory cells in the skin and joints, leading to inflammation , . Currently, conventional pharmacological treatments for psoriasis include corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and systemic agents such as methotrexate (MTX). MTX remains one of the most widely used and effective systemic drugs for psoriasis due to its strong immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory properties – . Dysregulation of transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) signaling has been reported in psoriasis, and recent research on transgenic mice has demonstrated that positive expression of TGFβ1 in the epidermis leads to skin inflammation . Chronic inflammation in psoriatic lesions causes ROS generation that leads to tissue damage. Additionally, disrupted homoeostasis between ROS production and antioxidant defense leads to disease progression in psoriasis , .

Imiquimod (IMQ) is a synthetic imidazoquinoline that modifies immune responses, acts as an agonist for Toll-like receptors (TLR), and activates NF-κB, leading to the generation of inflammatory factors and activation of innate and adaptive immune responses . Additionally, it triggers Th1-mediated antitumoral immune response and antigen-presenting cells , . Furthermore, IMQ promoted caspase-mediated pro-apoptotic activity at higher concentrations . IMQ activates the Th17 pathway, which causes increased production of IL-17 and IL-22, resulting in inflammation and subsequently keratinocyte increment, thickening of the epidermis, and immune cell infiltration .

Aloesin, a phytocompound found in Aloe vera , exhibits significant antioxidant properties. It has also been reported to mitigate lipid peroxidation and protect cells from oxidative damage . Moreover, a study revealed the anti-inflammatory effects of aloesin in a rat model by decreasing TNF-α levels . Furthermore, aloesin demonstrated notable wound healing properties by enhancing angiogenesis, collagen deposition, and tissue formation via activation of Smad and MAPK signaling pathways . No studies have been published on the therapeutic effects of aloesin in an IMQ-induced psoriasis mouse model. In this study, MTX was included as a positive standard control to benchmark the therapeutic effects of aloesin against an established anti-psoriatic drug. This study investigated the impact of aloesin on the severity Index (PASI) score, biochemical parameters, histopathology, and Western blotting (NF-κB) in a mouse model of psoriasis induced by IMQ.
