sections.methods:
Aloesin and IMQ were obtained from MSW Pharma (M.S., India) for the study. Inflammatory cytokines and markers, including IL-1β (MSW-IL-1β), IL-6 (MSW-IL-6), IL-17 (MSW-IL-17), IL-22 (MSW-IL-22), IL-23 (MSW-IL-23), NF-κB (MSW-NF-κB), ROS (ROS-MSW-01), and TGF-β (MSW-TGF-β) were also purchased from MSW Pharma, India. This study utilized high-grade chemicals of high purity to conduct the experiment.

In the current investigation, albino mice (18–20 g) were randomly assigned to separate experimental groups and housed in an animal facility with controlled environmental conditions. The temperature (22 ± 2 °C) and relative humidity (50 ± 5%) were maintained with a 12-h light/dark cycle. All rodents involved in the experiment had free access to drinking water and good-quality animal nutrition. All methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. The institutional research board of Batterjee Medical College, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, approved the research protocol with approval number (RES-2024–0026). The investigation was performed in compliance with the ARRIVE guideline . The experiments were conducted to minimize animal suffering and reduce the number of animals used.

Animals were simply randomized into five experimental groups as group 1 (control), group 2 (IMQ, 62.5 mg 5%), group 3 (20 mg/kg aloesin), group 4 (40 mg/kg aloesin), and group 5 (1 mg/kg, i.p. MTX) daily from Day 8 to 15 (Fig. ). Each group included eight animals. The control group received saline (pH 7.4) orally throughout the study. A depilatory cream was applied to remove the hair on the back of the experimental animals. Commercially available IMQ (62.5 mg) was applied to all animals, except the control group, for 6 days to induce disease characteristics mimicking psoriasis. After the appearance of psoriatic signs, including scales, patches, and erythema, 20 and 40 mg/kg aloesin was administered orally to animals in groups 3 and 4, respectively, for seven consecutive days. All animals were observed throughout the treatment period for clinical symptoms, and their weights were recorded weekly. Severity assessment was performed during this period based on the number of scales and patches on the skin. On the last day, the animals were sacrificed and the epidermis of the shaved area was gently removed. The removed skin was categorized into two parts. The first part was used for histopathological analyses by fixing it in 10% paraformaldehyde. The remaining portion was homogenized using phosphate saline buffer solution (pH 7.4), and subsequently centrifuged for 10 min at 4 °C (15,000 × g ) to obtain the supernatant, which was later used for biochemical tests .

PASI was used to evaluate psoriasis severity; animals were observed from days 1 to 6 during the disease development phase to classify the PASI according to the respective day. Erythema, thickness, inflammation, and scaling were assessed on a scale of 0 to 4, where 0 indicated absence, 1 denoted minimal presence, 2 represented moderate levels, 3 showed significant or high presence, and 4 denoted extreme or very high levels. Every day, the cumulative score ranged from 0 to 12, which was calculated by summing the three indices, and was used to estimate the degree of inflammation associated with the skin structure that mimics psoriasis. Moreover, skin hydration level was calculated using a skin moisture analyzer probe .

The supernatant of 10% of the tissue homogenate was used to measure the levels of inflammatory mediators, including IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22, IL-23, TNF-α, and NF-κB, as well as the apoptotic marker TGF-β, using commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. Cytokine levels in each skin tissue were expressed in picograms per milliliter (pg/mL).

For superoxide dismutase (SOD) estimation, the assay contains 10 µL of specimen to 100 µL of buffer composed of 0.050 M sodium pyrophosphate (pH 8.2), 10 µL of phenazine methosulfate, and 300 μL of nitro blue tetrazolium (NBT). NADH triggered a reaction that was terminated after 90 s using 100 μL of glacial acetic acid. The obtained colored product was then separated using centrifugation, and absorbance was recorded at 560 nm, with n-butanol used as the reference.

Glutathione (GST) was evaluated to determine the concentration of acid-soluble sulfhydryl groups by a colorimetric process using 5,5′-dithiobis-2-nitrobenzoic acid (DTNB). The homogenate supernatant was mixed with 4% sulfosalicylic acid in a 1:1 ratio and then centrifuged at 4000 rpm and 4 °C for 15 min. The reaction mixture consisted of 500 μL of DTNB, 2 mL of 0.1 M sodium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4), and the specimen supernatant. Spectrophotometric evaluation was conducted at a range of 412 nm, and the results are mentioned as μmol per gram of tissue.

Catalase (CAT) activity was evaluated. The reaction contained 2 mL of alkaline phosphate buffer of neutral pH, 50 μL of supernatant, and 1 mL of hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ). An aliquot was transferred to a cuvette for measurement of the optical density spectrophotometrically at a wavelength of 240 nm. The rate of decline in absorbance regarding H 2 O 2 decomposition was used to calculate CAT activity, and the results were expressed as micromoles of H2O2 consumed/minute per milligram of protein.

Lipid peroxidation was estimated using the thiobarbituric acid (TBA) method, with tetramethoxypropane as a standard for calibration. The reaction mixture was prepared by adding 250 μL of H 2 SO 4 (0.05 M) and 300 μL of 0.2% calibration standard to 200 μL of the specimen. The reaction mixture is then heated for 30 min using a water bath and immediately cooled by an ice bath, followed by the subsequent addition of n -butanol and centrifuged for 10 min (3500 × g ). The absorbance was measured at 532 nm, and the results were expressed as nanomoles per milligram of protein.

ROS levels in each group’s supernatant were measured using ELISA assay kits from a commercial supplier, following the manufacturer’s instructions.

For histological evaluation, the skin from the dorsal side of euthanized animals was carefully removed and fixed in 10% paraformaldehyde to preserve tissue integrity. The preserved tissue was subsequently embedded in paraffin and cut into 5-μm-thick sections. Further histological analysis was performed by observing tissue under a microscope coupled with a digital camera after staining with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E).

Protein was extracted from skin tissue. The tissue was washed with ice-cold PBS and then cut into small pieces. It was homogenized with cold protein lysis buffer and a protease inhibitor cocktail. Incubate the cell lysates on ice for 1 h with intermittent vortexing to total cellular proteins. Centrifuge the sample at 12,000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C. The total protein concentration was determined using the Lowry method. Western blot analysis was performed according to the previously described method. 35 In brief, 25–50 µg of protein from each group was separated by 10% SDS polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) and then electrophoretically transferred to nitrocellulose membranes (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA). The protein blots were incubated overnight at 4 °C for blocking. Thereafter, protein blots were incubated with primary antibodies against NF-κB p65 (Santa Cruz, CA) and peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature. For band visualization, the chemiluminescence method (GE Healthcare, Mississauga, Canada) is used, and β-actin bands are quantified using ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, USA). Image captured by using C-Digit chemiluminescent western blot scanner (LI-COR, Lincoln, USA).

Statistical analysis was performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test, except for PASI, which used two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni post hoc test. The results are shown as the data are expressed as mean ± SEM (n = 8) for the specified number of independent experiments. A normal (or Gaussian) distribution was used to evaluate whether numerical variables followed a normal distribution with the Shapiro–Wilk test. All variables had a normal distribution (P > 0.05). Based on these results, biochemical parameters have a normal distribution (P > 0.05). Significance levels were categorized as: P < 0.05 (significant); P < 0.01 (more significant). All statistical tests were performed using specialized software (GraphPad Prism version 8.0.2).
sections.results:
In the present study, aloesin’s effect on mice’s body weight was evaluated with respect to IMQ-induced pathological conditions. The experimental data suggest that IMQ application led to non-significant weight loss across all experimental groups, except the normal control group [F (4, 35) = 0.5209, (P = 0.7209)]. In addition, the group treated with the standard positive control, MTX (1 mg/kg, i.p.), exhibited no significant changes in body weight throughout the experimental period, similar to the aloesin groups. This confirms that neither aloesin nor MTX treatment induced adverse systemic effects, as indicated by stable body weights across all groups (Fig. ).

IMQ-treated mice exhibited a significant increase in psoriatic skin symptoms, including erythema, scaling, and increased skin thickness, which mimicked the symptoms observed in humans; however, normal control animals did not develop these symptoms. The severity of psoriatic progression in IMQ-treated animals was confirmed by a significant increase in the PASI score compared with that in normal control mice. Conversely, aloesin-treated animals exhibited a notable reduction in erythema [F (4, 210) = 472.0, (P < 0.0001)], skin thickness [F (4, 210) = 533.1, (P < 0.0001)], scale score [F (4, 210) = 528.6, (P < 0.0001)] and PASI [F (4, 210) = 523.7, (P < 0.0001)] as compared to IMQ-induced mice. Notably, including the MTX group allowed direct benchmarking of aloesin’s efficacy. MTX treatment significantly reduced erythema, skin thickness, scaling, and overall PASI scores compared to the IMQ group (p < 0.05). The degree of PASI score reduction in the MTX group was comparable to that observed in the aloesin-treated groups, reinforcing the anti-psoriatic capability of aloesin relative to a standard clinical agent (Fig. A–D).

The cytokine assay revealed a notable rise in the levels of IL-23 after IMQ application compared to the normal control group, which possibly drove the increase in IL-22 and IL-17 levels, subsequently amplifying the inflammatory cascade by exacerbating the production of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. However, aloesin treatment at both concentrations (20 and 40 mg/kg) effectively lowered the levels of IL-6 [F (4, 35) = 20.86, (P < 0.0001)], IL-17 [F (4, 35) = 21.12, (P < 0.0001)], IL-22 [F (4, 35) = 17.69, (P < 0.0001)], IL-23 [F (4, 35) = 17.03, (P < 0.0001)], IL-1β [F (4, 35) = 13.26, (P < 0.0001)], and TNF-α [F (4, 35) = 22.58, (P < 0.0001)] that could facilitate a smoother epidermal layer and comparatively reduced parakeratosis compared with the IMQ alone group. Similarly, animals treated with MTX exhibited robust suppression of proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22, IL-23, and TNF-α) compared to mice treated with IMQ only. The extent of cytokine downregulation in the MTX group paralleled that seen with doses of aloesin, indicating that aloesin and MTX exert comparable effects on the inflammatory cascade associated with psoriasis, as depicted in the histological assessment (Fig. A–F).

Furthermore, IMQ-induced mice demonstrated exaggerated NF-κB levels and decreased TGF-β levels compared to the control group. On the contrary, aloesin intervention at both 20 and 40 mg/kg concentrations significantly lowered NF-κB levels [F (4, 35) = 19.35, (P < 0.0001)], while TGF-β levels [F (4, 35) = 13.87, (P < 0.0001)] were upregulated. Consistent with the effects observed for aloesin, MTX administration significantly decreased NF-κB levels and restored TGF-β levels in skin tissues of IMQ-induced mice. These results further validate the anti-inflammatory potential of aloesin, which is comparable to the established efficacy of MTX in modulating key molecular mediators implicated in psoriatic pathology (Fig. A–B).

In this study, IMQ-induced mice showed disturbed oxidative homoeostasis, as the levels of antioxidants (SOD, GSH, and CAT) were markedly suppressed compared to controls; conversely, aloesin treatment at both 20 and 40 mg/kg doses efficiently reversed the effect of IMQ, improving the levels of antioxidants including SOD [F (4, 35) = 12.94, (P < 0.0001)], GSH [F (4, 35) = 16.60, (P < 0.0001)], and CAT [F (4, 35) = 17.12, (P < 0.0001)] as compared to IMQ group. The positive control group treated with MTX also showed a pronounced increase in antioxidant enzyme levels, with marked elevation in SOD, GSH, and CAT compared to the IMQ group. The magnitude of improvement in oxidative status with MTX was similar to that achieved by aloesin, suggesting equivalent antioxidant protective effects between these interventions (Fig. A–C).

IMQ administration markedly elevated both MDA and ROS levels in the experimental model. Treatment with aloesin at doses of 20 and 40 mg/kg significantly attenuated the concentrations of MDA [F (4, 35) = 30.88, P < 0.0001] as well as ROS [F (4, 35) = 6.462, P = 0.0005], demonstrating the compound’s ability to restore oxidative balance in treated animals. MTX treatment significantly reduced MDA and ROS concentrations in skin tissues of IMQ-treated mice, mirroring the antioxidative efficacy observed with aloesin. The restoration of oxidative balance by MTX was comparable to the effects seen in the high-dose aloesin group, demonstrating similar potency in mitigating IMQ-induced oxidative stress (Fig. D–E).

The figure depicts the efficacy of aloesin in the histological assessment of skin specimens. The epidermal layer of experimental mice exposed to IMQ developed severe acanthosis with increased epidermal hyperplasia, resembling the morphology of the psoriatic skin; however, these psoriatic phenotypes were absent in the control group. Furthermore, histological observations of both aloesin groups (20 and 40 mg/kg) revealed a smoother epidermis, a thinner epidermis, and reduced parakeratosis compared to the IMQ group . In the group treated with MTX, histopathological examination revealed substantial attenuation of epidermal hyperplasia, reduced parakeratosis, and decreased inflammatory infiltrate, paralleling the improvements seen with aloesin. Both MTX and aloesin-treated animals exhibited near-normal skin morphology relative to IMQ-only animals, further substantiating the therapeutic equivalence of these interventions in the context of psoriasis-like pathology (Fig. A–E).

The effect of aloesin on IMQ-induced psoriasis was evaluated by measuring the expression of NF-κB in skin tissue. There was a significant difference in the levels of NF-κB p65 transcription factors among the aloesin, MTX, and IMQ treatment groups (Fig. and Supplementary ). The IMQ group exhibited a marked increase in NF-κB p65 expression compared to the control group. In the groups treated with aloesin and MTX, the expression levels of NF-κB p65 were more inhibited at a dose of 40 mg/kg compared to the IMQ group [F (4, 10) = 75.62, (P < 0.0001)].
sections.discussion:
Psoriasis is a severe dermatological ailment that significantly impacts the physical and mental health of individuals. Psoriasis treatment remains a significant challenge due to its complex and multifaceted pathophysiology. Individuals with chronic psoriasis often experience devastating psychological, physical, and emotional conditions, which reduce their quality of life . Patients with psoriasis can have their self-image negatively affected by their visible characteristics . Extensive research has been conducted in preclinical psoriasis using the IMQ-induced mouse model. IMQ is an agonist of TLR7/8 that causes psoriasis-like skin lesions upon topical application . Aloesin is a phytocompound naturally found in Aloe species, with well-documented medicinal properties. In the present study, we analyzed the effect of aloesin on IMQ-caused psoriasis in a mouse model. Our results reveal that aloesin effectively reversed the detrimental effects of IMQ in vivo. It efficiently improved the skin of mice by reducing psoriatic lesions and the PASI score. In addition, aloesin treatment significantly downregulated the inflammatory responses and restored oxidative homeostasis.

The PASI is a commonly used method to assess the severity of psoriasis based on the degree of erythema, induration, and desquamation of lesions with an affected body surface , . The current experimental data showed a higher degree of PASI score in mice, consistent with previous studies that demonstrated IMQ application led to increased erythema and PASI scores, indicating the successful induction of psoriasis-like symptoms. The molecular mechanism of IMQ-induced erythema involves the activation of immune responses through TLR7 signaling, which subsequently triggers the release of pro-inflammatory mediators, including chemokine (C–C motif) ligand 2, IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. IMQ triggers the STAT3 and NF-κB pathways, exacerbating inflammation and facilitating keratinocyte proliferation, which contributes to epidermal thickening and enhanced blood circulation to the affected area. Another mechanism involves neo-angiogenesis and hypervascularity in the dermal tissue, which causes erythematous skin , . Aloesin may suppress TLR7 signaling, thereby arresting the subsequent cascade of inflammation and mitigating keratinocyte proliferation and acanthosis. Additionally, it may prevent neo-angiogenesis and reduce dermal vascularity, resulting in smoother skin, which underscores its anti-psoriatic effects in mice. These findings are supported by the histological observations in the current study, which demonstrated that IMQ application results in acanthosis and erythema of the skin. However, aloesin-treated mice demonstrated a smoother epidermal layer, reduced parakeratosis, and less epidermal thickening. Consistent with previous studies, the incorporation of MTX as a positive control group allowed direct benchmarking of aloesin’s efficacy. Notably, MTX-treated animals also demonstrated a substantial reduction in PASI scores, erythema, scaling, and skin thickness, comparable to the aloesin group – . This similarity underscores the potential of aloesin as a viable alternative to established systemic therapies for psoriasis, comparable to MTX in mitigating clinical symptoms.

Previous studies have indicated an activated NF-κB pathway after IMQ application that triggers the pro-inflammatory factors (IL-17, IL-22, IL-23, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6). IL-17 contributes to the accumulation of neutrophils and the formation of microabscesses in the epidermal layer of psoriatic lesions. Comparatively elevated levels of IL-17 have been reported in the serum and lesional skin of patients with psoriasis , . Similarly, IL-22 serum concentrations were significantly higher in individuals with psoriasis than in healthy individuals. Reportedly, IL-22 is associated with epidermal hyperplasia and keratinocyte proliferation and inhibits the terminal differentiation of keratinocytes , . The correlation between IL-23 and the pathogenesis of psoriasis involves a synergistic association with other cytokines, along with IL-23, which enhances psoriasis-like epidermal hyperplasia by inducing prominent inflammation. The association between IL-23 and psoriasis is further supported by the efficacy of IL-23 inhibitors in treating psoriatic conditions , . IL-1β is a vital inflammatory mediator in the skin microenvironment. Previous studies have shown that while IL-1β is crucial in local skin inflammation, its systemic levels may not always be linked to disease severity , . IL-6 activates the AKT/STAT3 signaling pathway, leading to abnormal proliferation and differentiation of epidermal keratinocytes . Unlike other cytokines, TNF-α is involved in the progression of PsA, as it promotes the recruitment of inflammatory cells to the skin and joint tissues, leading to bone and cartilage degradation . Cumulatively, this leads to skin inflammation, infiltration of immune cells, and epidermal hyperplasia, the characteristic morphological features of psoriasis – . NF-κB is a crucial factor in the inflammatory response associated with different skin diseases, including psoriasis. It has also been shown to play a role in the dysregulation observed in psoriasis . Under normal conditions, NF-κB typically exists as a homo- or heterodimer, with the p50-p65 heterodimer being the most prevalent. In resting cells, this heterodimer remains inactive in the cytoplasm, forming a trimer complex with the inhibitory protein IκB. Previously reported that NF-κB is highly expressed in psoriasis skin lesions and is significantly activated in psoriatic keratinocytes . These findings align with our results, which demonstrated elevated levels of NF-κB and inflammatory mediators in mice after IMQ application . Conversely, aloesin intervention significantly downregulated the levels of these inflammatory mediators, thereby acting as anti-inflammatory agents in IMQ-induced psoriasis in mice. In line with earlier studies, parallel reductions in pro-inflammatory cytokines were observed in the MTX group , . The extent of downregulation was analogous to that attained by high-dose aloesin, reinforcing the equivalence of their immunomodulatory effects. Thus, aloesin suppression of the psoriasis-associated cytokine network is not only robust but is also comparable to current first-line systemic intervention.

Previously, TGF-β has been shown to exhibit anti-inflammatory effects in IMQ-induced psoriasis, downregulating the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Reportedly, the IMQ application was associated with a decline in the expression of TGF-β, while anti-psoriatic therapy resulted in elevated levels, which is similar to the present study, in which aloesin reversed the effect of IMQ by increasing the suppressed levels of TGF-β, demonstrating its role as an anti-inflammatory agent , . Similar to previous findings, in the present study, MTX also upregulated TGF-β levels . TGF-β plays a dual role in psoriasis, acting as a potent immunomodulator and promoter of tissue repair when balanced, but potentially contributing to epidermal inflammation and hyperproliferation when dysregulated. Restoration of TGF-β by both MTX and aloesin aligns with clinical findings that normalization of TGF-β signaling is associated with symptom improvement in psoriasis. Thus, both agents appear to favorably adjust the TGF-β axis, supporting effective resolution of inflammation and epidermal pathology.

In this study, increased levels of MDA and ROS were observed in IMQ-administered rodents, whereas the levels of antioxidant enzymes (SOD, GSH, and CAT) were reduced in IMQ-treated skin. These results agree with the current findings – . Emerging evidence indicates that homeostatic disruption between ROS and antioxidants is not only a marker of oxidative stress but also an upstream driver of inflammation-mediated signaling cascades, including the activation of NF-κB in immune cells , . Consequently, changes in ROS levels (through direct or surrogate measures, such as MDA) can reliably reflect the activity status of NF-κB signaling. In the present study, aloesin restored oxidative balance by reducing MDA and elevating antioxidant enzymes, which is mechanistically consistent with suppression of the ROS-driven NF-κB pathway. The NF-κB pathway, central to inflammatory gene regulation and immune cell recruitment in psoriasis, was also significantly suppressed by MTX treatmenty , paralleling the effect of aloesin. Both interventions reduced NF-κB levels within psoriatic tissues, which likely underpins much of the observed decrease in proinflammatory cytokines and improved skin histology. The comparable inhibition of NF-κB by MTX and aloesin demonstrates that aloesin can target essential inflammatory cascades in psoriasis with efficacy equivalent to that of established systemic therapies.

In this study, the effects of aloesin may be attributed to its regulatory influence on inflammatory factors associated with the pathophysiology of psoriasis. IMQ administration significantly triggers the production of proinflammatory modulators, such as IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17, IL-22, IL-23, TNF-α, and NF-κB, which are crucial in keratinocyte hyperproliferation, immune cell infiltration, and chronic skin inflammation. However, aloesin reversed the effects of IMQ by downregulating the release of these inflammatory molecules, underscoring its potential in arresting the inflammatory cascade and restoring immune balance. Notably, aloesin also elevates levels of TGF-β, a cytokine known for its central role in modulating immune suppression and promoting regulatory mechanisms in tissue repair. Moreover, aloesin enhances the activity of key antioxidant enzymes (SOD, CAT, GST) while reducing the concentrations of oxidative stress markers, such as MDA and ROS, suggesting a capacity to preserve cellular homeostasis in response to psoriatic challenge. MTX, a reference anti-psoriatic agent, achieves similar normalization of the antioxidant system and reduction in oxidative stress, highlighting the comparable antioxidative mechanism of aloesin within this experimental model. Similar results were seen with aloesin and MTX, highlighting the potential of aloesin to address both inflammation and oxidative stress in psoriasis.

Although this study revealed the effect of aloesin on IMQ-induced psoriasis in mice, it has several limitations. This study employed a short-term IMQ-induced mouse model to evaluate the impact of aloesin. Although the model replicates key histopathological and immune features, its brief duration limits relevance to chronic disease progression. Thus, observed outcomes mainly reflect acute responses and may not indicate long-term efficacy. Aloesin improved PASI scores, cytokine levels, and oxidative stress markers in a short-term study. However, longer-term studies with extended treatment and follow-up are needed to evaluate sustained effects and relapse prevention. Future research should utilize chronic psoriasis models to elucidate the therapeutic potential and mechanisms of aloesin under persistent inflammation.

In conclusion, the present study demonstrated that aloesin effectively alleviated IMQ-induced psoriasis in a mouse model, with effects comparable to those of the standard anti-psoriatic agent, MTX, by inhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway. Aloesin intervention markedly reduced PASI scores, indicating a decrease in psoriatic severity. Decreased psoriatic lesions observed in the histological assessment further support the therapeutic potential of aloesin. Additionally, the favorable modulation of inflammatory and antioxidant molecules enhances aloesin’s anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. The comparative approach using MTX highlights aloesin promise as a candidate for further preclinical development in psoriasis. However, further detailed studies are needed to fully explore the mechanisms underlying its anti-psoriatic effects.

title: The clinically applied PARP inhibitor talazoparib ameliorates imiquimod-induced psoriasis in mice without reducing skin inflammation.
abstract: Background Considering the role PARPs play in inflammation, we assessed the effect of PARP inhibition in an inflammatory skin condition, psoriasis, to explore novel avenues for the potential repurposing of PARP inhibitors that are currently used in tumour therapy. Methods The imiquimod (IMQ)-induced model of psoriasis was applied in BALB/c mice. Mice received daily intraperitoneal injection of either one of four PARP inhibitors or their vehicle prior to treatment of the shaved back skin of mice with IMQ-containing cream or control cream for four days. The appearance of the skin of mice was scored daily according to the extent of erythema, induration and scaling. The most effective PARP inhibitor was selected for detailed studies on mouse skin and in a human keratinocyte cell line. Results Of the PARP inhibitors, talazoparib and rucaparib improved the imiquimod-induced symptoms on mouse skin. Application of talazoparib in the psoriasis model resulted in maintained terminal differentiation and reduced proliferation of epidermal keratinocytes. Conversely, talazoparib also enhanced the production of pro-inflammatory chemokines in the skin of mice. These effects of talazoparib was associated with increased mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen species and a consequent activation of pro-apoptotic and pro-inflammatory pathways in keratinocytes. Conclusion PARP inhibition by talazoparib promotes terminal differentiation of epidermal keratinocytes that may be beneficial in psoriasis. Despite the fact that talazoparib exerted a pro-inflammatory effect in the skin, which is not unprecedented in anti-psoriatic therapy, these findings may advance the conduction of pre-clinical and clinical trials with PARP inhibitors in psoriasis management.

sections.other:
PARP activation was first described in relation to DNA damage response, during which PARP1 cleaves NAD + to yield ADP-ribose residues that it transfers to target proteins, building up poly (ADP-ribose) (PAR) chains (; ; ). A couple of decades later, a second PARP enzyme, PARP2 was shown to exert similar catalytic activity (; ). In the early 2000s, it was recognized that tumour cells with defective homologous recombination DNA repair pathways, such as BRCA1/2-deficient cancer cells, are highly sensitive to the inhibition of PARP activity (; ). That realization gave a significant boost to research and development efforts with PARP inhibitors, and currently olaparib, rucaparib, niraparib and talazoparib have FDA approval as anti-cancer agents. All of these PARP inhibitors display simultaneous inhibition of PARP1 and PARP2 (; ), the two isoforms with highest activity, as PARP1 covers 85%–95%, while PARP2 covers 5%–15% of total cellular PARP activity depending on the model used (; ).

As a result of intense studies conducted on the PARP field during the past decade, now ample evidence demonstrates that PARP activation and PAR synthesis are involved in a plethora of biological processes beyond DNA repair. These processes involve energy metabolism and mitochondrial biology (), lipid metabolism (), transcriptional and translational regulation (), cell death (; ), differentiation and inflammation (; ). In accordance, the clinically used PARP inhibitors displayed beneficial effects in several models of non-oncological, inflammatory pathologies, such as asthma (), sepsis (), alcoholic hepatitis (; ), acute pancreatitis (), burn injury (), and acute lung injury (). Hence, it has been postulated that PARP inhibitors could be repurposed for the treatment of non-oncological diseases ().

Psoriasis is one the most common inflammatory skin diseases, to which currently there is no cure. Psoriasis manifests under specific genetic and environmental factors, and it is characterized by the hyperproliferation and aberrant terminal differentiation of epidermal keratinocytes. This results in the formation of thickened, red plaques on various skin areas. (). Psoriatic skin lesions contain a robust immune cell infiltrate, and psoriasis is considered primarily an immune-mediated disorder. It is widely accepted that T helper (Th)17 cells and the IL17 cytokine family has a prominent role in activating those signalling circuits in keratinocytes that sustain chronic inflammation in psoriasis (; ).

Psoriasis has several animal models, among them, the most widely utilized in psoriasis-related studies is the imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasiform dermatitis (). We previously studied this model in PARP1 −/− and PARP2 −/− mice. Surprisingly, we found that the dermatitis upon IMQ treatment was more severe in PARP1 −/− mice than in wild-type mice (), while PARP2 −/− mice displayed a protected phenotype against the IMQ-induced symptoms (). In the current study, we aimed to test the effect of PARP inhibitors, which target PARP1 and PARP2 in equal measure, in the IMQ-induced psoriasis model.

The distribution of data was analysed by Shapiro-Wilk test. If two groups were compared, we used independent t-test (two-tailed), as the Shapiro–Wilk test showed normal distribution. If the distribution was not normal, Mann-Whitney test was used. When we compared more than two groups and if the distribution was normal, we used ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. In case the data did not show a normal distribution, Kruskal–Wallis test were applied complemented by Dunn’s post hoc test. The significance level was set at 0.05. sections.methods:
BALB/c mice were bred at the animal facility of the University of Debrecen, Hungary. No more than six mice were housed in each cage (standard block shape 365 × 207 × 140 mm, surface 530 cm 2 ; 1284 L Eurostandard Type II. L from Techniplast, Milan, Italy) with Lignocel Select Fine (J. Rettenmaier und Söhne, Rosenberg, Germany) as bedding. Mice had ad libitum access to water (sterilized tap water) and food (chow diet - Safe, Augy, France), and were kept under a 12/12-h dark/light cycle. Only male mice were used in the study at the age of 8–10 weeks. Mice had paper tubes to enrich their environment. Cages were changed once a week, on the same day. The animal facility was overseen by a veterinarian.

Mice were housed separately during the experiment. Two days prior to the start of the study, the back of mice was shaved in a 2 × 2 cm area, then mice were weighed and divided into different cohorts. Each day, mice received 200 μL intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of either vehicle (VEH) (solvent composed of 4% dimethyl-sulfoxide, 5% polyethylene glycol 300 in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS)) or one of the following PARP inhibitors: talazoparib (S7048) solution (2 mg kg -1 ·day -1 ); olaparib (S1060), (20 mg kg -1 ·day -1 ) rucaparib (S4948) (50 mg kg -1 ·day -1 ); niraparib (S2741) (10 mg kg -1 ·day -1 ) (all from Selleck Chemicals, Houston, TX, United States) 1 h prior to topical treatment with either 62.5 mg of Aldara cream (5% imiquimod (IMQ), Meda AB, Solna, Sweden) or a control cream (CTL) for four consecutive days. The severity of the lesions, including induration, erythema and scaling, was scored daily by two experienced researchers (one of them was a dermatologist), each on a scale from 0 to 4, where 0 denotes no symptoms and 4 denotes the most severe symptoms. On day 5, 2 h prior to sacrifice, mice received 5-bromo-2-deoxyuridine (ab142567; Abcam, Cambridge, United Kingdom) (BrDU, 100 mg/kg of body weight i. p.), then mice were sacrificed, and skin biopsies were taken for further analyses. The study was approved by the Veterinary Centre of the University of Debrecen, Hungary (study registration No. 5/2023/DEMÁB).

Histology analyses were performed on 4 μm thick sections cut from formalin fixed, paraffin embedded mouse skin samples, similar, as in (). Section were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). For immunohistochemistry (IHC), blocked tissue sections were incubated with specific primary antibodies (RelA/NFkB p65 [p Ser276]: NB100-82086; Involucrin: 924401, Biolegend (San Diego, Ca, United States); Caspase-3: 9662, Cell Signaling Technology (Danvers, MA, United States)). Protein expression was detected with Mouse and Rabbit Specific HRP/DAB (ABC) Detection IHC kit (ab64264; Abcam, Cambridge, United Kingdom) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. For detection of BrdU, a commercial IHC kit was used (ab125306, Abcam). Negative controls were obtained by omitting the primary antibodies. Slides were digitalized with the PANNORAMIC confocal slide scanner (3DHISTECH Ltd., Budapest, Hungary). Scanned slides were studied by the SlideViewer 2.8 for Windows 11 software of 3DHISTECH Ltd. Epidermal thickness of mouse skin was measured in the SlideViewer 2.8 software.

Cell culture studies were performed on the HPV-Ker human keratinocyte cell line. Human keratinocytes were immortalized with the HPV-E6 oncogene by researchers of the University of Szeged, Hungary in collaboration with Creative Laboratory Ltd., Szeged, Hungary (), and the thereby generated HPV-Ker cells were kindly provided by Creative Laboratory Ltd. Cells were maintained in Keratinocyte serum-free medium (SFM) supplemented with Bovine Pituitary Extract (BPE) (50 μg/mL), human recombinant Epidermal Growth Factor (rEGF) (5 ng/mL) (17005042, Gibco, Thermo-Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, United States), 1% penicillin/streptomycin (P4333, Merck Millipore, Burlington, MA, United States) and 1% L-glutamine solutions (59202C, Merck) in 5% CO 2 humidified air at 37°C. For differentiation of HPV-Ker keratinocytes, post-confluent cells were kept in antibiotics-free culture media supplemented with 1.7 mM Ca 2+ for 3 days. Cells were exposed to treatments with TAL (100 nM); IL17A (200 ng/mL; 7955-IL, R&D systems, Minneapolis, MN, United States); TNFα (10 ng/mL; GF023, Merck Millipore). Treatment schemes are highlighted in Figure legends.

HPV-Ker cells were washed with PBS solution and were then harvested in RIPA lysis buffer (50 mM Tris, 150 mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS, 1 mM EDTA, 1 mM Na 3 VO 4 , 1 mM NaF, 1 mM PMSF and protease inhibitor cocktail, all from Merck Millipore) on ice. DNA-protein complexes in cell lysates were disrupted by sonication (Branson Sonifier, Emerson Electric, Pasig, Philippines) for 3 × 20 pulses, 15-s intervals. Protein isolates were separated from debris by centrifugation for 10 min at 10,000 x g, 4°C. Protein lysates were boiled with 5x SDS sample buffer (310 mM Tris-HCl, pH 6.8, 50% glycerol, 10% SDS, 100 mM DTT, 0.01% bromophenol blue, all from Merck Millipore) supplemented with 5% 2-mercaptoethanol for 10 min. Protein extracts (20–30 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes. Membranes were blocked with 5% BSA in TBS-Tween or 5% non-fat milk in TBS-Tween for 1 h at room temperature and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4°C. Membranes were probed with a peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody for 1 h at room temperature. Signals were visualized by enhanced chemiluminescence reaction and captured by ChemiDocTM Touch Imaging System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, United States). Bands were quantified by densitometry using Fiji ImageJ software (). The following antibodies were used in immunoblots: anti-caspase-3 (9662, Cell Signaling Technology, 1:1000), recombinant anti-cytokeratin 10 (Abcam, ab76318, 1:1000), anti-β-actin-peroxidase (Merck, A3854, 1:20000), anti-mouse IgG, HRP-linked (Merck Millipore, A9044, 1:2000), anti-rabbit IgG, HRP-linked (Cell Signaling Technology, 7074S 1:1000).

Mouse skin samples were flash frozen in liquid nitrogen after excision. Before protein extraction, tissues were weighed and rinsed with PBS. Tissues were homogenized in PBS containing protease inhibitor cocktail (S8830, Merck Millipore) using 5 mm stainless steel beads at 30 Hz for 8 min in a TissueLyser II device (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). Afterwards, Triton X-100 was added to the samples to reach 1% final concentration. The samples were then centrifuged at 10,000 × g for 5 min at 4°C to remove any debris. The supernatant was saved, and protein content was quantified using a Pierce BCA protein assay kit (23225, Thermo Fisher Scientific). 300 μg protein of each samples within a treatment group was pooled and used for the mouse cytokine array according to the protocol provided by the manufacturer (Proteome Profiler Array, No. ARY006, R&D Systems/Bio-Techne). The immunoblot images were captured and visualized using a ChemiDoc™ Touch Imaging System (Bio-Rad Laboratories) and the integrated intensity of each spot in the images was analyzed using CellProfiler for non-cell images analysis software (Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard) ().

HPV-Ker cells were exposed to various treatments, subsequently apoptotic cells were detected using eBioscience Annexin V Apoptosis Detection Kit FITC with propidium iodide (PI) (88–8005-72/74, Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, United States) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, supernatants of cells were removed and put aside. Cells were washed with PBS, trypsinized and washed with the supernatant media complemented with fetal bovine serum (FBS) into polystyrene tubes, then cells were pelleted by centrifugation (2000 rpm, 5 min, 4 °C). Cells were washed again with PBS, centrifuged, and stained with FITC-conjugated Annexin V and PI (5–5 μL/100 μL binding buffer/2 × 10 5 cells) for 15 min at room temperature. Samples were then diluted with PBS and subsequently analysed by a NovoCyte Flow Cytometer (Agilent Technologies, San Diego, CA, United States).

For microscopy, HPV-Ker cells were seeded on coverslips in 24-well plates, and were exposed to various treatments. Cells were incubated in culture media containing 100 nM MitoTracker Red CMXRos dye (M7512, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30 min, washed three times with culture media, then cells were fixed with 4% formaldehyde. After washing three times with PBS, nuclei of cells were counterstained with Hoechst 33342 dye (Thermo Fisher Scientific), subsequently, cells were observed in a TCS SP8 confocal microscope (Leica, Wetzlar, Germany). For flow cytometry, HPV-Ker keratinocytes were seeded in 6-well plates. Cells were trypsinized, washed with fetal bovine serum-containing culture media, centrifuged, and incubated in culture media with 100 nM MitoTracker Red CMXRos dye for flow cytometry (M46752, Thermo Fisher Sceintific) for 30 min at 37°C for 30 min. Afterwards, cells were washed twice with PBS, then analyzed by Novocyte Flow Cytometer (Agilent Technologies).

To detect mitochondrial ROS, HPV-Ker cells were seeded in 6-well plates and were subjected to various treatments. Cells were trypsinized, washed with FBS-containing culture media, centrifuged, and incubated in culture media with 5 μM MitoSOX Red mitochondrial superoxide indicator ( M36008 , Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 37°C for 30 min. Afterwards, cells were washed twice with HBSS buffer, then analyzed by Novocyte Flow Cytometer (Agilent Technologies).

Total RNA from cells was isolated using PureLink RNA kit (12183018A; Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA samples were treated with Ambion DNase I (AM2222; Thermo Fisher Scientific), afterwards, samples were reverse transcribed using a High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (4368813; Thermo Fisher Scientific). The RT-qPCR reactions were performed in a Light-Cycler 480 Detection System (Roche, Bazel, Switzerland) using TaqMan assays: ATF3 (Hs00231069_m1); IL6 (Hs00174131_m1); IL1β (Hs01555410_m1); CXCL8 (Hs00174103_m1). RT-qPCR data was quantified by calculating normalized gene expressions using the ΔΔCt method. GAPDH (Hs02786624_g1) was used as an internal control gene for normalization. Taqman assays were from Thermo Fisher Scientific.
sections.results:
To test if PARP inhibition can affect IMQ-induced psoriasis-like dermatitis in mice, first we performed a pilot study with the four clinically available inhibitors. We included only male mice in this study for several reasons. Multiple studies show that psoriasis changes in women during pregnancy, postpartum and with menopause, indicating that psoriasis is influenced by estrogen hormones (; ). In addition, a recent study provided evidence that estradiol suppresses IMQ-induced psoriasis in mice (). Since female mice have estrous cycle, it is possible that the hormonal status of female mice could interfere with the development and severity of IMQ-induced symptoms. To note, studies suggest that the effects of PARP inhibitors also depend on the sex of the animals, with male mice being more responsive than females (; ).

We found in the pilot experiment that, in the applied doses, only rucaparib and talazoparib reduced the extent of induration, erythema and scaling of the skin caused by IMQ treatment, while olaparib and niraparib did not affect the visual appearance of dermatitis compared to the cohort that received only vehicle (VEH) in i. p. injection before treatment of their skin with IMQ (VEH IMQ) ().

It is interesting that not all PARP inhibitors influenced the IMQ-induced psoriasiform lesions. This discordance may have several explanations. For one, we tested the inhibitors in a dosage selected based on oncological studies. However, it has been suggested that the optimal dose of PARP inhibitors in non-oncological conditions may be lower than the doses used in oncological indications (), and that the inhibitors may have bell-shaped dose-responses (). Another feasible explanation may be the known difference in the pharmacological and pharmacokinetic profiles of the compounds (). For example, niraparib and talazoparib have longer half-lives than olaparib and rucaparib, hence only niraparib and talazoparib are used in a once-daily dosing in therapy (). Talazoparib goes through minimal hepatic metabolism but its dosage should be reduced in patients with impaired renal function, while niraparib requires dose adjustments in patients with hepatic impairment (). In our experiments we formulated the PARP inhibitors for i. p. injection. Administration via oral gavage may have been closer to the tablet formulation how PARP inhibitors are applied in clinical therapy currently, and may have yielded different results.

Nevertheless, based on our findings and considering that talazoparib is the most potent PARP inhibitor (), we chose the talazoparib-treated cohort for mechanistic studies. shows the back skin of mice that received either VEH or talazoparib daily i. p. injection prior to topical IMQ treatment (VEH IMQ and TAL IMQ, respectively) as compared to mice that received VEH i. p. and were treated with a control cream (VEH CTL) on day 5 of the experiment. The IMQ-evoked epidermal thickening was less pronounced in the skin of mice that received talazoparib (), as is visible on skin sections after hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining ().

Immunohistochemical analyses of skin samples revealed premature and smeared expression of the terminal differentiation marker involucrin (IVL) in those mice that received only VEH in i. p. injection before IMQ treatment (VEH IMQ) (). In talazoparib-administered mice (TAL IMQ), although the staining zone broadened, involucrin expression displayed a sharp appearance in the granular layer, more closely resembling normal skin (VEH CTL) (). In addition, analysis of nuclear BrdU incorporation showed fewer proliferating basal keratinocytes in mice that received talazoparib prior to IMQ application (). Next, we performed cytokine array from whole skin lysates. Since visually, the severity of lesions seemed reduced in the talazoparib-treated cohort, it was surprising to find that expressions of inflammatory markers did not change in the skin of these mice compared to the IMQ reference cohort (VEH IMQ). Moreover, inflammation-related chemokines CXCL1 and CCL12 could only have been detected in the samples of talazoparib-treated mice (TAL IMQ), and not in the skin of VEH IMQ mice, suggesting a slight pro-inflammatory effect of talazoparib in the skin (). In accordance, talazoparib did not lessen IMQ-evoked NF-κB activation as determined by detection of phosphorylated p65 positive nuclei in skin sections ().

Given that PARP1 has much higher average activity than PARP2 (85%–90% compared to 5%–15% of total cellular PARP activity), it may be interesting how the phenotype resulted from talazoparib application in the IMQ model channels more aspects of the PARP2 −/− phenotype than the PARP1 −/− phenotype in the same model. Namely, the skin of PARP2 −/− mice similarly displayed maintained terminal differentiation, reduced proliferation and overall alleviated symptoms, but also reduced inflammation after IMQ application compared to wild-type mice (). Conversely, PARP1 −/− mice displayed more severe psoriasis-like dermatitis and enhanced inflammatory marker expression than the wild-type mice in the IMQ model (). In this regard, it has to be noted that not all functions of PARPs depend on their catalytic activity, some of their functions rely only on their physical presence and interactions with other proteins (). The latter functions can only be observed in knock-out model systems and are out of the scope of PARP inhibitors. Characterization of enzymatic activity dependent and independent roles of PARP1 and PARP2 in psoriasis should be elucidated in future studies in order to better understand what signalling mechanisms could be targeted by PARP inhibitors that are relevant in psoriasis.

The phenotype observed upon talazoparib treatment can be explained by its pro-apoptotic effect (; ), as it has been reported that apoptosis has a crucial role in balancing proliferation and terminal differentiation of epidermal keratinocytes (), and that psoriasis features dysfunctional keratinocyte apoptosis (). As the apoptotic effector caspase-3 was shown to be activated during keratinocyte apoptosis and terminal differentiation (; ; ), we studied caspase-3 expression in the skin of mice. In VEH CTL mice we detected caspase-3 positivity in the basal and lower spinous layers, which was similar in IMQ-treated mice receiving VEH i. p. injection (). In the TAL IMQ cohort, caspase-3 showed strong and even expression in epidermal layers (), indicating enhanced apoptosis in the skin upon talazoparib administration.

Next, we aimed to study the role of talazoparib in human keratinocyte differentiation. Differentiation of HPV-Ker human keratinocyte cultures in talazoparib-containing media resulted in higher expression of terminal differentiation marker keratin 10, which was accompanied by increased caspase-3 expression (). In addition, Annexin V/propidium iodide dual staining of differentiated keratinocytes revealed an increment in late apoptotic population when the cells were under talazoparib stimulation either alone, or in combination with psoriasis-mimicking cytokines IL17A and TNFα (). These data indicate that talazoparib improves keratinocyte differentiation by activating caspase-mediated programmed cell death. Then we further studied the possible underlying mechanisms of these findings. We have previously shown that PARP1 and PARP2 regulate mitochondrial biogenesis (; ). Since higher mitochondrial content correlates with greater tendency of cells to undergo caspase-mediated apoptosis (), we studied mitochondrial parameters in keratinocytes upon PARP inhibition with talazoparib. We detected higher MitoTracker () and MitoSox () fluorescence in talazoparib-treated HPV-Ker keratinocytes, indicative of increased mitochondrial mass and higher mitochondrial production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Also, we found that talazoparib treatment caused a significant upregulation in pro-inflammatory cytokine mRNA expressions in human keratinocytes, which was even more pronounced when talazoparib was applied together with the combination of IL17A and TNFα (). Although this pro-inflammatory effect of PARP inhibition is somewhat surprising, it is not without precedent. We have previously reported that a combined treatment of HPV-Ker cells with olaparib and IMQ caused higher increase in IL6 mRNA expression than IMQ alone (). In a different study, olaparib enhanced UVB-induced TNFα and IL8 mRNA expression in human keratinocytes (). Moreover, olaparib treatment increased ROS production in human tumour macrophages, which essentially promoted pro-inflammatory and anti-tumour function of macrophages (). The exact molecular mechanisms through which talazoparib increased both terminal differentiation and inflammation in keratinocytes is not yet clarified. In this regard, it may be important that we found a marked elevation in the expression of the stress-responsive transcription factor activating transcription factor 3 (ATF3) in talazoparib-treated keratinocytes (). ATF3, depending on context, can either positively or negatively regulate various signalling pathways involved in apoptosis and inflammation (). Mitochondrial ROS-induced ATF3 has been associated with the induction of caspase-3-mediated apoptosis and pro-inflammatory response (; ; ). We assume that higher ROS production in talazoparib-treated keratinocytes caused the upregulation of ATF3, and consequently, the activation of caspase-mediated apoptosis and induction of inflammatory gene expression. Ultimately, higher apoptotic rate led to better terminal differentiation of keratinocytes, which, at least partly, could explain the amelioration of IMQ-induced symptoms in mice. The pro-inflammatory response observed upon talazoparib treatment calls into question the overall beneficial effect of talazoparib in the IMQ-induced psoriasis model. However, the afore-presented mode of action of talazoparib is very similar to what was described in the case of the commonly used anti-psoriatic topical drug dithranol (anthralin). That is, dithranol was shown to act by inducing mitochondria-driven apoptotic pathways (; ; ), while also producing skin inflammation, due to the generation of ROS (; ).

Taken together, this study raises the notion that PARP inhibitors may have an anti-psoriatic effect, but several questions remain unanswered. First, from a translational point of view, it may be a limitation to our study that we used a co-treatment approach with PARP inhibitors and IMQ, through which talazoparib inhibited the full development of psoriatic symptoms, but that does not answer the question if PARP inhibitors could be effective in alleviating an already developed psoriasis, which is when treatment of the disease is typically initiated. We used this approach mainly because one of our aims with this study was to compare the application of PARP inhibitors in mice with the application of PARP1 −/− and PARP2 −/− mice that we used in our previous studies in the IMQ model. This approach may more closely mimic the potential preventive effects of PARP inhibitors on psoriasis flares and on the development of more serious symptoms.

Second, it has to be stressed that in this work only keratinocyte-related effects were studied, despite the fact that talazoparib was administered in i. p. injection in mice. Psoriasis is considered primarily an immune-mediated disease. Since PARP1 and PARP2 regulate various aspects of innate and adaptive immune responses (; ), the skin phenotype we have seen in the psoriasis model in mice upon talazoparib treatment probably involves both immune-modulatory and the hereby presented keratinocyte-specific effects of talazoparib. How PARP inhibition affects immune responses in psoriatic conditions has to be determined in further studies in order to fully evaluate the potential of PARP inhibitor repurposing in psoriasis.

title: Inactivation of cofilin-1 in Mcpt5-Cre-nf-Cfl1fl/fl mice prevents the formation of connective tissue mast cells without affecting basophils: a new tool to investigate the specific role of CTMCs in disease.
abstract: Actin-binding proteins play a critical role in regulating the dynamic rearrangement of the actin cytoskeleton, which is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis and facilitating various processes in eukaryotic cells. Cofilin-1 (Cfl1), an actin-binding protein, promotes the severing and depolymerization of actin filaments. To investigate the function of Cfl1 in mast cells, we generated Mcpt5-Cre-nf-Cfl1 fl/fl knock-in mice, expressing a non-functional form of Cfl1 (nf-Cfl1) instead of wildtype Cfl1 under the control of the connective tissue mast cell (CTMC)-specific promoter mast cell protease 5 (Mcpt5). Expression of nf-Cfl1 resulted in the complete absence of CTMCs. Notably, normal numbers of basophils were observed, in contrast to other mast cell-deficient mice. Interestingly, an inducible knock-in of nf-Cfl1 in mature mast cells did not affect the survival of mature mast cells. The Mcpt5-Cre-nf-Cfl1 fl/fl mice lacking CTMCs showed impaired induction of systemic anaphylaxis. However, they remained fully susceptible to 1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene-induced contact hypersensitivity and imiquimod-induced psoriasis-like dermatitis. In addition, clearance of vaccinia virus skin infection was unaltered. Thus, this study demonstrates that CTMCs are not essential in these inflammatory skin diseases. Deviating results in some other mast cell-deficient models suggest that the concomitant lack of basophils or residual CTMCs in these mouse models influence disease outcome. Taken together, the complete absence of CTMCs and the preserved presence of basophils in Mcpt5-Cre-nf-Cfl1 fl/fl mice establishes this model as a valuable tool for studying the specific role of CTMCs in different diseases.
