sections.results:
We have previously reported that autonomous activation of IL-17R signaling mediated by increased SHP2 expression sustains inflammation and nullifies anti-IL-17A efficacy . However, despite the upregulation of SHP2 in skin samples of psoriatic patients, they do exhibit a positive response to anti-IL-17 therapies. Psoriasis is characterized by persistent inflammation and aberrant keratinocyte hyperproliferation, supported by gene analysis showing enrichment in the cell cycle and IL-17 signaling pathways (Supplementary Fig. ). Interestingly, our study demonstrated that SHP2 overexpression in keratinocytes mainly contributed to the abundance of chemokines, rather than the key pathological change of sustained cell hyperproliferation and migration (Supplementary Fig. ). A clinical study further identified increased expression of genes related to cell cycle and keratinocyte function in individuals with weak response to immunomodulatory agents for inflammatory skin diseases . Based on these findings, we propose that the IL-17A pathway in psoriatic keratinocytes may carry a distinct pattern for the pathogenesis of psoriasis.

To unravel this, we analyzed microarray data from skin biopsies of patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis. KEGG pathway analysis revealed that genes up-regulated in psoriatic lesions but failed to revert following etanercept treatment, a biologic TNF inhibitor approved for the treatment of moderate to severe plaque psoriasis , , were enriched in IL-17 pathway (Supplementary Fig. ). Four IL-17RA-binding molecules were chosen from the related genes, following a comparison with a published molecular database (Supplementary Fig. ). Among these four genes, only KLK8 , encoding kallikrein related peptidase 8 (KLK8), was identified as a skin-specific molecule . We confirmed that KLK8 was primarily expressed in human and mouse skin tissues, with nearly exclusive expression in skin keratinocytes (Supplementary Fig. ). Protein docking predictions revealed the binding of KLK8 to the transmembrane region of IL-17RA (Supplementary Fig. ). It interacted with IL-17RA in HEK293T cells exogenously transfected with Flag-IL-17RA and Myc-KLK8 (Supplementary Fig. ). More importantly, the expression of KLK8 was significantly increased in keratinocytes of skin tissues from psoriasis patients (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ) and imiquimod-induced psoriatic mice (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ), and positively correlated with the PASI score in etanercept-non-responding psoriasis patients (Supplementary Fig. ). In responsive patients, KLK8 expression was significantly reduced after treatment to levels comparable to normal skin, whereas in non-responding patients, it only partially decreased and remained significantly higher than in normal skin (Supplementary Fig. ). We then stimulated HaCaT cells with IL-17A and observed a time-dependent increase in both gene and protein levels of KLK8 (Supplementary Fig. ). In contrast, other inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-6, IL-17E, and IFN-γ) had minimal impact on KLK8 expression, except for a mild increase observed with TNF (Supplementary Fig. ). Moreover, anti-IL-17A antibody GR1501 specifically suppressed IL-17A-induced KLK8 upregulation, whereas etanercept did not inhibit TNF-induced KLK8 expression (Supplementary Fig. ). Similarly, both secukinumab and anti-mIL-17A antibody greatly inhibited KLK8 expression in the skin of psoriatic patients and mice, respectively (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). These findings may explain why anti-IL-17 antibodies are more effective than anti-TNF antibodies in the clinical treatment of psoriasis and highlight the specific induction of KLK8 by IL-17A in keratinocytes, suggesting its unique role in psoriasis.

To further investigate the role of KLK8 in psoriatic keratinocytes, we preformed classification of keratinocytes in psoriasis patients based on their levels of KLK8 expression, resulting in the identification of two distinct populations: a population with low KLK8 expression ( KLK8 low) and a population with high KLK8 expression (Fig. ). Further analysis using cellular pathway enrichment revealed that the KLK8 high population was primarily associated with cell cycle regulation, in contrast to the KLK8 low population (Fig. ). In vitro experiments confirmed that KLK8 knockdown in HaCaT cells significantly inhibited IL-17A-induced proliferation and migration (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ), but did not affect the expression of chemokines, cytokines and antimicrobial peptides downstream of the classical IL-17 pathway (Fig. ), while overexpression increased the percentage of cells in the S and G2M phases (Supplementary Fig. ). Subsequently, we topically applied gel emulsifier containing si- Klk8 to the back of imiquimod-induced psoriasis mice and found that treatment with si- Klk8 significantly suppressed psoriasis progression (Supplementary Fig. ). To specifically silence KLK8 in skin keratinocytes, we utilized the adeno-associated virus (AAV)-promoter of Krt14 -sh Klk8 (Supplementary Fig. ). This targeted knockdown led to notable reductions in clinical scores and epidermis thickness, while also inhibiting inflammation, tissue destruction, and the expression of proliferation-related molecules (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). However, it did not reduce the expression of pro-inflammatory factors downstream of the classical IL-17A signaling pathway in the epidermal layer (Supplementary Fig. ), which was consistent with our in vitro findings in Fig. . These results suggest that KLK8 regulates psoriasis progression predominantly by orchestrating IL-17A-mediated proliferation and migration of keratinocytes, independent of the classical downstream chemokines production. Therefore, despite the upregulation of classical chemokines in psoriasis, inhibiting KLK8 expression with anti-IL-17A antibodies successfully attenuates the hyperactivation of keratinocytes.

To further elucidate the regulatory mechanisms of KLK8 on IL-17A-stimulated keratinocytes, we analyzed single-cell RNA sequencing data (scRNA-seq) from psoriasis patients and IMQ-induced psoriatic mice. Our analysis revealed the enrichment of the HIF-1 signaling pathway and glycolysis in psoriatic keratinocytes (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). HIF1A and enzymes related to the glycolytic pathway ( LDHA , PGK1 , ALDOA , HK2 , and TPI1 ) were significantly elevated in skin tissues of psoriasis patients and mice, whereas HIF1A’s inhibitor HIF1AN showed marked downregulation (Supplementary Fig. ). We then performed high-throughput metabolomics on the culture medium of IL-17A-stimulated HaCaT cells after KLK8 knockdown. Notably, we found that IL-17A induced lactate production in cells to a greater extent compared to other metabolites, and this effect was significantly suppressed by KLK8 knockdown (Fig. , and Supplementary Fig. ). Besides, IL-17A increased expression of the lactate transporter MCT1 (encoded by SLC16A1 ) (Fig. ), which was suppressed by anti-IL-17A antibody GR1501 (Supplementary Fig. ). Consistent with these findings, elevated expression of MCT1 was observed in psoriatic patients (Fig. ) and mice (Fig. ), particularly in psoriatic keratinocytes (Supplementary Fig. ). Furthermore, SLC16A1 expression correlated with PASI scores in patients who did not respond to etanercept treatment (Supplementary Fig. ). Moreover, specific knockdown of KLK8 in keratinocytes almost completely suppressed lactate levels in skin tissues and serum of IMQ-induced psoriasis mice (Fig. ), suggesting that keratinocytes are likely the main contributors to lactate production through the activity of KLK8. This knockdown also reduced the expression of key enzymes in the glycolytic pathway in IL-17A-treated HaCaT cells and skin tissues of IMQ-induced psoriasis mice (Fig. ). These observations were further supported by the pronounced correlation between KLK8 and these genes in psoriasis patients (Fig. ). These findings underline the critical involvement of KLK8 in regulating glucose metabolism and lactate transport specifically within psoriatic keratinocytes.

In addition, the production of lactate induced by IL-17A was also reduced after knockdown of SLC16A1 or inhibition of MCT1 with the inhibitor AZD3965 in HaCcaT cells (Supplementary Fig. ). Meanwhile, si- SLC16A1 or AZD3965 significantly blocked IL-17A-induced keratinocyte proliferation and migration (Supplementary Fig. ). Treatment with AZD3965 also displayed significant inhibition against imiquimod-induced psoriasis, including reductions in skin thickness, lactate levels, and inflammatory factor production in the skin lesions (Supplementary Fig. ).

Clinical data indicate a frequent association between psoriasis and metabolic disorders, including an increased susceptibility to obesity and diabetes mellitus – . Patients with metabolic syndrome (MetS) tend to have a reduced response to anti-IL-17A antibodies and have been reported to have significantly elevated levels of lactate in skin tissue and serum ,, , suggesting the potential involvement of lactate overproduction from multiple sources within the disease microenvironment. To replicate this, we established a psoriasis model using type 2 diabetic ob/ob mice. Compared to wild-type mice, IMQ-induced ob/ob mice exhibited increased body weight and blood glucose level (Fig. ). These mice displayed more severe dorsal skin lesions and increased skin thickness, along with a significantly diminished response to anti-mIL-17A antibody administration (Fig. ). In psoriatic wildtype mice, elevated lactate levels in serum and epidermis skin tissues (Fig. ), as well as increased skin expression of MCT1 and KLK8 (Fig. ), were observed, which were reduced after anti-mIL-17A antibody treatment. These elevations were particularly pronounced in ob/ob psoriatic mice, but the suppressive effect of anti-mIL-17A antibody was almost attenuated (Fig. ). In addition, we examined single-cell data obtained from the forearm skin of normal individuals and patients with diabetes. We observed that KLK8 exhibited significantly higher expression levels in keratinocytes from the diabetic forearm skin (Fig. , j), suggesting that KLK8 and its regulated lactate have the potential to influence the efficacy of anti-IL-17A therapies for treating psoriasis, particularly in individuals with comorbid metabolic diseases.

To further explore how the environmental lactate acts on psoriatic keratinocytes, we supplemented lactate to the cell culture medium in vitro. The addition of lactate increased its content in both the cytoplasm and culture medium (Fig. ), which almost completely antagonized the inhibitory effects of anti-IL-17A antibody on keratinocyte proliferation (Fig. ), migration (Fig. ), and expression of inflammatory factors (Fig. ). Next, we administered lactate to imiquimod-induced psoriasis mice. Interestingly, we found that both subcutaneous and intradermal supplementation of lactate exacerbated skin inflammation (Fig. , and Supplementary Fig. ) and increased epidermal thickness (Fig. ), with comparable efficacy between the two administration routes. Lactate levels were significantly elevated in the epidermis and dermis of psoriatic mice, particularly in the epidermis, with subcutaneous and intradermal injections further increasing lactate accumulation, the latter resulting in slightly higher lactate levels in the epidermis compared to subcutaneous injection (Fig. ). Notably, the additional administration of lactate reduced the efficacy of anti-mIL-17A antibody in ameliorating psoriasis (Fig. ), as evidenced by increased epidermal thickness (Fig. ), elevated lactate levels (Fig. ), and enhanced expression of inflammatory and proliferative genes in the skin tissues (Supplementary Fig. ). Taken together, these findings demonstrate that excess lactate produced from multiple cellular sources within skin microenvironment determines disease progression and resistance against anti-IL-17A therapy.

Given that elevated environmental lactate levels compromise the therapeutic efficacy of anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibodies, we explored whether inhibiting lactate transport could restore efficacy. The increased cytoplasmic lactate content was significantly attenuated by treatment with the MCT1 inhibitor AZD3965 (Fig. ), indicating that it inhibited the transport of lactate into cells under high extracellular lactate conditions. We then combined AZD3965 with anti-mIL-17A antibody treatment in lactate-administered psoriasis mice. The impaired efficacy of anti-mIL-17A antibody caused by elevated lactate levels was significantly improved by AZD3965 administration, regardless of whether lactate was administered via intradermal (Fig. ) or subcutaneous injection (Supplementary Fig. ). This suggests promising potential for the clinical application of MCT1 inhibitors in treating psoriasis patients with obesity or abnormal lactate metabolism.

The functional significance of lactate as a metabolic waste product remains overlooked until the discovery of histone lactylation, a newly identified epigenetic modification derived from lactate , . Considering that KLK8 promotes lactate production and transport, we set out to determine whether the accumulation of lactate induces lactylation in psoriatic keratinocytes. The expression of pan-lactylation was significantly increased in skin lesions of imiquimod-induced mice (Supplementary Fig. ) and IL-17A-induced HaCaT cells (Supplementary Fig. ). In addition, lactate levels were significantly correlated with IL-17A but not with CXCL1 in skin tissues (Fig. ). The correlation between pan-lactylation and IL-17A was also confirmed (Fig. ). The observed augmentation of pan-lactylation in psoriatic mice, particularly near the 17 kDa position, suggests a potential association with histones. Using an alkylated lactate probe for click chemistry (Fig. ), we observed a notable upregulation of histone H4 lactylation in HaCaT cells (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). Notably, only the lactylation of histone H4 lysine 12 (H4K12la) was significantly up-regulated in IL-17A-stimulated HaCaT cells and skin epidermal keratinocytes of imiquimod-induced psoriatic mice (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). The upregulation of H4K12la expression was then confirmed in human psoriatic skin tissues (Fig. ) and IL-17A-stimulated keratinocytes (Supplementary Fig. ). As expected, the silencing of KLK8 effectively suppressed the IL-17A-induced increases in H4K12la levels in human primary keratinocytes and HaCaT cells (Fig. , k and Supplementary Fig. ). In addition, both in vitro and in vivo, treatment with anti-IL-17A antibody resulted in a reduction of H4K12la expression, whereas the addition of lactate counteracted this inhibitory effect (Fig. ). Similarly, the H4K12la expression in mice with psoriasis was significantly inhibited when treated with the MCT1 inhibitor AZD3965 (Fig. ). Gel encapsulating si- Klk8 and intradermal injection of a keratinocyte-specific Klk8 knockdown adenovirus also effectively suppressed H4K12la expression (Fig. ). These results suggest that H4K12la induced by IL-17A is dependent on KLK8, which may be a key event in the keratinocyte activation and psoriasis progression.

Using H4K12la-targeted CUT&Tag-seq analysis (Supplementary Fig. ), we identified three distinct clusters of H4K12la-binding peaks in IL-17A-stimulated HaCaT cells (Fig. ). Approximately 42% of higher H4K12la-binding peaks were located in the promoter region (Fig. ). Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that the genes with enhanced H4K12la after IL-17A stimulation were primarily related to cell cycle regulation (Fig. ). Next, we performed multi-omics analyses by combining data from lesional skin samples of psoriasis patients, ear skins from IMQ-treated mice, and H4K12la-targeted CUT&Tag-seq. Thirteen genes displayed elevated mRNA levels in psoriasis and enhanced H4K12la binding to their promoter regions after IL-17A stimulation (Fig. ). Among these genes, FOXM1 , CCNB2 and CDC25C , which play crucial roles in cell cycle regulation, were identified (Fig. ). Increased expression of these three genes was observed in skin lesions from psoriasis patients (Fig. ) and mice (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ), as well as IL-17A-stimulated HaCaT cells (Supplementary Fig. d). Furthermore, the analysis of scRNA-seq data showed that the upregulation of FOXM1 , CCNB2 and CDC25C was predominantly observed in keratinocytes (Supplementary Fig. ). Clinical trials also indicated a significant decrease in FOXM1 , CCNB2 and CDC25C expression in patients treated with anti-IL-17RA antibody brodalumab (Supplementary Fig. ). Knockdown of KLK8 in HaCaT cells (Fig. ) and human primary keratinocytes (Fig. ), as well as knockdown of SLC16A1 (Supplementary Fig. ) or treatment with AZD3965 (Supplementary Fig. ) to inhibit H4K12la levels, significantly suppressed the IL-17A-induced increase in FOXM1 , CCNB2 and CDC25C expression. This reduction was also observed in psoriatic mice applied with AAV- Krt14 -sh Klk8 or si- Klk8 (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). Moreover, there was a significant correlation between KLK8 and these three genes, as well as between SLC16A1 and these three genes, observed in both normal and psoriatic individuals (Supplementary Fig. ). In contrast, the addition of lactate, which enhanced H4K12la levels, not only promoted the expression of FOXM1 , CCNB2 , and CDC25C in vitro and in vivo, but also blocked the inhibitory effect of anti-IL-17A antibodies on these three genes (Fig. ).

Furthermore, apart from cell cycle-related genes, significantly increased H4K12la peaks were observed in the promoter regions of multiple inflammatory factors and their receptors, including IL17RA (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). The upregulation of IL-17RA expression was confirmed in IL-17A-stimulated keratinocytes (Supplementary Fig. ) and at the site of skin lesions in human psoriatic skin tissues (Supplementary Fig. ). In addition, in the promoter region of KLK8 , we also found and verified a remarkable augmentation of H4K12la peak in the IL-17A group (Fig. ). Chromatin precipitation experiments demonstrated that knockdown of KLK8 resulted in reduced H4K12la binding within the promoter region (Fig. ). Considering the dependence of H4K12la on KLK8, the interaction between KLK8 and IL-17RA, as well as the promotion of IL17RA and KLK8 expression by H4K12la modification, there may exist a positive feedback loop involving IL-17RA, KLK8, and H4K12la. This feedback loop drives IL-17A-mediated accelerated keratinocyte division throughout the cell cycle, sustaining excessive keratinocyte proliferation and activation, and continuously impelling the progression of psoriasis.

We used bioinformatics approaches to investigate several candidate acetyltransferases , including EP300 , KAT2A and KAT8 , which have been proposed as “writers” of histone lactylation – . Among these, only HAT1 was significantly up-regulated in skin tissues of both psoriasis patients and imiquimod-induced psoriasis mice (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). Further analysis revealed that HAT1 exhibited higher expression levels in the skin compared to other acetyltransferases, primarily in the psoriatic keratinocytes (Supplementary Fig. ). Our results demonstrated a significant increase in the expression of both HAT1 mRNA (Fig. ) and protein (Fig. ) in dorsal skin tissue of imiquimod-induced psoriasis mice.

While HAT1 is known to catalyze histone acetylation – , there is currently no report suggesting its involvement in lactylation. Molecular docking analysis indicated that lactyl-coenzyme A can interact with lysine 12 of histone H4, involving glutamate at position 187 of HAT1 (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). We next confirmed the interaction between HAT1 and H4K12la (Fig. , f and Supplementary Fig. ). Furthermore, IL-17A greatly induced upregulation of HAT1 but not KAT2A , KAT8 and EP300 (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). The HAT1 expression was significantly decreased after treatment with secukinumab and brodalumab in the clinic (Fig. ). Knockdown of HAT1 led to a remarkable reduction in IL-17A-induced H4K12la in human primary keratinocytes and HaCaT cells (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ), but not H4K12ac (Supplementary Fig. ). Next, we found that HAT1 expression was upregulated in FOXM1 + , CCNB2 + , and CDC25C + keratinocytes populations from psoriasis patients sc-RNA data (Supplementary Fig. ) compared to other histone acetyltransferases, and showed a significant correlation between FOXM1 , CCNB2 and CDC25C in psoriasis patients skin tissues (Supplementary Fig. ). Moreover, the knockdown of HAT1 significantly inhibited IL-17A-induced proliferation and migration (Fig. , m) and resulted in decreased expression of H4K12la-targeted genes FOXM1 , CCNB2 and CDC25C both in HaCaT cells and human primary keratinocytes (Fig. ).

In psoriasis mice, the binding of HAT1 to H4K12la in skin tissues was higher compared to control mice (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). Similarly, the co-localization of HAT1 and H4K12la also showed an elevation in skin tissues of psoriasis patients (Fig. ), suggesting the specific role of HAT1 as a writer of H4K12la in keratinocytes. Moreover, we also silenced HAT1 in an imiquimod-induced psoriasis model. Treatment with si- Hat1 significantly attenuated the severity of psoriasis, as evidenced by diminished epidermal thickness and attenuated inflammation and tissue destruction (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). Moreover, it led to a reduction in levels of lactate (Fig. ), H4K12la and KLK8 (Fig. ), as well as the expression of cell cycle genes regulated by H4K12la (Fig. ). Taken together, HAT1 expression and its ability to write lactylation into H4K12 is very important for keratinocyte hyperactivation in the pathogenesis of psoriasis.

Given the finding that IL-17A-induced H4K12la drives hyperactivation of keratinocytes, we sought to target this mechanism using rational pharmacological approaches. To this end, we focused on inhibiting lactate production by oxamate (an LDHA inhibitor) and 2-DG (a HK2 inhibitor). Treatment with oxamate or 2-DG significantly reduced IL-17A-induced H4K12la expression (Supplementary Fig. ) and effectively inhibited the proliferation and migration of IL-17A-stimulated HaCaT cells (Supplementary Fig. ). Furthermore, we examined the expression of genes regulated by H4K12la and found that both oxamate and 2-DG significantly reduced the expression of cell cycle-related genes, including FOXM1 , CCNB2 and CDC25C (Fig. ).

In the imiquimod-induced mouse model of psoriasis, treatment with oxamate and 2-DG exhibited significant therapeutic effects, including reduced skin inflammation, PASI score, skin epidermal layer thickness, and lactate content in skin tissues (Fig. ). Treatment with these inhibitors also downregulated H4K12la expression and inhibited PCNA expression associated with cell proliferation (Fig. ). In addition, they inhibited the expression of inflammation- ( Il17a , Il23a , Tnf and Il6 ) and proliferation-related ( Pcna , Mki67 , Foxm1 , Ccnb2 , and Cdc25c ) genes (Fig. ). Furthermore, oxamate and 2-DG treatment led to a significant reduction in the expression of Hat1 (Supplementary Fig. ) and Slc16a1 (Supplementary Fig. ). Tissue immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated that drug treatment suppressed the expression and co-localization of H4K12la and HAT1 (Supplementary Fig. ). Co-administration of anti-mIL-17A antibody (30 μg/mouse) and 2-DG (0.3 g/kg) effectively suppressed psoriasis development, showing stronger efficacy in reducing PASI score, skin thickening, and H4K12la expression than either treatment alone (Fig. and Supplementary Fig. ). These results suggest that targeting IL-17A-induced H4K12la in keratinocytes could be a promising strategy for alleviating psoriasis (Fig. ).
sections.discussion:
IL-17 signaling is known to be deeply involved in the pathogenesis of various autoimmune diseases. However, the exact role of IL-17 signaling in the different manifestations of different diseases remains unknown. In this study, we focused on unraveling the detailed mechanism of IL-17A signaling in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. Our results identified KLK8 as a keratinocyte-specific protein that mediated IL-17A-driven keratinocyte hyperactivation, independently of IL-17A-induced canonical chemokine production. This non-canonical IL-17A signaling pathway involved IL-17RA/KLK8 interaction, lactate production, H4K12la catalyzed by HAT1, and subsequent upregulation of cell cycle gene expressions. We provide insights into the distinction between IL-17A-induced pro-inflammatory factor production and keratinocyte hyperproliferation in psoriasis, highlighting the role of KLK8-mediated regulation of IL-17A signaling on keratinocyte hyperproliferation. We further characterized H4K12la as a key mechanism of the non-canonical IL-17A signaling pathway, contributing to the main pathology of psoriasis by inducing the upregulation of various cell cycle-related genes (e.g., FOXM1 , CCNB2 , and CDC25C ), resulting in accelerated proliferation of psoriatic keratinocytes. In addition, H4K12la was found to increase the expression of both KLK8 and IL-17RA in IL-17A-stimulated keratinocytes. Thus, our study uncovers the existence of a positive feedback loop in non-canonical IL-17A signaling that drives psoriasis progression through IL-17RA/KLK8/H4K12la/cell cycle genes.

Histone lactylation is a tightly regulated process, yet the specific “writers” responsible for distinct lysine modifications and their molecular mechanisms remain largely uncharacterized. We found that only H4K12la was significantly upregulated in skin epidermal keratinocytes from imiquimod-induced psoriatic mice and IL-17A-stimulated HaCaT cells. This selective induction of H4K12la by IL-17A may involve multiple interrelated factors. First, IL-17A selectively upregulated HAT1 but not EP300 or KAT2A (reported to be associated with H3K18 modifications , ), implying that enzyme availability could dictate site specificity. Prior studies indicate that acyltransferases form distinct complexes which exhibit substrate preferences for specific acylation types , . By analogy, HAT1 could interact with other proteins, thereby preferentially lactylating H4K12, but this hypothesis requires experimental validation. In addition, acetylation and lactylation both target lysine ε-amine groups, raising the possibility of competition . For example, the pre-existing modification of H3K9ac could antagonize lactylation, potentially influencing the outcome of histone modification at the same site. Future studies, including both biochemical and structural analyses of HAT1 and its substrate preferences, will be critical to uncover the precise mechanism by which IL-17A drives selective lactylation of H4K12.

On the other hand, lactate is a well-known metabolic intermediate involved in the regulation of multiple cellular functions. The lactate secrets into the local skin microenvironment could influence the functions of other cell types, such as immune cells and fibroblasts, thereby synergistically regulating local inflammation. Recent studies suggest that lactate can modulate immune cell functions. For example, highly proliferative epidermal cells produce large amounts of lactate, which affects the activity of γ δ T T cells and promotes the production of IL-17A by γ δ T cells, forming a crosstalk between keratinocytes and immune cells . Accumulated lactate can also be taken up by CD4 + T cells in inflamed tissue, reshaping their effector phenotype to enhance IL-17 production . Besides, epidermal-derived lactate mediates aseptic skin inflammation by modulating macrophage function . In addition to keratinocytes, other cell types, such as immune cells and fibroblasts, also contribute to the alteration of local lactate dynamics. Thus, lactate from multiple cellular sources in the skin microenvironment not only fuels keratinocyte dysfunction but also broadly primes immune cells or other cells, creating a feedforward cycle that exacerbates psoriatic pathology.

We then found that the administration of lactate exacerbated imiquimod-induced skin inflammation, which was also observed in ob/ob mice with elevated serum lactate levels. MCT1, one of the key transporters of lactate, is reported to exhibit typically constitutive expression but can be inducible under specific pathological conditions, exhibiting bidirectional lactate transport dictated by concentration gradients ,– . Our experiments showed that in the context of psoriasis, IL-17A stimulated keratinocytes to enhance lactate production, which fueled intracellular H4K12 lactylation. Simultaneously, IL-17A upregulated MCT1 expression to extrude excess lactate into the extracellular microenvironment, preventing intracellular acidification. The secreted lactate in the skin microenvironment may further modulate neighboring immune cells and fibroblasts, thereby indirectly amplifying local inflammation. Conversely, MCT1 facilitated lactate import under high extracellular lactate conditions, demonstrated by increased intracellular lactate levels during incubation with lactate and reduced levels with AZD3965 treatment. In psoriasis patients with comorbid metabolic disorders such as diabetes, systemic lactate elevation is likely to contribute to localized lactate accumulation in keratinocytes via MCT1 import, potentially exacerbating intracellular lactylation and inflammation. Thus, MCT1’s function in psoriasis is context-dependent: it exports lactate under typical psoriasis conditions but shifts to importing lactate in metabolic syndrome-associated psoriasis, worsening disease severity.

In addition, the excessive accumulation of lactate in the skin microenvironment reduced the effectiveness of monoclonal antibody targeting IL-17A. Indeed, clinical variations in the response to biologics for psoriasis treatment are often observed in patients with comorbid metabolic disorders like obesity, diabetes, and hypertension – . These patients usually show higher skin and blood lactate levels , , and tend to exhibit reduced efficacy when treated with biologic agents with unknown reason . Therefore, our study highlights the crucial role of H4K12la in psoriasis pathogenesis with bidirectional effects. On one hand, H4K12la acts as the “driving force” to cause the hyperactivation of keratinocytes in an IL-17A-dependent manner, making the cells sensitive to the anti-IL-17A therapy. On the other hand, the accelerated H4K12la driven by elevated environmental lactate from multiple cellular sources impairs the therapeutic efficacy of anti-IL-17A therapy.

Finally, the present study introduced a therapeutic approach targeting lactate and H4K12la. We found that the combination treatment with an anti-IL-17A antibody and the lactate transport inhibitor AZD3965 significantly alleviated severe skin inflammation associated with elevated lactate levels, thereby reversing the diminished efficacy of the anti-IL-17A antibody. In addition, the glycolysis inhibitor 2-DG also restored the effectiveness of the anti-IL-17A antibody, even when the dose of the antibody was reduced. These findings provide insights into why higher doses are often needed when administering monoclonal antibodies to overweight psoriasis patients.

In conclusion, our study highlights the crucial role of keratinocyte-specific KLK8 and lactylation in driving psoriasis progression through IL-17A-dependent but non-canonical IL-17A signaling. The KLK8 and lactylation-based feedback loop not only contributes to psoriasis progression but also determines the therapeutic efficacy of anti-IL-17A therapy, particularly in individuals with comorbid metabolic diseases influenced by lactate levels. These findings shed light on the complicated pathology of psoriasis and offer potential therapeutic options for psoriasis patients with metabolic syndrome and other IL-17A-associated diseases that are resistant to anti-IL-17A therapies.
sections.methods:
Female C57BL/6 mice (Strain NO. N000013) and male ob/ob mice (Strain NO. T001461) were purchased from GemPharmatech. All experimental and control animals were co-housed and bred under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions. All experimental mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation. All animal experiments were carried out according to the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Academies Press, 2011) and were approved by the Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee of Nanjing University (No. IACUC-2407012).

8–10 weeks male ob/ob mice and 6–8 weeks female C57BL/6 mice were shaved on backs in advance. To induce psoriasis-like symptoms in the skin of mice, the shaved skin areas were treated for 4-5 consecutive days using 62.5 mg cream containing 5% imiquimod (Aldara, 3 M Health Care Limited, UK).

The PASI scoring criteria are as previously described ,, . For the back skin, disease severity was assessed every day with a scoring system considering scaling, erythema, and skin thickness, similar to the human Psoriasis Area and Severity Index, but not taking the area into account because it is defined by the experimenter. A cumulative score was generated from the three mentioned parameters. The PAIS scores range from 0 to 4 points, 0 points: none; 1 point: mild; 2 Points: moderate; 3 points: obvious; 4 points: extremely obvious. In order to ensure the objectivity of the scoring results, the whole scoring process adopted the method of averaging the scores after scoring separately by two different experimenters.

For cytokines stimulation, HaCaT cells were stimulated with 50 ng/mL IL-17A (C021, Novoprotein, China), 10 ng/mL TNF (300-01 A, PeproTech, USA), 10 ng/mL IL-6 (200-06, PeproTech, USA), 50 ng/mL IL-17E (200-24, PeproTech, USA), or 10 ng/mL IFN- γ (300-02, PeproTech, USA) for 24 h.

For humanized monoclonal antibody treatment, HaCaT cells were stimulated with 10 ng/mL TNF or 50 ng/mL IL-17A for 2 h before treatment with 20 μg/mL etanercept (Pfizer Inc., USA) or 10 μg/mL GR1501 (Genrix Biopharmaceutical Company, China) for 24 h.

For drug treatment, the anti-mIL-17A monoclonal antibody (A2120, Selleck Chemicals, USA) was administered by subcutaneous injection (s.c.) every three days at a dose of 50 μg per mouse or a low dose of 30 μg per mouse. AZD3965 (HY-12750, MedChem Express, USA) is administered intraperitoneally at a dose of 2.5 mg/kg daily. 2-DG (HY-13966, MedChem Express, USA) is administered intraperitoneally at a dose of 0.5 g/kg daily or a low dose of 0.3 g/kg daily. Oxamate (S123221, Aladdin, China) is administered intraperitoneally at a dose of 0.5 g/kg daily. Nala (E011079, Energy Chemical, China) is a daily subcutaneous injection (s.c.) or intradermal injection (i.d.) of 25 μL of 0.5 mg/mL. All drugs were administered from the day before imiquimod treatment until the mice were sacrificed. The body weight of mice was measured, and skin condition was scored before daily administration.

For siRNA topical treatment, siRNA duplexes targeting mouse Klk8 (si- Klk8 ) and Hat1 (si- Hat1 ), or nonsense mouse control siRNA (si-Ctrl) were designed and applied as reported . Briefly, duplexes were suspended in a 3:5 mixture of cream emulsifier (Johnson’s Baby Lotion; Johnson & Johnson, USA) and water at a final concentration of 12.5 μM. The shaved area was pretreated with 30 μL si- Klk8 and si- Hat1 , or si-Ctrl for one day and then once a day for four consecutive days. One hour following siRNA treatment, imiquimod cream was applied. The sequences of si-RNA were presented in Supplementary Table . All sequences of RNAi were purchased from General Biosystems (China).

For AAV viruses specifically targeting keratinocytes, the viruses were purchased from HANBIO at a titer of 1 × 10 12 , and the method was as previously described . Briefly, the animals were injected intradermally with an insulin needle at a distance of 0.5 cm from a spot, and a total of 9 spots were injected, each spot 10 μL. As the viral vector was tagged with zsgreen, the animals were anaesthetized after 4 weeks, and in vivo fluorescence imaging was performed to observe viral amplification and skin tissue was collected for immunoblotting to verify knockdown of protein levels. If strong fluorescence was observed and the target protein was clearly knocked down, experiments could be carried out according to the experimental requirements.

For cell lines, HaCaT cells (SCSP-5091, National Collection of Authenticated Cell Cultures, China), HEK293T cells (SCSP-502, National Collection of Authenticated Cell Cultures, China), Hela cells (SCSP-504, National Collection of Authenticated Cell Cultures, China), NIH3T3 cells (SCSP-515, National Collection of Authenticated Cell Cultures, China) were cultured in DMEM (C3103-0500, Viva Cell, China) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (C04001-500, Viva Cell, China) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (C0222, Beyotime, China). All cells were cultured at 37 °C in a 5% (v/v) humidified CO 2 incubator (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA).

Primary human keratinocytes (CP-H113, Procell, China) were isolated from the foreskin and then cultured in Human keratinocyte serum-free complete medium (CM-H113, Procell, China) at 37 °C in a 5% (v/v) humidified CO 2 incubator.

All human studies were approved by the Ethics Institutional Review Board of West China Hospital, Sichuan University. Psoriatic patients were recruited by the Department of Dermatology and Venereology at West China Hospital under protocol 2019-R-513. All recruited volunteers provided written informed consent.

The isolation of mouse epidermal tissue was carried out by an enzymatic digestion method as described previously . Briefly, the same area of dorsal skin was clipped from normal and imiquimod-induced psoriasis mice, and the isolated skin was incubated dermis side down in dispase digestion buffer (CD4691, Coolaber, China) (2.0 U/mL) at 4 °C for 18 h. After being washed with PBS and lysed with lysis solution, the tissues were quantified to the same concentration. The lactate content of each skin layer was determined by using a lactate detection kit.

HaCaT, HEK293T and Hela cells were cultured overnight, and transfection was performed when the cell density reached 70%. For small interfering sequences, 10 μL of freshly mixed small interfering solution and 5 μL of transfection reagent (40802ES03, Yeasen, China) were added to serum-free medium, transfected, and cultured for 48 h. The sequences of si-RNA were presented in Supplementary Table . For plasmid transfection, 1 μg of plasmid mixed with 1 μL of transfection reagent and 100 μL of opti-MEM medium (11058021, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) was added to serum-free medium, transfected, and cultured for 24 h. Subsequently, the medium was changed to complete medium with stimulation and drug treatment as required.

The primary antibodies used in our study were as follows: anti-L-Lactyl Lysine Rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IF or IHC, PTM-1401RM, PTM, China), anti-Lactyl-Histone H3 (Lys9) Rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, PTM-1419RM, PTM, China), anti-Lactyl-Histone H3 (Lys14) Rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, PTM-1414RM, PTM, China), anti-L-Lactyl-Histone H3 (Lys18) Rabbit mAb-ChIP Grade (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IF, PTM-1427RM, PTM, China), anti-L-Lactyl-Histone H4 (Lys5) Rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IF, PTM-1407RM, PTM, China), anti-L-Lactyl-Histone H4 (Lys8) Rabbit pAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IF, PTM-1415RM, PTM, China), anti-L-Lactyl-Histone H4 (Lys12) Rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IF or IHC, PTM-1411RM, PTM, China), anti-L-Lactyl-Histone H4 (Lys16) Rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IF, PTM-1417 RM, PTM, China), anti-histone H3 rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, PTM-1001RM, PTM, China), anti-Histone H4 Rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, PTM-1015RM, PTM, China), anti-Histone H4 Rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, A19815, ABclonal, China), anti-HAT1 Mouse mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IF, PTM-5195, PTM, China), anti-KAT1/HAT1 Rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, A4423, ABclonal, China), anti-MCT1 Rabbit mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, PTM-6973, PTM, China), anti-MCT1 (H-1) (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IHC, sc-365501, Santa Cruz, USA), anti-CK14 Rabbit pAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IF, A24481, ABclonal, China), anti-Acetyl-Histone H4-K12 Rabbit pAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, A14227, ABclonal, China), anti-LDH-A Antibody (E-9) (1:1000 dilution for WB, sc-137243, Santa Cruz, USA), anti-IL-17R Antibody (G-9) (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IF, sc-376374, Santa Cruz, USA), anti-PCNA Antibody (F-2) (1:1000 dilution for WB, sc-25280, Santa Cruz, USA), anti-DYKDDDDK tag Polyclonal antibody (1:1000 dilution for WB, 20543-1-AP, Proteintech, USA), anti-KLK8 (1:1000 dilution for WB, 1:100 dilution for IF or IHC, 68247-1-Ig, Proteintech, USA), anti-GAPDH Monoclonal antibody (1:5000 dilution for WB, 60004-1-Ig, Proteintech, USA), anti-Myc-Tag (9B11) Mouse mAb (1:1000 dilution for WB, 2276, Cell Signaling Technology, USA), anti-beta-Actin Antibody (1:5000 dilution for WB, T0022, Affinity, USA), anti-beta-Tubulin Monoclonal Antibody (1:5000 dilution for WB, E-AB-20033, Elabscience, China).

Cells were collected and lysed with RIPA lysis (P0013K, Beyotime, China), and then quantified by the BCA kit (23227, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). SDS-PAGE was used for protein separation and then electrophoretically transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride membranes. The membranes were probed with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C and incubated with a horse radish peroxidase-coupled secondary antibody at room temperature for 1 h. Detection was performed using a LumiGLO chemiluminescent substrate system (Vazymes, China) and chemiluminometers (BioRad, USA).

Total RNA was extracted by RNAiso Plus (9109, Takara, Japan), and concentrations were measured with Nanodrop (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Reverse transcription was carried out according to the kit instructions (R323-01, Vazyme, China), and qPCR was performed using SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Q321-02, Vazyme, China) on CFX96 (Bio-Rad, USA). The sequences of PCR primer pairs were presented in Supplementary Table .

The lactate assay was carried out according to the instructions provided with the kit (A019-2-1, Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, China). Briefly, the sample obtained is diluted proportionally, the reagents are added sequentially according to the instructions, and the reaction is carried out in a water bath at 37 °C for 10 min. After 10 min, the termination solution is added. After mixing, the absorbance was measured at 530 nm. Distilled water was used as a blank control and 3 mM lactate solution was used as a standard.

HaCaT cells were pre-transfected with si- HAT1 or si-NC as a control. They were then inoculated into 12-well plates at 500/well. Three days after IL-17A induction, crystal violet staining was performed.

HeLa cells were pre-transfected with KLK8-Myc plasmid (Purchased from General Biosystems, China) or empty vector as a control group, and flow cytometry was performed to detect cell cycle changes after 24 h of IL-17A induction according to the instructions of the Cell Cycle Detection Kit (KGA9101-20, KeyGEN, China).

For sample preparation, HaCaT cells were stimulated with fresh medium containing 50 ng/mL IL-17A after transfection with si-NC and si- KLK8 for 24 h. The cell supernatants were collected after 24 h for metabolite detection. In brief, samples were thawed at 4 °C, and 100 μL of each sample was mixed with 10 μL isotope internal standards and 400 μL of cold methanol/acetonitrile solution (1:1, v/v), adequately vortexed, then ultrasounded for 30 min at low temperature, followed by incubation at 20 °C for 1 h. The mixture was centrifuged for 20 min (14000 rcf, 4 °C). The supernatant was dried in a vacuum centrifuge. For LC-MS analysis, the samples were re-dissolved in 100 μL acetonitrile/water (1:1, v/v) and adequately vortexed, and then centrifuged (14000 rcf, 4 °C, 15 min). The supernatants were collected for LC-MS/MS analysis.

For HPLC analysis, analyses were performed using a UHPLC (1290 Infinity LC, Agilent Technologies) coupled to a QTRAP (AB Sciex 6500 +). The mobile phase contained A = 50 mM CH3COONH4 in water + 1.2% NH4OH and B = 1% acetylacetone in ACN. The samples were in the automatic sampler at 4 °C, and the column temperatures were kept constant at 35 °C. The gradients were at a flow rate of 300 μL /min, a 2 μL aliquot of each sample was injected. The gradient was 70% B in 0–1 min, and then was reduced to 60% in 1–10 min, and then to 30% in 10–12 min, and kept for 12.1 15 min. Then the B was increased up to 70% in 15-15.1 min and kept for 15.1–22 min. The QC samples were used to test and evaluate the stability and repeatability of this system. At the same time, they served as the standard mixture of metabolites for correcting chromatographic retention times.

For MS/MS Analysis, in ESI negative modes, the conditions were set as follows: source temperature 450 °C, Ion Source Gas1 (Gas1): 45, Ion Source Gas2 (Gas2): 45, Curtain gas (CUR): 30, ionSapary Voltage Floating (ISVF) -4500 V; Adopt the MRM mode detection ion pair.

For data processing, the Multiquant software was used to extract chromatographic peak area and retention time. The standards’ correct retention time was used to identify the metabolites.

Probe synthesis and in vitro click chemistry experiments were performed as described previously . Briefly, probe-incubated HaCaT cells were harvested and lysed to obtain protein supernatants. Preconfigured click chemistry reaction solutions were then added for reaction. Immunoprecipitation with biotinylated magnetic beads was performed at the end of the reaction to obtain a sample of probe-labeled protein for SDS-PAGE gel electrophoresis, and finally, staining was performed by either Kormas Brilliant Blue or immunoblot, depending on the experimental needs.

CUT&Tag was performed with the Hyperactive In-Situ ChIP Library Prep Kit for Illumina (pG-Tn5) (TD901, Vazyme, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, HaCaT cells were collected with IL-17A-untreated and IL-17A-treated for 24 h, and then combined with beads coated with Concanavalin A. Subsequently, the cells were re-suspended in antibody buffer and incubated sequentially with primary and secondary antibodies against H4K12la. The samples were incubated with pA-Tn5 transposase. After transposon activation and labeling, DNA was isolated, amplified, and purified to construct libraries. Libraries for sequencing were constructed, and purification steps were performed using VAHTS DNA cleaning beads (N411, Vazyme, China). Sequences of qPCR primer pairs are shown in Supplementary Table .

For Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, mice were sacrificed on the fourth day, and dorsal skin was taken and fixed overnight in 4% paraformaldehyde before paraffin-embedded sections were stained for H&E.

For IHC, different primary and secondary antibodies (KIT-9710, MXB, China) are used for labeling and DAB stain development (DAB-0031, MXB, China), depending on the experimental requirements.

For cells, differently treated HaCaT cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 0.5 h at room temperature, followed by 0.5% Triton X-100 (T0010-100, Sun Shine Bio, China) for 15 min at room temperature. 5% BSA was used for blocking for 1 h at room temperature, and the primary antibody was incubated overnight at 4 °C. The next day, cells were washed and incubated with the corresponding secondary antibody combination for 1 h. Finally, cells were incubated with DAPI solution (C1002, Beyotime, China) at room temperature for 5 min for nuclear staining.

For tissue sections, baked slices were dewaxed, gradient hydrated, and then repaired with sodium citrate antigen repair solution at 95 °C for 20 min. After cooling to room temperature, 0.5% Triton X-100 was applied for 15 min at room temperature. 5% BSA was used for blocking at room temperature for 1 h, and primary antibodies were incubated overnight at 4 °C. The next day, the cells were washed and incubated with the appropriate secondary antibody combination for 1 h. Finally, DAPI solution was used for nuclear staining for 5 min at room temperature.

The secondary antibodies were used as follows: Goat anti-Rabbit IgG (H + L) Highly Cross-Adsorbed Secondary Antibody, Alexa Fluor 488 (1:200, A11034, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Goat anti-Mouse IgG (H + L) Highly Cross-Adsorbed Secondary Antibody, Alexa Fluor 594 (1:200, A11032, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Images were captured using a fluorescence microscope or laser confocal microscopy (Zeiss, Germany). The corresponding fluorescence intensity was measured using ImageJ.

HaCaT cells proliferation experiments were performed in 96-well culture plates. Briefly, 2.0 × 10 3 cells were seeded into each well and cultured overnight. The cells were then subjected to the desired treatment. At the end of the experiment, the medium was discarded, and a staining solution consisting of 20 μL freshly prepared 5 mg/mL MTT solution (ST316, Beyotime, China) and 200 μL DMEM medium was added to each well. The cells were incubated for 4 h at 37 °C with 5% CO2. After incubation, the plate was centrifuged at 300 x g for 5 min, and the solution was aspirated. The precipitate was dissolved by adding 200 μL of DMSO to each well, followed by shaking at 350 rpm for 10 min at room temperature to dissolve the precipitate. Absorbance was measured at 570 nm.

HaCaT cells were cultured in 6-well plates overnight. After the cells grew to 100% fusion, the cells were scratched from the top to the bottom of the plate wells with a 200 μL pipette tip perpendicular to the cell surface. Microscopic observation and record were performed in bright field, and the cell scratch width was counted at 0 h. Then, the corresponding culture system was configured with medium containing 2% FBS and the culture was continued for 24 h. Software OlyVIA (Olympus, Japan) was used to calculate the scratch width and to calculate the cell migration rate.

1-2 mg protein lysates from cells or tissues were incubated with primary antibody overnight at 4 °C. 40 μL of protein A/G magnetic beads or 10 μL tag magnetic beads (MedChem Express, USA) were pre-washed, to which the protein solution is added after incubation with the antibody. Then incubated with the beads at room temperature for a further 2 h. After 2 h, the beads were washed 6 times with washing buffer. Aspirated the liquid and 45 µl of 1 × loading solution was added to each tube and heated for 10 min at 100 °C. Finally, the sample solution was aspirated for electrophoretic detection.

The collected skin tissue lysates were analyzed with IL-17A (900-M392, PeproTech, USA) and CXCL1 ELISA kits (900-M127, PeproTech, USA) according to the kit instructions.

HaCaT cells were incubated with or without 10 mM lactate for 24 h, then the cells were collected and subjected to Cellular Thermal Shift Assay (CETSA) assay. Briefly, incubated cells were equally divided into 10 parts, each parts got heated for 3 min under different temperatures (37, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 70, 75, 80 °C), then the heated cells were put into room temperature for 3 min. Then, cells were put into − 80 °C for 5 min and put into 37 °C for 5 min, repeated one more time. After that, cell lysates were extracted by centrifuged at 20,000 × g for 20 min. Expression of HAT1 was detected by western blot.

The molecule Lactyl-CoA (compound CID: 3081970) was downloaded from PubChem ( https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov ), the structure of HAT1 and histone H4 complex (2P0W) was downloaded from RCSB Protein Data Bank (RCSB PDB) ( https://www.rcsb.org ), and the full-length structures of KLK8 and IL-17RA were predicted by AlphaFold.

Molecular docking was performed by MOE software. Protein docking was performed by GRAMM and handled by PyMol software and PDBePISA ( https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/pisa/ ).

Statistical analysis was performed using Prism 10.0.3 software (GraphPad), and the data are presented as the mean ± SD. The number of independent replicates (n) and the method used to analyze statistical significance ( P -value) are reported in the respective figure legends.

Further information on research design is available in the linked to this article.

title: Sulfotransferase SULT2B1 contributes to the epithelial-immune microenvironment homeostasis in imiquimod-induced psoriatic dermatitis.
abstract: Introduction Skin protects the body from external threats by constituting an epithelial-immune microenvironment. Sulfotransferase family 2B member 1 (SULT2B1) converts cholesterol to cholesterol sulfate (CS). We previously reported that CS acts as an endogenous dedicator of cytokinesis 2 (DOCK2)-inhibitory metabolite suppressing immune cell migration and activation by inhibiting DOCK2-mediated Rac activation. Despite being located in the epidermis, pathophysiological roles of CS in cutaneous inflammation remain unknown. Methods We evaluated the Sult2b1 -producing cells in the dorsal skin of wild-type mice and compared the degree of cutaneous inflammation between wild-type and Sult2b1 knockout mice using a psoriatic dermatitis model induced by topical imiquimod (IMQ). We also examined SULT2B1 gene expression levels in human epidermal keratinocytes to assess the effects of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Results Sult2b1 expression levels and CS production gradually increased in the skin of psoriatic dermatitis model mice. IMQ-induced dermatitis and neutrophil recruitment were exacerbated in the Sult2b1 knockout mice with a complete loss of CS. Furthermore, genetic deletion of Dock2 or intravenous administration of neutrophil-depleting antibodies alleviated IMQ-induced dermatitis in Sult2b1 knockout mice. Notably, CS was more abundant in the skin samples of patients with psoriasis than in the healthy control samples. Primary normal human epidermal keratinocytes exhibited significantly elevated SULT2B1 levels after Th1 cytokine treatment. Discussion These findings suggest that increased SULT2B1 levels in the skin under psoriatic conditions may be involved in a negative feedback mechanism that helps to limit excessive skin inflammation, thereby potentially contributing to the maintenance of epithelial-immune microenvironment homeostasis. Overall, our results raise the possibility that SULT2B1 plays an important role in cutaneous inflammation and could serve as a useful indicator or potential target in psoriasis.
