title: PEGylated Peptide for Targeted Inhibition of Human Antigen R as a Novel Therapeutic Strategy for Psoriasis: A Proof-of-Concept Study.
abstract: Introduction Psoriasis, characterized by dermatological manifestations, exhibits a systemic impact through its association with serious comorbidities, including inflammatory arthritis, cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, and psychiatric disorders. Current high-cost traditional therapies primarily involve antibodies against psoriasis-associated cytokines. Human antigen R (HuR), an RNA-binding protein that regulates the expression of upstream inflammatory cytokines, is overexpressed in immune disorders. Oligopeptide-based drugs that specifically interact with proteins to block downstream gene expression via structural interactions have garnered significant attention. In this study, we report a peptide-based polymer to target HuR and evaluated their efficacy in treating imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasis-like dermatitis in mice ears. Methods Specifically, the HuR-inhibiting peptide (HIP) is PEGlated to obtain methoxypolyethylene glycol- block -poly(γ-benzyl glutamate) (mPEG- b -PBLG) amphiphilic block copolymer. The self-assembly of the mPEG- b -PBLG block copolymer facilitates the formation of polymeric nanoparticles (NPs) in aqueous solutions, resulting in the improvement of the stability and bioactivity of the oligopeptide. Results Macroscopic and histological analyses demonstrated that the oligopeptide significantly alleviates the symptoms in psoriasis model mice. Furthermore, the levels of the key cytokine IL-23 and the growth factor VEGF are downregulated. Notably, the HIP effectively targeted the ear skin and did not induce apparent organotoxicity. Discussion The promising results demonstrated in this proof-of-concept study provide strong evidence supporting the targeted inhibition of HuR via PEGylated peptide. The observed efficacy in mitigating key inflammatory markers (VEGF and IL-23) highlights the potential of this approach to offer superior specificity and reduced systemic side effects compared to current broad-spectrum immunosuppressants. This HuR-targeting strategy offers a potentially low-cost and effective therapeutic approach for psoriasis patients.

sections.other:
Psoriasis, a chronic and disfiguring immune-mediated skin disease, presents a significant global health burden, affecting an estimated 125 million individuals worldwide. Beyond its dermatological manifestations, psoriasis is associated with a heightened prevalence of several serious comorbidities, including inflammatory arthritis, cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, as well as psychiatric disorders, underscoring its systemic impact. The pathogenesis of psoriasis is characterized by the dysregulation of the immune system and the overproduction of key pro-inflammatory cytokines, notably tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-12 (IL-12), interleukin-17 (IL-17), and interleukin-23 (IL-23)., While topical therapies remain the foundational treatment approach for patients with mild psoriasis, moderate-to-severe cases often necessitate systemic interventions. The advent of biologic therapies has revolutionized psoriasis treatment, offering targeted inhibition of specific inflammatory pathways. These biologics include agents directed against TNF-α, the shared p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23, IL-17, and the p19 subunit specific to IL-23., Additionally, an oral phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitor provides another systemic treatment option. The development and utilization of highly selective drugs capable of precisely targeting cytokine expression within the psoriatic inflammatory cascade hold significant promise for improving the quality of life for affected individuals by offering enhanced efficacy and potentially reducing the systemic side effects associated with broader immunosuppression.

The treatment landscape for inflammatory diseases has historically relied on non-specific small molecule drugs (such as methotrexate), often associated with a spectrum of undesirable side effects. Recognizing the limitations of this approach, significant research efforts have shifted towards the development of alternative and more selective anti-inflammatory therapies, with peptides emerging as promising candidates. Indeed, peptides have gained prominence as lead compounds for numerous therapeutic targets due to their inherent high specificity and the continuous advancements in innovative synthetic strategies. Notably, several endogenous peptides (such as αMSH and cortistatin) identified during the inflammatory response exhibit intrinsic anti-inflammatory activity by directly inhibiting, reducing, and/or modulating the expression and activity of key inflammatory mediators. This inherent bioactivity underscores their potential as targeted therapeutics. However, the clinical translation of these promising peptide candidates is often hampered by inherent physicochemical and pharmacokinetic limitations, including rapid clearance from the circulation, poor aqueous solubility, and low metabolic stability, primarily due to their susceptibility to enzymatic degradation. To overcome these significant challenges and enhance their therapeutic utility, structural modification of peptides has become a widely accepted and actively pursued strategy. Among the various modification techniques, the covalent attachment of polyethylene glycol (PEG), a process known as PEGylation, has demonstrated considerable success in improving peptide drug properties., The conjugation of PEG chains to a peptide significantly increases its effective hydrodynamic volume. This increased size reduces the rate of renal filtration in the glomeruli, leading to prolonged circulation times and consequently, a reduced clearance rate. Furthermore, the bulky and highly hydrated PEG moiety creates a steric barrier around the peptide, effectively hindering the access of proteolytic enzymes and thus providing significant protection against enzymatic degradation. This enhanced stability translates to a longer in vivo half-life, potentially improving the efficacy and reducing the frequency of drug administration.

Human antigen R (HuR), also known as ELAV-like protein 1 (ELAVL1), is a crucial RNA-binding protein with multifaceted roles in post-transcriptional gene regulation. It exerts control over the stability, translation efficiency, and nucleocytoplasmic trafficking of its diverse target messenger RNAs (mRNAs). Under normal cellular conditions, HuR primarily resides within the nucleus, where it is known to bind nascent mRNAs containing adenylate-uridylate rich elements (AREs), typically located in the 3’ untranslated region (3’UTR). Subsequently, HuR escorts these target mRNAs from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, acting as a key chaperone in their export and subsequent protection from degradation by cytoplasmic ribonucleases. In response to various physiological or stress stimuli, HuR undergoes a dynamic redistribution, shuttling from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. Upon translocation to the cytoplasm, HuR binds to the AREs present in the 3’UTR of its target transcripts, thereby modulating their half-life and/or translational output. Notably, a significant proportion, approximately ninety percent, of chemokine and cytokine mRNAs contain AREs in their 3’UTRs, highlighting the critical importance of HuR-mediated post-transcriptional gene regulation during the intricate processes of the immune response., Specifically, during inflammation, HuR plays a prominent role in stabilizing the mRNAs of a wide array of pro-inflammatory cytokines, leading to their increased expression. Consequently, HuR is recognized as a potential anti-inflammatory therapeutic target. Prior research has demonstrated that HuR directly binds to the 3’UTR mRNAs of key pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-17. Furthermore, studies have shown that the translation of these cytokines can be effectively blocked through the use of chemical inhibitors targeting HuR or in HuR-deficient Th17 cells.,

Previously, our group demonstrated that several aromatic peptides exhibited potent anti-inflammatory activity via the blockage of the mRNA binding site of HuR and downstream signaling, evidenced by the results from the molecular modeling and in vitro/in vivo experiments. These aromatic peptides were capable of binding to the RNA-binding site of HuR, resulting in the reduction of antibody recognition and the exhibition of anti-inflammatory activity without adverse effect. Building upon our prior investigations, this study further explored the therapeutic potential of the poly(γ-benzyl glutamate) (PBLG) peptide, designated as the HuR-inhibiting peptide (HIP), in a murine model of psoriasis. The PBLG HIP was conjugated with methoxypolyethylene glycol (mPEG) to obtain mPEG- b -PBLG amphiphilic block copolymer, rendering the formation of polymeric nanoparticles (NPs) in aqueous solutions via self-assembly. The assembled NPs with the mPEG on the corona exhibited stealth property to prevent the peptide degradation, ensuring the delivery of the PBLG HIP to block the mRNA binding site of HuR. Through comprehensive in vitro and in vivo analyses of key cytokines, our findings demonstrated that HIP effectively suppressed the expression of pro-inflammatory mediators critical in psoriasis pathogenesis, including TNF-α, IL-17, and IL-23, as well as the pro-angiogenic factor VEGF. This downregulation of key inflammatory and angiogenic drivers correlated with a significant alleviation of psoriatic symptoms in the treated mice ears, evidenced by reduced erythema, thickness, and scaling. Furthermore, the observed distribution of HIP within the ear skin provides a mechanistic basis for its localized therapeutic efficacy in this model.
sections.methods:
Imiquimod (R837) from MedChemExpress and quercetin from Sigma-Aldrich were used in this study. Antibodies against HuR (Santa Cruz), caspase-3 (Cell Signaling), polyethylene glycol (PEG, Abcam), and GAPDH (GeneTex) were utilized for protein detection. Mouse IL-23, VEGF, and TNF-α levels were quantified using ELISA kits from R&D Systems. The RAW264.7 murine macrophage cell line (Bioresource Collection and Research Center, Hsinchu, Taiwan), the HaCaT human epidermal keratinocyte, and the B16-F10 murine melanoma cell lines (the latter two from the American Type Culture Collection) were used for in vitro experiments. Aldara ® 5% imiquimod cream (Inova Pharmaceuticals, Austria) induced psoriatic skin changes in 8–10-week-old male C57BL/6 mice (National Laboratory Animal Center, Taiwan). All the chemicals and solvents are ACS grade, unless otherwise noted.

γ-benzyl L-glutamate N-carboxyanhydride (BLG NCA), the activated monomer for polypeptide synthesis, was prepared according to a previously established protocol. Subsequently, the mPEG 112 - b -PBLG 5 block copolymer was synthesized via ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of BLG NCA. This polymerization was initiated by methoxypolyethylene glycol amine (mPEG 112 -NH 2 , Sigma-Aldrich), which served as a macroinitiator with a stated molecular weight of 5000 g mol −1 (corresponding to approximately 112 ethylene glycol repeating units, hence mPEG 112 ). The polymerization was conducted with a feed molar ratio of mPEG 112 -NH 2 macroinitiator to the BLG NCA monomer of 1: 5, indicating an intended average degree of polymerization of 5 for the PBLG block.

Polymeric NPs were prepared via a dialysis-based self-assembly process. In a typical procedure, 10 mg of the mPEG 112 - b -PBLG 5 amphiphilic block copolymer were initially dissolved in 1 mL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, Sigma-Aldrich), a water-miscible organic solvent. To induce NP formation and remove the organic solvent, the polymer solution was then subjected to dialysis against a phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solution (pH 7.4, ionic strength 0.15 N). This dialysis was performed using a cellulose dialysis membrane with a molecular weight cutoff (MWCO) of 3.5 KDa (Sigma), ensuring retention of the relatively high molecular weight block copolymer while allowing the smaller DMSO molecules to diffuse out the cellulose dialysis membrane over a period of 24 hrs. To facilitate efficient solvent exchange and ensure complete removal of DMSO, the PBS solution was replenished at specific intervals: every 30 min for the initial 3 hrs, followed by exchanges every 2 hrs for the subsequent 6 hrs, and finally every 6 hrs for the remaining duration of the dialysis process.

The 1 H NMR spectrum of the block copolymer was recorded at a BRUKER AVANCE III HD nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectrometer operating at 600 MHz (Bruker Corporation, Germany) with TFA- d 1 (Sigma-Aldrich) as the solvent. The hydrodynamic diameter (particle size) was determined by dynamic light scattering (DLS) analysis at a 90° angle using an Otsuka ELSZ-1000 system (Otsuka Electronics, Japan). The autocorrelation function was analyzed using the cumulant method and CONTIN algorithms within the software. Measurements were performed in triplicate (n = 3), and data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed on a Hitachi H7500 microscope with a tungsten filament at an accelerating voltage of 120 kV. A sample aliquot was deposited onto a carbon-coated copper grid, excess solution was removed with filter paper, and the grid was air-dried overnight prior to TEM analysis.

Raw264.7, HaCaT and B16-F1 cells (4 x 10 5 ) were seeded in each well of a 6-well cell culture plate. The following day, the culture medium was replaced with 900 μL of serum-free DMEM and 100 μL of HIP (1 mg mL −1 ). After a 3-hr treatment period, the cells were further stimulated by the addition of IMQ at a concentration of 10 μg mL −1 and supplemented with 10% FBS. Twelve hrs post-stimulation, the cell samples were harvested, and total RNA was extracted using the REzol C&T RNA extraction Kit (Protech Technology). Two micrograms (2 μg) of the extracted total RNA were then reverse-transcribed into complementary DNA (cDNA) using the High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems). The resulting cDNA was utilized as a template for real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using qPCRBIO SyGreen Mix (PCR Biosystems) and performed on a StepOne Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems). The PCR amplification protocol consisted of an initial denaturation step at 95°C for 3 min, followed by 50 cycles of denaturation at 95°C for 5 seconds and annealing/extension at 60°C for 30 seconds. The primer sequences used for the amplification of target genes and the housekeeping gene are listed below:

Human GAPDH: Forward (F): 5’-GTCTCCTCTGACTTCAACAGCG-3’ / Reverse (R): 5’-ACCACCCTGTTGCTGTAGCCAA-3’

Human IL-17: Forward (F): 5’-CGGACTGTGATGGTCAACCTGA-3’ / Reverse (R): 5’-GCACTTTGCCTCCCAGATCACA-3’

Human IL-23: Forward (F): 5’-GAGCCTTCTCTGCTCCCTGATA-3’ / Reverse (R): 5’-GACTGAGGCTTGGAATCTGCTG-3’

Human TNFα: Forward (F): 5’-CTCTTCTGCCTGCTGCACTTTG-3’ / Reverse (R): 5’-ATGGGCTACAGGCTTGTCACTC-3’

Mouse GAPDH: Forward (F): 5’-CATCACTGCCACCCAGAAGACTG-3’ / Reverse (R): 5’-ATGCCAGTGAGCTTCCCGTTCAG-3’

Mouse IL-17: Forward (F): 5’-CAGACTACCTCAACCGTTCCAC-3’ / Reverse (R): 5’-TCCAGCTTTCCCTCCGCATTGA-3’

Mouse IL-23: Forward (F): 5’-CATGCTAGCCTGGAACGCACAT-3’ / Reverse (R): 5’-ACTGGCTGTTGTCCTTGAGTCC-3’

Mouse TNFα: Forward (F): 5’-GGTGCCTATGTCTCAGCCTCTT-3’ / Reverse (R): 5’-GCCATAGAACTGATGAGAGGGAG-3’

The relative gene expression levels of IL-17, IL-23, and TNF-α were normalized to the expression of the housekeeping gene, GAPDH, and the fold change in expression was calculated using the 2 −ΔΔCt method.

RAW264.7 cells were pretreated with HIP at concentrations of 25, 50, and 100 μM for 1 hr, followed by stimulation with 10 μg mL −1 imiquimod (IMQ) for 18 hrs. Cells were then lysed in RIPA buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, pH 8.0, 1 mM Na 3 VO 4 , 20 μg mL −1 leupeptin, 20 μg mL −1 aprotinin, 1 mM PMSF, and 50 mM NaF). Protein lysates were analyzed by immunoblotting using primary antibodies against caspase-3, and GAPDH, followed by appropriate secondary antibodies. For organ lysates from mice, the organs were weighed and then homogenized in RIPA buffer. The resulting homogenates were subsequently centrifuged to obtain the supernatant, which was then used for PEG expression analysis. The Immunoreactive protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence (ECL) (Pierce Biotechnology, Rockford, IL). Band intensities were normalized to GAPDH and quantified using ImageJ software ( https://imagej.net/ij/ ).

Histochemical analysis was conducted on ear skin, liver, and spleen samples obtained from both control and HIP-treated mice. Following fixation in 4% paraformaldehyde, the tissues were embedded in paraffin and sectioned at a thickness of 4 μm. To visualize the distribution of HuR or PEG, tissue sections were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through a graded series of ethanol solutions to distilled water. Antigen retrieval was performed by heating the sections in citrate buffer (pH 6.0) in a boiling water bath for 20 min. Non-specific binding was blocked by incubating the tissue sections with 5% bovine serum albumin (BSA) at room temperature for 1 hr. Subsequently, sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with either an anti-HuR antibody or an anti-PEG antibody, both diluted in KPL 10% BSA Diluent/Blocking Solution (Seracare). After washing with PBST (0.05% Tween-20), the sections were incubated at room temperature with the appropriate horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody diluted in 15% BSA Diluent. The enzymatic signal was developed using diaminobenzidine (DAB) as a chromogenic substrate. Finally, the sections were counterstained with hematoxylin to visualize tissue morphology.

The animal study protocol was approved by the Laboratory Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC Approval No. 108050, National Cheng Kung University), adhering to the Animal Protection Act of Taiwan. All animal procedures were conducted in strict accordance with the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) Guidelines for the Euthanasia of Animals (2020). For anesthesia, subjects were placed in an induction chamber containing 5% isoflurane in oxygen. Following induction, anesthesia was maintained with 2% isoflurane delivered via a nose cone. Euthanasia was performed via an overdose of sodium pentobarbital (150 mg kg −1 , administered intraperitoneally) after which the absence of reflexes and breathing was confirmed. IMQ, a ligand for TLR7/8, was previously used as an antiviral drug. However, increasing research indicates that patients using IMQ cream experience transient psoriasis-like symptoms. Consequently, IMQ cream is widely used in animal models of psoriasis. In these models, IMQ applied to the lesional skin of mice induces the expression of Th1 and Th17-related cytokines and presents dermatitis with psoriasis-like characteristics. Following the psoriasis animal model described by Jabeen et al, eight-week-old BALB/c mice were topically treated with 13.88 mg of IMQ (5% Aldara cream) on both ears from day 0 to day 9. Starting from day 5, HIP, saline, or quercetin was administered via intraperitoneal injection daily until day 10. The severity of psoriasis was observed daily, and the mice were sacrificed on day 10 for subsequent analysis.

The Psoriasis Area Severity Index (PASI) clinical scoring system was employed to evaluate the inflammatory status of the dorsal skin in all mice over the 8-day experimental period. This assessment involved the visual examination of three key clinical parameters on the back skin of each animal: erythema (redness), induration (thickness), and desquamation (scaling). Each parameter was independently scored by two researchers (n = 6 evaluations per parameter) on a scale ranging from 0 to 4, where 0 indicated no presence, 1 represented slight manifestation, 2 denoted moderate severity, 3 indicated marked inflammation, and 4 signified very marked involvement. The scores for the three parameters were then summed to yield a cumulative PASI score ranging from 0 to 12 for each mouse at each time point. The final PASI score for each animal was determined by calculating the mean of the values obtained from the two independent researchers.

The inhibitory effect of the PEGylated peptide on inflammatory cytokine secretion was assessed by ELISA. Murine macrophage Raw264.7 cells were specifically chosen for this assay, as macrophages are the primary source of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α and IL-23, central to the inflammatory cascade in psoriasis pathogenesis. Raw264.7 cells were seeded and pre-incubated for 1 hr either in the absence (blank) or presence of varying concentrations of HIP. Following this pre-treatment, the cells were stimulated with 10 μg mL −1 IMQ for an 18-hr period. Subsequently, cell-free supernatants were collected, and the levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-23 were quantified using commercially available ELISA kits from R&D Systems, following the manufacturer’s instructions. In a separate experiment, tissue lysates were prepared from mouse ear samples that had been treated with or without HIP. The expression levels of a panel of cytokines and chemokines in these tissue lysates were then analyzed using the Proteome Profiler™ Mouse Cytokine Array Panel A, also obtained from R&D Systems, according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

Results are expressed as means with their corresponding standard deviations (SD). The sample size (n) for each experimental group is clearly reported in the figure legends and/or results section. Statistical comparisons between groups were performed using Student’s unpaired t -test, and significance was defined as p < 0.05. All statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism version 10.1.2.
sections.results:
The amphiphilic block copolymer mPEG 112 - b -PBLG 5 was synthesized through PEGylation of the PBLG HIP. In aqueous solutions, polymeric NPs were formed through the self-assembly of this copolymer, as shown in . The PBLG HIP within these NPs was investigated, initially, to assess its ability to suppress pro-inflammatory mediators. Subsequently, the HIP administration was evaluated in vivo for ameliorating IMQ-induced psoriasis-like symptoms.

The as-synthesized mPEG 112 - b -PBLG 5 block copolymer was confirmed by H NMR analysis, and all the protons could be assigned to all the chemical shifts ( Figure S1 ). The degree of polymerization (DP) of PBLG was calculated based on the ratio of the benzyl group (–OCH 2 C 6 H 5 ) on PBLG to the ethylene group (–(CH 2 ) 2 O–) on mPEG ( Figure S1 ), which was determined to be 5. Using a dialysis-based self-assembly process, the mPEG 112 - b -PBLG 5 block copolymer self-assembled to form polymeric NPs in an aqueous solution due to its amphiphilic nature. The DLS analysis revealed that the hydrodynamic diameter (particle size) of the assembled NPs in a PBS buffer solution was measured to be 92.0 ± 3.5 nm ( Figure S2 ). The TEM analysis confirmed the formation of NPs, and the size of the assembled NPs was smaller than that measured by DLS analysis ( Figure S3 ), which was attributed to the dehydration of the sample, leading to the shrinkage of the NPs upon drying during the sample preparation.

To investigate the impact of PBLG HIP on the expression of key inflammatory cytokines implicated in psoriasis – TNF-α, IL-17, and IL-23 – murine macrophage Raw264.7 cells, human keratinocyte HaCaT cells, and murine melanoma B16-F1 cells were pre-treated with the polymeric NPs comprised of PBLG HIP before induction with IMQ to evaluate RNA expression levels. Three distinct cell lines were employed in this study to comprehensively evaluate the effect of the PEGylated peptide on psoriasis-relevant pathological mechanisms. The HaCaT cell line, an immortalized human keratinocyte line, was utilized to model the hallmark feature of psoriasis: keratinocyte hyper-proliferation and epidermal thickening. The Raw264.7 murine macrophage cell line represented the core immuno-inflammatory component of the disease, allowing us to assess the peptide’s inhibitory effect on the secretion of key pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-α and IL-6. Furthermore, the B16-F1 cell line was included primarily for general pharmacological characterization, specifically to determine the cellular uptake and internalization kinetics of the PEGylated peptide, ensuring the integrity of the preliminary drug data. Collectively, these cell lines covered the critical aspects of both epidermal dysregulation and immune response abnormalities central to psoriasis pathogenesis, thus supporting a complete evaluation of the target peptide’s mechanism of action. As depicted in , HIP treatment alone stimulated the expression of these three cytokines in Raw264.7 cells, but not significantly in HaCaT or B16-F1 cells. Notably, HIP pre-treatment significantly suppressed the IMQ-induced expression of these three cytokines across all three cell lines, suggesting a broad inhibitory effect of HIP on cytokine expression following IMQ stimulation. The observation that HIP alone induced cytokine expression specifically in Raw264.7 macrophages suggests a potential cell activation mechanism, possibly related to the physical characteristics (eg, particle size of NPs), potentially leading to the activation of phagocytosis.

Having established that the PBLG HIP inhibits the expression of IMQ-induced inflammatory cytokines at the RNA level, we next investigated the corresponding protein expression and downstream signaling pathways. As depicted in and , HIP demonstrated a dose-dependent inhibition of TNF-α and IL-23 secretion in IMQ-stimulated Raw264.7 macrophages. This inhibitory effect extended to key cellular processes, as evidenced by the observation of DNA condensation, a morphological hallmark of apoptosis, and the increased expression of cleaved caspase-3, a critical executioner of apoptosis ( and ). This apoptotic outcome in macrophages treated with HIP and IMQ could be attributed to multiple mechanisms. Firstly, HIP has previously demonstrated ability to block the function of HuR, an RNA-binding protein known to stabilize cytokine mRNAs and promote cell survival, likely contributes to the observed decrease in cytokine production and potentially sensitizes cells to apoptotic stimuli [24]. Secondly, HIP might exert an inhibitory effect on pathways crucial for activating cell growth and survival signals that are normally triggered during inflammatory response. Consequently, the dual action of HIP – suppressing pro-inflammatory mediators and hindering macrophage survival – suggests its potential as a therapeutic agent for psoriasis, a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by excessive immune cell activation and cytokine production.

To evaluate the in vivo therapeutic efficacy of HIP, an IMQ-induced psoriasis-like murine model was established. Following 10 days of IMQ cream application to the ears, mice were intraperitoneally administered HIP (at doses of 20 and 100 mg kg −1 ) or quercetin (a positive control at 50 mg kg −1 ) starting from day 5 of the experiment (). Macroscopic observation of both sides of the mice’s ears revealed that treatment with HIP (at both concentrations) and quercetin significantly attenuated the visible signs of psoriasis compared to the saline-treated control group (). Clinical scoring using a Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI)-like system further demonstrated that HIP and quercetin treatment significantly reduced individual symptom scores for erythema (), thickness (), and scaling () in comparison to the saline group. Daily measurement of ear thickness using a vernier caliper also confirmed a significant reduction in ear swelling in both the HIP- and quercetin-treated groups compared to the saline group (). Analysis of the cumulative psoriasis severity score indicated that both HIP and quercetin significantly ameliorated IMQ-induced psoriasis symptoms, with no statistically significant difference observed between the lower dose of HIP (20 mg kg −1 ) and quercetin (). On day 10, serum levels of key pro-inflammatory mediators, VEGF and IL-23, were quantified. Both HIP (at 20 and 100 mg kg −1 ) and quercetin significantly inhibited VEGF expression compared to the saline group. However, while HIP significantly reduced IL-23 levels, quercetin treatment did not show a statistically significant inhibitory effect on IL-23 expression ( and ). These results provide compelling evidence that HIP has potent anti-psoriatic effects in vivo, comparable to quercetin, and may act through mechanisms involving the suppression of key pro-inflammatory mediators like VEGF and, importantly, IL-23.

To further elucidate the anti-psoriatic mechanisms of HIP, histological analysis and HuR expression profiling were performed on ear skin tissue. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining revealed a marked increase in epidermal proliferation in IMQ-treated mice compared to the saline control (). Notably, both HIP and quercetin significantly reduced this IMQ-induced epidermal hyperplasia. Quantitative analysis of epidermal thickness and the number of epidermal layers demonstrated that high-dose HIP (100 mg kg −1 ) exhibited the most potent anti-proliferative effect, while the lower dose of HIP (20 mg kg −1 ) showed comparable efficacy to quercetin ( and ). Furthermore, immunohistochemistry analysis demonstrated a correlation between cytoplasmic HuR expression levels and the observed epidermal proliferation, suggesting a potential link between HuR and the anti-proliferative effects of HIP. These histological and molecular findings further support the anti-psoriatic efficacy of HIP in the IMQ-induced murine model, highlighting its ability to reduce epidermal hyperproliferation, potentially through mechanisms involving the modulation of cytoplasmic HuR expression.

To determine if the systemic distribution of HIP correlated with its therapeutic effects, we quantified HIP levels in various organs of psoriasis model mice using immunoblotting (). This analysis demonstrated a distinct distribution pattern, with the highest concentration of HIP observed in the spleen, followed by significant levels in the inflamed ear skin and the liver. Minimal HIP was detected in other organs examined. This distribution profile was further confirmed through PEG antibody staining of tissue biopsies from the spleen, ear skin, and liver (). To evaluate potential organ toxicity, especially in the liver where HIP accumulated, we measured serum levels of the liver enzymes alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate transaminase (AST) in HIP-treated mice (). Notably, treatment with either HIP or the known anti-inflammatory compound quercetin resulted in a significant reduction in both serum ALT and AST levels in the psoriasis model mice. Immunoblotting and immunohistochemistry showed that HIP preferentially distributed to spleen, inflamed ear skin, and liver in psoriasis model mice. Importantly, despite hepatic accumulation, HIP treatment did not elevate serum ALT levels, a key indicator of liver damage. Instead, both HIP and quercetin significantly reduced ALT, suggesting a lack of liver toxicity and potential protective effects against psoriasis-associated liver inflammation. Similarly, reduced AST levels further supported the absence of widespread cellular damage following HIP treatment.
sections.discussion:
In the context of diseases characterized by overactive immune cells, microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy in recent years due to their ability to specifically inhibit the expression of aberrant genes. However, significant challenges remain in the efficient delivery and cost-effectiveness of miRNA-based therapies., This present study builds upon our previous research involving the PBLG HIP and its application in the treatment of psoriasis patients. The PBLG HIP was feasibly PEGylated via ROP of BLG NCA using mPEG 112 -NH 2 as the macroinitiator. The formation of polymeric NPs via the self-assembly of the PEGylated HIP in aqueous solutions is highlighted to improve the stability and bioactivity of the PBLG HIP and, consequently, ensure the delivery of the PBLG HIP. Our in vitro data reveal that the PBLG HIP might exert dual action of suppressing pro-inflammatory mediators and hindering macrophage survival via block function of HuR and exerting an inhibitory effect on pathways crucial for activating cell growth and survival signals (). The HIP effectively ameliorates the clinical manifestations of psoriasis via suppressing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (). Beyond its targeted therapeutic efficacy, our findings indicate that the PEGylated component of the HIP formulation distributes within the affected ear skin and internal organs such as the spleen and liver ( and ). Importantly, the HIP treatment did not induce liver inflammation or damage to other organs (). These results strongly suggest that HIP holds potential as a cost-effective and efficacious alternative anti-inflammatory therapy by competitively inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokine mRNAs.

The promising results demonstrated in this proof-of-concept study provide strong evidence supporting the targeted inhibition of HuR via PEGylated peptide as a novel and viable therapeutic strategy for psoriasis. The observed efficacy in mitigating key inflammatory markers (VEGF and IL-23) highlights the potential of this approach to offer superior specificity and reduced systemic side effects compared to current broad-spectrum immunosuppressants. Looking ahead, the immediate future direction of this research involves rigorous pharmacokinetic and toxicology assessments in larger animal models to determine the safety profile and optimal dosing regimen. Ultimately, the author’s expectation is that this method could be successfully translated into a next-generation, targeted biological agent for the long-term management of chronic plaque psoriasis, paving the way for eventual pre-clinical development and human clinical trials.

In summary, this study demonstrated the therapeutic potential of the PBLG HIP for psoriasis. The PBLG HIP was conjugated with mPEG to facilitate the formation of polymeric NPs in aqueous solutions and to improve the stability and bioactivity of the PBLG HIP. Our experimental results revealed that the PBLG HIP effectively suppressed IMQ-induced inflammatory cytokine production at both transcriptional and translational levels in vitro. The in vivo experiments demonstrated that the intraperitoneal administration of HIP significantly ameliorated psoriasis-like symptoms in IMQ-treated mice, evidenced by the reduction in erythema, scaling, thickness, and secretion of VEGF and IL-23. Mechanistically, this suppression correlated with HuR blockade and a subsequent decrease in epidermal proliferation. The observed distribution of HIP in the spleen, inflamed skin, and liver suggested an inflammation-targeting capacity. Furthermore, the reduction in serum ALT and AST levels indicated a low risk of organotoxicity. Collectively, these findings propose the PBLG HIP as a promising alternative therapeutic strategy for psoriasis. Our approach, which targets the post-transcriptional stability of key inflammatory mediators (such as VEGF and IL-23) via HuR inhibition, offers a mechanism fundamentally distinct from current biologic therapies that rely on neutralizing circulating cytokines (eg, monoclonal antibodies against IL-17 or IL-23). This mechanistic differentiation suggests that HuR inhibitors could potentially complement current anti-cytokine biologics, particularly in patients who exhibit incomplete or diminishing responses to single-pathway blockade. We anticipate that a HuR-based treatment, perhaps formulated for topical delivery given the skin-localized nature of the disease, could serve as a valuable combination therapy or an alternative targeted agent to expand the current treatment options for moderate-to-severe psoriasis.

title: The impact of biologics targeting the IL-17 and IL-23 pathways on metabolic indicators in plaque psoriasis.
abstract: This study aims to compare the efficacy of IL-17 and IL-23 biologics in the treatment of plaque psoriasis (Psoriasis vulgaris) in patients with metabolic syndrome (MetS) and to explore the effects of different biologics on metabolic indicators, particularly regarding the differences in efficacy during long-term treatment. This is a randomized controlled clinical trial involving 120 moderates to severe plaque psoriasis patients, of which 60 have metabolic syndrome and 60 do not. The patients were randomly assigned to three groups: IL-17 biologics group, IL-23 biologics group, and cyclosporine control group. Treatment lasted for three months, with evaluation indicators including psoriatic lesion assessment (PASI score), blood glucose levels, lipid profile (triglycerides, HDL-C), inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, IL-6), etc. Patients were assessed at baseline, after one month, and after three months of treatment for both clinical efficacy and changes in metabolic indicators. Both IL-17 and IL-23 biologics demonstrated superior efficacy compared to cyclosporine in treating plaque psoriasis. After one month and three months of treatment, PASI scores in the IL-17 and IL-23 groups were significantly lower than in the control group, and the therapeutic effects were more pronounced (P < 0.05). The IL-17 and IL-23 groups also showed better improvements in blood glucose, blood lipids (TG and HDL-C), and inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR, IL-6) compared to the control group. After three months of treatment, fasting blood glucose, fasting insulin, triglycerides, and CRP levels were significantly lower in the IL-17 and IL-23 groups than in the control group (P < 0.05). Metabolic syndrome had some impact on treatment outcomes, with the efficacy of IL-17 and IL-23 biologics being lower in patients with metabolic abnormalities compared to those without metabolic syndrome. However, the IL-23 biologic showed less impact from metabolic syndrome. IL-17 biologics had a rapid effect in the short term, while IL-23 biologics demonstrated superior efficacy in long-term treatment, particularly at the three-month mark, where both efficacy and metabolic improvements were better than the IL-17 group. Both IL-17 and IL-23 biologics are more effective than cyclosporine in treating plaque psoriasis and can improve metabolic indicators in patients. Although metabolic syndrome impacts the efficacy of IL-17 biologics, IL-23 biologics are less affected by metabolic syndrome and demonstrate better long-term efficacy. Therefore, IL-23 biologics are recommended for long-term treatment in plaque psoriasis patients with metabolic syndrome.

title: Icotrokinra induces early and sustained pharmacodynamic responses in phase IIb study of patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis.
abstract: BACKGROUNDIcotrokinra is the first and only targeted oral peptide that selectively binds the IL-23 receptor with high affinity to precisely inhibit IL-23 signaling. Icotrokinra demonstrated high rates of complete skin clearance and durable disease control in the phase IIb trial, FRONTIER-1, and its long-term extension, FRONTIER-2, in participants with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. This study evaluated systemic and skin pharmacodynamic response of icotrokinra and its relationship to clinical response in FRONTIER participants.METHODSFRONTIER-1 participants received icotrokinra or placebo for 16 weeks. FRONTIER-2 followed participants for up to 1 year of treatment; placebo participants transitioned to icotrokinra after week 16. Systemic pharmacodynamic changes were assessed in serum through week 52. Skin pharmacodynamic changes were assessed using transcriptomic analysis of skin biopsies and protein quantification in tape-strip samples through week 16.RESULTSIcotrokinra dose-dependently reduced serum levels of the IL-23/IL-17 axis and psoriasis disease biomarkers through week 52, with maximal reductions observed with the highest 100 mg twice-daily dose. Proteomic analyses showed icotrokinra selectively blocked IL-23-driven inflammation without broader impacts on circulating proteins, including serum IL-23 levels. Sixteen weeks of icotrokinra, but not placebo, reduced expression of psoriasis-associated genes in lesional skin. Icotrokinra treatment also reduced psoriasis-relevant proteins in week 16 lesional skin tape-strips to levels comparable to nonlesional samples.CONCLUSIONIcotrokinra induced a dose-dependent pharmacodynamic response, with early (week 4) and sustained (week 52) reductions in biomarkers of IL-23 pathway activation and psoriasis disease severity, which correlated with clinical response.TRIAL REGISTRATIONClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05223868, NCT05364554.FUNDINGJohnson & Johnson.

sections.abstract: BACKGROUNDIcotrokinra is the first and only targeted oral peptide that selectively binds the IL-23 receptor with high affinity to precisely inhibit IL-23 signaling. Icotrokinra demonstrated high rates of complete skin clearance and durable disease control in the phase IIb trial, FRONTIER-1, and its long-term extension, FRONTIER-2, in participants with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. This study evaluated systemic and skin pharmacodynamic response of icotrokinra and its relationship to clinical response in FRONTIER participants.METHODSFRONTIER-1 participants received icotrokinra or placebo for 16 weeks. FRONTIER-2 followed participants for up to 1 year of treatment; placebo participants transitioned to icotrokinra after week 16. Systemic pharmacodynamic changes were assessed in serum through week 52. Skin pharmacodynamic changes were assessed using transcriptomic analysis of skin biopsies and protein quantification in tape-strip samples through week 16.RESULTSIcotrokinra dose-dependently reduced serum levels of the IL-23/IL-17 axis and psoriasis disease biomarkers through week 52, with maximal reductions observed with the highest 100 mg twice-daily dose. Proteomic analyses showed icotrokinra selectively blocked IL-23-driven inflammation without broader impacts on circulating proteins, including serum IL-23 levels. Sixteen weeks of icotrokinra, but not placebo, reduced expression of psoriasis-associated genes in lesional skin. Icotrokinra treatment also reduced psoriasis-relevant proteins in week 16 lesional skin tape-strips to levels comparable to nonlesional samples.CONCLUSIONIcotrokinra induced a dose-dependent pharmacodynamic response, with early (week 4) and sustained (week 52) reductions in biomarkers of IL-23 pathway activation and psoriasis disease severity, which correlated with clinical response.TRIAL REGISTRATIONClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05223868, NCT05364554.FUNDINGJohnson & Johnson.
sections.other:
Psoriasis is a common, chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory disease affecting around 2%–4% of the population in Western countries (), with plaque psoriasis accounting for about 90% of cases (). The pathogenesis of psoriasis involves a complex interplay between T cells, innate immune cells, and keratinocytes (). Cytokines and other inflammatory mediators secreted by immune cells drive leukocyte infiltration and keratinocyte proliferation (). This cutaneous inflammation results in the clinical appearance of psoriatic skin lesions that are histologically characterized by loss of keratinocyte terminal differentiation, epidermal hyperproliferation, and thickening ().

Conventional systemic oral therapies, including methotrexate, cyclosporine, and fumaric acid esters, have limited efficacy and may be associated with serious side effects (). Despite the availability of multiple advanced systemic oral and biologic treatment options, a significant portion of eligible patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis are not on advanced therapy, due to safety concerns, lower efficacy of advanced oral therapies, and/or patient preference (). Biologic therapies targeting several cytokine pathways, including tumor necrosis factor (TNF), IL-12/23, IL-17, and IL-23 signaling, have been approved for treating psoriasis and generally deliver greater efficacy but are limited by the need for intravenous or subcutaneous injections (, ). Two advanced oral therapies, apremilast (phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor) and deucravacitinib (tyrosine kinase 2 inhibitor), have been recently approved for psoriasis but show lower efficacy or safety/tolerability concerns relative to biologics, limiting their use (–). Thus, for patients with psoriasis, there is a significant unmet need for an oral therapy with higher efficacy and a more favorable safety and tolerability profile.

The IL-23 receptor (IL-23R) signaling pathway plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. Genetic studies have shown that polymorphisms in the IL-23 pathway are associated with an increased risk of developing psoriasis (, ). IL-23 is predominantly secreted by myeloid cells and can activate IL-23R + pathogenic T cells (T helper 17, T cytotoxic 17, and tissue-resident memory T cells) and innate immune cells (mucosal-associated invariant T cells, innate lymphoid cells, γδ T cells, and natural killer cells) to drive skin inflammation (–). Furthermore, evidence supports a role for IL-23R signaling in differentiating pathogenic versus nonpathogenic cells across autoimmune diseases (). IL-23 pathway inhibition with monoclonal antibodies targeting the p19 subunit of IL-23 or the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23 is clinically validated and has high therapeutic efficacy in psoriasis (–). However, the IL-23R has not previously been a therapeutic target for psoriasis, and there are no approved, oral therapies that selectively target the IL-23 pathway. Icotrokinra (previously JNJ-77242113) is the first and only targeted oral peptide that selectively binds IL-23R with high affinity to precisely inhibit proximal IL-23R signaling and downstream cytokine production (). Preclinical studies found icotrokinra to be a stable and bioavailable oral peptide with no risk of drug-drug interaction (). Unlike currently approved IL-23 inhibitors that target the soluble IL-23 ligand (e.g., guselkumab, risankizumab, and tildrakizumab), icotrokinra is a competitive antagonist of the IL-23R and blocks IL-23 signaling, differentiating this compound from currently approved advanced therapies in psoriasis.

In the recently completed phase IIb, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging, 16-week study (FRONTIER-1, NCT05223868 ) in participants with moderate-to-severe psoriasis, icotrokinra showed a significant dose-response relationship ( P < 0.001) (). In this study 79% of participants receiving 100 mg twice daily achieved at least 75% reduction in the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index score (PASI 75), and 40% achieved complete skin clearance (PASI 100) at week 16 (). In the 36-week long-term extension (LTE) study (FRONTIER-2, NCT05364554 ), no new adverse events or safety signals were identified, and clinical responses were sustained through 52 weeks of treatment (). Here, modulation of systemic and tissue pharmacodynamic (PD) biomarkers and its relationship to clinical response was evaluated to develop a deeper understanding of targeting IL-23R for therapeutic benefit in psoriasis.

sections.results:
To characterize the PD response in participants with psoriasis treated with icotrokinra, serum samples were analyzed from consenting FRONTIER-1 ( n = 248) and FRONTIER-2 LTE ( n = 227) participants (). Among participants with available serum samples, no statistically significant differences were noted in baseline demographics or clinical characteristics among treatment groups, with mean age ranging from 42.0 to 45.7 years, body weight from 85.1 to 92.1 kg, and psoriasis disease duration from 15.3 to 21.7 years. Females comprised a larger proportion of participants in the placebo (41.9%) than combined icotrokinra (28.3%) groups. Also, 22.9% of participants in the combined icotrokinra dose groups had severe psoriasis, as assessed by Investigator Global Assessment (IGA), versus 11.6% in the placebo group. Serum beta-defensin-2 (BD-2) (median levels: 2,614–3,836 pg/mL), IL-17A (0.8 pg/mL for all), IL-17F (3.0–4.6 pg/mL), IL-22 (15.0–28.6 pg/mL), and IL-23 (0.5–0.6 pg/mL) levels were generally balanced across treatment groups ().

Baseline demographics were comparable, and no statistically significant differences were noted, among the 60 (29 placebo and 31 icotrokinra 100 mg twice daily [BID]) participants from whom tape-strip samples were analyzed for BD-2 (; supplemental material available online with this article; https://doi.org/10.1172/jci.insight.193563DS1 ) or among the subset of 46 (20 placebo and 26 100 mg BID) FRONTIER-1 participants from whom Olink Explore HT–based broad proteomic data were generated from tape-strip samples (), with similar differences in demographics as observed in the serum cohort. Among participants with available tape-strip samples, there was a larger proportion of female participants in the placebo (55.2%) than in the 100 mg BID icotrokinra group (35.5%); 25.8% of participants in the icotrokinra dose groups had severe psoriasis, as assessed by IGA, versus 6.9% in the placebo group; however, none of these differences were statistically significant ().

Fewer participants consented to skin biopsy sampling (placebo N = 3; icotrokinra N = 22), and as a result there were more differences in baseline characteristics of participants who provided skin biopsy samples for transcriptomic analyses (). Similar to the serum and skin-tape cohorts, there was a higher proportion of females in the placebo group (66.7%) than the icotrokinra group (18.2%). A higher proportion of icotrokinra-treated participants with skin biopsies had severe psoriasis (40.9%), while all placebo participants had moderate psoriasis, as assessed by IGA. Additionally, there were differences in prior therapies, with 36.4% of participants receiving icotrokinra receiving prior phototherapy and 0.0% in the placebo group. Findings from skin biopsy transcriptomics datasets should be interpreted within this context.

Activation of the IL-23 pathway in psoriasis is associated with increased serum levels of IL-23 pathway biomarkers IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22 (). Additionally, inflammatory burden in psoriatic skin has been shown to increase serum levels of antimicrobial peptides, like BD-2 (). Serum levels of these biomarkers correlate with disease severity and treatment response, including therapies that inhibit IL-23 (, ). Reductions from baseline for IL-17A, IL-17F, IL-22, and BD-2 were observed for all icotrokinra doses relative to placebo, with the largest reductions in the 100 mg BID dose cohort. Importantly, reductions in serum biomarkers with icotrokinra treatment were observed as early as week 4 and were sustained through week 52, with similar reductions from week 16 to week 52 in the placebo group after transition to icotrokinra 100 mg once daily (QD; ).

Other receptor antagonist therapeutics have been shown in clinical studies to increase systemic levels of their respective ligands (, ). Despite reducing psoriasis-relevant biomarkers, blocking IL-23R with icotrokinra did not result in a change of serum levels of its ligand, IL-23, from baseline through week 52 (). Broad proteomic analysis of serum samples showed that, of the 5,420 proteins quantified on the Olink HT platform, only 11 proteins were significantly downregulated with icotrokinra after 52 weeks of treatment (FDR < 0.05; log 2 fold change [FC] < –1; ). Eight of these 11 downregulated proteins (PI3, IL-19, BD-2, IL-17A, IL-17C, IL-22, GPR15LG, and SERPINB4) are directly relevant to psoriasis or IL-23 pathway activation (–). While the log 2 FC of the other 3 proteins (ENTHD1, CAMK1G, and FKBP1B) were less than –1, the –log 10 P value was much lower than the aforementioned 8 psoriasis-relevant proteins.

Taken together these results show icotrokinra induced a dose-dependent systemic PD response with early and sustained reductions in systemic biomarkers of IL-23 pathway activation and psoriasis disease severity. Furthermore, icotrokinra selectively inhibited IL-23–driven psoriatic inflammation without broad modulation of circulating proteins, including serum IL-23 levels.

Effective treatment response in psoriasis, including IL-23 pathway inhibition, is associated with normalization of the transcriptome in lesional psoriatic skin (). To characterize the skin PD response of icotrokinra, whole transcriptome analysis with enrichment of biological pathways and processes was performed on lesional and nonlesional skin biopsy samples. Given the limited number of participants consenting to the skin biopsy substudy, only qualitative descriptive analysis of placebo- versus pooled icotrokinra-treated participants was performed. Week 16 lesional skin samples from icotrokinra-treated, but not placebo-treated, participant samples were more similar to week 0 nonlesional skin samples (). Icotrokinra treatment induced transcriptional changes, with modulation of gene sets associated with multiple cell types (e.g., T cells, keratinocytes) and disease-relevant cytokine signaling pathways (e.g., IL-23, IL-12, IFN-γ, and TNF-α). Importantly, icotrokinra attenuated well-characterized psoriasis-associated gene sets, including meta-analysis derived-3 (MAD-3) up and MAD-5 up, which contain genes that are upregulated in lesional compared with nonlesional psoriasis samples across multiple studies (), as well as IL-23/IL-17 signaling. This analysis also showed increased expression of well-characterized gene sets that are downregulated in disease (e.g., MAD-3 down, MAD-5 down; ) (). Thus, icotrokinra treatment induced transcriptional changes that are consistent with IL-23 pathway inhibition and normalization of inflammation in lesional skin.

Skin tape-strip sampling, a relatively minimally invasive technique, has shown promise in differentiating transcriptional signatures between psoriasis and atopic dermatitis skin (). To further characterize icotrokinra skin PD effects, proteins derived from lesional and nonlesional skin tape-strip samples collected through week 16 were compared between participants receiving icotrokinra 100 mg BID versus placebo.

The sensitivity of tape-strip based analysis was assessed by evaluating changes in skin levels of BD-2, a serum biomarker responsive to icotrokinra (). BD-2 protein levels were elevated in week 0 lesional skin in both icotrokinra 100 mg BID and placebo groups. Icotrokinra 100 mg BID treatment, but not placebo, significantly reduced BD-2 levels in lesional skin to levels approaching those seen in nonlesional and healthy control skin ().

To further characterize changes in proteins collected via tape-strip sampling, broad proteomics was performed using the Olink Explore HT platform (>5,420 proteins assessed). At baseline, the protein landscape in lesional tape-strip samples was markedly differentiated from nonlesional samples, with enrichment of several psoriasis-relevant proteins. A total of 2,684 proteins were upregulated and 18 proteins were downregulated in lesional samples relative to nonlesional samples. The upregulated proteins included known IL-23/IL-17 pathway biomarkers (IL-19, IL-17A, BD-2, IL-22, and IL-17F; ). Similar differences in protein expression patterns were also observed when comparing week 0 lesional skin with skin samples from healthy volunteers (). A paired analysis of week 16 versus week 0 lesional samples showed that 100 mg BID icotrokinra treatment downregulated disease-relevant proteins, with 2,366 downregulated and 13 upregulated proteins after 16 weeks of treatment (). Importantly, a paired analysis of week 16 lesional versus week 0 nonlesional samples in icotrokinra-treated participants showed 5,406 out of 5,415 proteins were comparable at week 16, and of the 9 proteins that were different between these groups, none are known to be related to the pathogenesis of psoriasis ().

To further evaluate the impact of icotrokinra on psoriasis-relevant proteins, protein sets were generated from well-characterized or published psoriasis and IL-23 pathway activation gene sets (, –). In this GSVA, the icotrokinra-treated week 16 lesional samples were more similar to healthy control and nonlesional samples than both week 0 lesional and placebo-treated week 16 lesional samples (). Thus, icotrokinra normalized psoriasis-associated protein signatures in lesional skin to levels observed in nonlesional skin by week 16, suggesting normalization of skin inflammation with treatment.

To understand the exposure-response relationship of icotrokinra PD and its correlation with clinical response, the pharmacokinetic (PK)/PD relationship coupled with clinical response was assessed. Log 2 FC in serum BD-2 levels strongly correlated with percentage PASI improvement ( R = –0.6, P < 2.2 × 10 –16 ; ). Furthermore, higher reductions in serum BD-2 levels were associated with higher levels of PASI improvement (). Similar results were obtained with IL-22, with serum levels correlating with PASI response ( R = –0.4, P < 2.2 × 10 –16 ; ).

Population PK/PD modeling was performed to evaluate the relationship between icotrokinra treatment on PASI scores and serum BD-2 levels over time. Sequential population PK/PD modeling with indirect response models for PASI scores and log 2 BD-2 levels fit the data well (visual predictive check based on simulation of N = 1,000 shown in ). The precision of the parameter estimate for the concentration at half of the maximum effect (EC 50 ) improved slightly by including BD-2 levels in the model, compared with a model including PASI scores alone. The time course and magnitude of effect of icotrokinra concentrations on PASI scores and BD-2 levels were similar. These results demonstrate that the exposure-clinical response and exposure-biomarker relationships were similar with icotrokinra. Thus, there was a strong correlation between exposure, PD changes, and the observed clinical response with icotrokinra.
sections.discussion:
Use of conventional oral therapies approved for psoriasis can be constrained by lower efficacy and safety/tolerability concerns (). Monoclonal antibodies targeting the IL-23 p19 subunit or the IL-12/23 p40 subunit have been shown to be safe and highly efficacious in treating psoriasis (, , , ); however, many patients prefer oral therapies or have needle phobia, which limit the overall use of injectable biologics (). The more recently approved advanced oral therapies for psoriasis, apremilast and deucravacitinib, have demonstrated lower efficacy or safety/tolerability concerns relative to biologics (, ). While several psoriasis treatments block the IL-23 pathway by targeting the IL-23 cytokine ligand, currently no available drugs bind the IL-23R. In the FRONTIER-1 and -2 studies, icotrokinra, the first and only targeted oral peptide that selectively binds IL-23R, demonstrated high rates of durable skin clearance through 52 weeks in participants with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. In these studies, rates of adverse events were similar across the icotrokinra and placebo groups, and no additional adverse events or safety signals were identified through 52 weeks of treatment (, ). Preclinical studies also found no risk of drug-drug interactions and no major metabolites (). The present study showed that selective targeting of IL-23R signaling with icotrokinra induced an early and sustained PD response in participants with psoriasis.

Since IL-23R has not been previously targeted for therapeutic efficacy, it was important to confirm that icotrokinra induced PD changes, both in the systemic circulation and the target skin tissue in patients with psoriasis. Oral dosing of icotrokinra, as early as week 4, substantially reduced psoriasis-relevant biomarkers in serum across all dosing regimens compared with placebo. In line with clinical responses seen in FRONTIER-1 and -2 studies, the greatest reductions in serum biomarkers were observed with the icotrokinra 100 mg BID regimen. This systemic PD response with icotrokinra was dose dependent and sustained through week 52. While some receptor antagonists have been shown to increase their respective ligand levels in serum (, ), icotrokinra induced these systemic PD changes without increasing serum levels of IL-23 through 1 year of treatment. Previous studies showed that icotrokinra potently and selectively inhibits IL-23 signaling (), and the results presented here further confirm that icotrokinra selectively blocks IL-23–driven inflammation in patients with psoriasis without broader impacts on circulating proteins.

In addition to these systemic PD changes, icotrokinra drove PD changes in the target tissue with attenuation of transcriptional skin biomarkers that are relevant to disease and IL-23 pathway activation in psoriasis. Furthermore, icotrokinra downregulated psoriasis-associated proteins in tape strips of lesional skin to levels observed in nonlesional skin. Icotrokinra’s PD response was positively correlated with increasing exposures, as well as the clinical response, suggesting a strong relationship between the PD and clinical exposure-response. Ongoing phase III trials of icotrokinra (ICONIC-LEAD [ NCT06095115 ], ICONIC-TOTAL [ NCT06095102 ], ICONIC-ADVANCE 1 [ NCT06143878 ], and ICONIC-ADVANCE 2 [ NCT06220604 ]) in broad populations of adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis will further confirm and provide additional details regarding safety and efficacy profiles, including patient reported outcomes and how they correlate to biomarker changes in larger patient cohorts.

In addition to defining the magnitude of skin PD response with icotrokinra, these analyses suggests that tape-strip sampling can provide a minimally invasive alternative to skin biopsies for evaluating disease biology and treatment response in participants with psoriasis. Tape-strip sampling offers several advantages over full-thickness biopsies, including its minimally invasive technique and ease of sample collection, making it a more convenient option for patients. Additionally, tape-stripping allows for real-time analysis of changes in the skin, making it suitable for monitoring disease progression or treatment responses.

The results reported here have some limitations. In addition to reported numerical differences in baseline characteristics of participants in this serum and tissue biomarker analysis, only a small number of participants consented to the optional skin biopsy substudy. As such, there were more differences in baseline characteristics of participants who consented to skin biopsy sampling, and results should be interpreted within this context. Due to these limitations, reported skin transcriptional changes were qualitative; therefore, no quantitative interpretations among dosing regimens or the magnitude of the effect could be drawn. Tape-strip sampling also has some notable limitations, including that it only samples the outer epidermal layers, so deeper layers of skin are not profiled as can be done with full-thickness biopsies. Additionally, similar to skin biopsy collections, tape-strip sampling could be influenced by factors such as operator technique and skin condition. Despite these limitations, our results clearly show that icotrokinra selectively induced dose-dependent systemic PD responses, characterized by early (week 4) and sustained (week 52) reductions in objective biomarkers of IL-23 pathway activation and disease severity. Icotrokinra also attenuated psoriasis biomarkers to normalize inflammation in the skin and drive disease improvement in participants with psoriasis. Taken together, the data strongly suggest that icotrokinra has a PD profile that is consistent with its mechanism of action of selectively inhibiting IL-23–driven inflammation and has the potential to be an oral therapy that will broaden the treatment options for patients with psoriasis.
sections.methods:
Sex was not considered as a biological variable.

FRONTIER-1 study design, patient eligibility criteria, and initial results have been previously reported (). Briefly, FRONTIER-1 participants with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis were randomized 1:1:1:1:1:1 to receive icotrokinra at a dose of 25 mg QD, 25 mg BID, 50 mg QD, 100 mg QD, 100 mg BID, or placebo for 16 weeks. FRONTIER-2 was the LTE study, during which participants randomized to icotrokinra continued their assigned treatment through week 52 and those receiving placebo crossed over to 100 mg QD icotrokinra after week 16 (). Concomitant treatments for psoriasis were prohibited, except for shampoos containing salicylic acid and nonmedicated topical moisturizers.

Blood samples were collected through week 52. Serum IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-23 concentrations were measured using commercially available kits from EMD Millipore Corporation and analyzed on the SMCxPRO instrument. The IL-22 assay was developed internally on the SMC platform and run on the SMCxPRO instrument. A custom BD-2 assay, developed by Mesoscale Discovery (MSD), was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol and read on the MESO QuickPlex SQ120 MSD instrument. A broad evaluation of protein expression was also conducted on these serum samples, using the Olink Explore HT platform (Olink Proteomics).

The protocol for protein extraction from tape-strip samples was optimized using the method described by Clausen et al. (). See for protocol details. Briefly, 20 tape-strips were collected from lesional or nonlesional skin using D-squame tape discs at each sampling time point (lesional and nonlesional at baseline; lesional at week 16). Protein was extracted from the last 4 tape-strips of each patient to sample the deepest layers of skin. BD-2 and broad proteomics were performed using MSD and Olink Explore HT platform assays per manufacturer’s protocol.

Skin biopsies for RNA sequencing were collected from a subset of patients. See for protocol details.

Participant and disease characteristics at baseline were compared between placebo and combined icotrokinra participants with available serum samples using 1-way ANOVA for continuous variables and χ 2 for categorical variables. Due to small sample sizes, comparisons between placebo and 100 mg BID icotrokinra participants with available Olink tape-strip data were performed using Kruskal-Wallis for continuous variables and χ 2 for categorical variables, except baseline IGA 3/4, whose P value was calculated using Fisher’s exact test.

Log 2 FC from baseline and comparisons between all icotrokinra doses and baseline for serum biomarkers through week 52 were calculated directly using a linear mixed effects model with main and interaction fixed effects of treatment arm, time, and participant random effect, using post hoc estimated marginal mean.

Differential protein analyte analysis was performed using the R package OlinkAnalyze (DOI: 10.32614/CRAN.package.OlinkAnalyze). Statistical testing was performed using the olink_ttest function from this package, which applied a Welch 2-sample t test or paired t test at confidence level 0.95 for every protein for a given grouping variable, correcting for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method. Volcano plots for both serum and tape-strip samples were generated in R using ggplot2 with intensity-normalized protein expression values. GSVA was also performed on Olink proteomic data from tape-strip samples by generating protein sets from the gene sets described under the transcriptomic analysis.

RNA sequencing data analysis and GSVA were performed with the GSVA R package (). Gene sets used for GSVA were from published data (, –), BioCarta pathways, and MSigDB hallmark pathways. Given the limited number of individuals participating in the skin biopsy substudy, only pooled icotrokinra versus placebo analysis was performed.

Data from weeks 0–52 for all participants were pooled, and PASI percentage improvement was evaluated for correlation with BD-2 and IL-22 serum levels using Pearson’s correlation. These data were also grouped into 6 PASI percentage improvement categories, <25%, 25%–49%, 50%–74%, 75%–89%, 90%–99%, and 100%, and adjusted P values were calculated using Tukey’s test for multiple comparisons of means.

Data from all FRONTIER-1 and -2 participants were included in this analysis. Indirect response models involving a simultaneous fit of BD-2 levels and PASI scores were used to describe the longitudinal population PK/PD of the PASI and biomarker time courses having a common drug concentration resulting in EC 50 . The model for the drug effect on continuous PASI accounted for a placebo effect.

The study was approved by each site’s institutional review board(s)/ethics committee for all sites. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their participation in the study.

title: Long-Term Efficacy of Tildrakizumab in the Treatment of Psoriasis.
abstract: The pathogenesis of psoriasis has been linked to autoimmune and autoinflammatory traits that result in atypical cytokine and keratinocyte activation and proliferation. Many cytokine pathways are involved in the development of inflammation with interleukin-23 (IL-23) playing a significant role in plaque-type psoriasis. Biologic agents that target specific cytokines have shown to be effective therapies in the treatment of plaque-type psoriasis over other conventional treatments such as systemic retinoids. Tildrakizumab is an immunoglobulin G1-kappa monoclonal antibody that inhibits the IL-23/IL-17 pathway and has demonstrated through two three-part randomized Phase 3 clinical trials (reSURFACE 1 and reSURFACE 2) and their extension trials to be an efficacious and safe therapy for the targeted treatment of moderate-to-severe plaque-type psoriasis.

title: Cedirogant in adults with psoriasis: a phase II, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
abstract: Background Dysregulated interleukin (IL)-17/IL-23 signalling contributes to psoriasis pathogenesis. Cedirogant is an inverse agonist of nuclear receptor ROR-gamma isoform 2 (RORyt), a key transcription factor responsible for IL-17 synthesis and a regulator of the T helper 17 cell lineage programme. Objectives To evaluate the efficacy and safety of cedirogant to treat moderate-to-severe psoriasis. Methods In this phase IIb, multicentre, double-blind, 16-week study (NCT05044234), adults aged 18-65 years were randomized 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 to once-daily oral cedirogant 75 mg, 150 mg, 375 mg or placebo. Efficacy results based on observed cases were summarized descriptively. Results Of 156 enrolled patients, most were male (70.5%); 39 patients were randomized to each treatment. Only 47 patients completed the study; the study was terminated early owing to preclinical findings. At week 16, PASI 75 achievement rates (primary endpoint) were 29%, 8% and 42% in the cedirogant 75-mg, 150-mg and 375-mg groups, respectively, and 0% in the placebo group. AE rates were similar in the cedirogant 75-mg, 150-mg and placebo groups, and higher in the cedirogant 375-mg group; most AEs were mild or moderate. Conclusions Patients with psoriasis who received cedirogant showed PASI improvement, and cedirogant was generally well tolerated. The results should be interpreted in the context of early study termination. Cedirogant development has been discontinued.

title: Risk of Cutaneous T Cell Lymphoma with Psoriasis Biologic Therapies.
abstract: Background The risk of developing cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL) in patients using psoriasis biologics has not been well characterized. The goals of this review were to investigate the incidence of CTCL in patients with psoriasis receiving biologic therapy in clinical trials and psoriasis registries, and to review cases of CTCL and biologic use reported in scientific publications. Methods The US National Library of Medicine clinical trials database (clinicaltrials.gov) was queried to identify phase 3 and 4 clinical trials of the 12 biologic agents currently FDA approved for psoriatic disease. The incidence of CTCL in these trials was examined and summarized. To examine the incidence of CTCL in psoriasis registries, a Medline search was conducted. Finally, we performed a systematic review of CTCL cases reported in the literature. Results Only two cases of CTCL were reported in 35,801 subjects with psoriasis receiving a biologic agent in the active arm of 108 psoriasis phase 3 clinical trials. One of these CTCL cases was determined by the investigator to be CTCL misdiagnosed as psoriasis prior to randomization. No cases of CTCL were reported in 5440 subjects with psoriasis in 34 phase 4 clinical trials. Only one case of CTCL was identified in 34,111 registry subjects. In the literature, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors had the highest number of reported cases of CTCL (34 cases), followed by interleukin (IL)-17 inhibitors (7 cases), and IL-12/23 inhibitors (6 cases). No cases of CTCL were found to be reported with IL-23 inhibitors. Conclusion Our findings indicate that the development of CTCL is rare in the setting of psoriasis biologic use. Of the limited number of cases of CTCL found, most were in the setting of TNF inhibitor use and no cases of CTCL were reported in the setting of IL-23 inhibitor use.

sections.other:
Psoriasis is a common, multisystem inflammatory disease characterized by erythematous, scaling patches, and plaques. Psoriasis affects roughly 125 million people worldwide (3% prevalence) and is associated with comorbidities such as psoriatic arthritis, cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, and obesity [, ]. The underlying pathogenesis involves dysregulated cutaneous immunity with dysfunction of T1 and T17 cells, dendritic cells, keratinocytes, fibroblasts, and macrophages. This results in keratinocyte hyperproliferation and the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-17, IL-23, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNFα), and interferon-gamma (IFNγ) [, , ].

Our improved understanding of the inflammatory molecular pathways involved in psoriasis has led to the development and US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval of multiple biologic therapies. These therapies target the cytokine-mediated pathogenesis of psoriasis and are approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe psoriasis []. The main classes of biologics include TNFα inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, IL-23 inhibitors, and IL-12/23 inhibitors.

An important consideration for using biologic agents is their safety profiles. The efficacy of a biologic agent in treating psoriasis must be weighed against potential adverse events []. Through clinical trials and post-marketing surveillance, multiple adverse events have been reported. Reported events include injection site reactions, infections, heart failure, and malignancy [, ]. The goal of this review is to focus on one particular type of malignancy, which is cutaneous T cell lymphoma (CTCL).
