sections.other:
Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated, proliferative, inflammatory skin condition that predominantly involves the skin, nails, and joints . According to the Global Psoriasis Atlas, approximately 60 million people have psoriasis worldwide . Psoriasis not only is limited to the skin but is also a multisystem disease associated with psoriatic arthritis (PsA), increased hyperlipidemia, hypertension, coronary artery disease, diabetes mellitus (DM), and a higher body mass index (BMI). This disease can also cause adverse effects on overall quality of life, including an impact on psychological and mental health . Many treatments are available for psoriasis management, ranging from simple topical treatment to systemic biological treatment. Considering the role played by neuroendocrine signaling, corticotropin-realizing factor (CRF) and its first receptor (CRFR-1) in psoriasis pathogenesis, Andrzej T. Slominski et al. , predict that they may be new psoriasis treatment targets.

Biological therapy has become one of the main treatments for psoriasis and has played an active and effective role in treating severe, refractory, and special types of psoriasis . Several biologic agents, such as etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab (ADA), ustekinumab (USTE), guselkumab (GUSE), secukinumab (SECU), and ixekizumab (IXE), have been approved for the treatment of psoriasis in China .

Different tools are used to assess psoriasis severity. Salgado-Boquete et al. presented a classification algorithm composed of various disease measures that classify psoriasis patients into three categories: mild, moderate, and severe.

With the gradual increase in the number of biological drugs approved for the treatment of psoriasis in China, considering the high prevalence of tuberculosis and hepatitis B (HBV) in the Chinese population, the rational use of safe and effective biological drugs has become a priority among physicians . Hence, real-world data in China regarding the actual effectiveness, tolerability and safety of different biologics remain limited.

The disease severity of psoriasis is mainly assessed subjectively via the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI), Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) and body surface area (BSA). The same tools are used to evaluate treatment efficacy in clinical settings, but an optimal measure of treatment response may overlook systemic response in psoriasis patients under treatment. There is not only a need to compare different biologics to quickly guide dermatologists but also to assess biologic treatment efficacy using objective parameters such as metabolic and inflammatory biomarkers.

We conducted simple randomized sampling and follow-up of all psoriatic patients receiving biological treatment from January 2023 to June 2024 on the basis of four time points: baseline (time point 1, TP1), week 4 (time point 2, TP2), week 12 (time point 3, TP3) and week 24 (time point 4, TP4). Five biologics were given to patients during our study. These antagonists included one tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) antagonist (ADA), one interleukin IL-12/23 inhibitor (USTE), one interleukin-23 inhibitor (GUSE), and two IL-17 antagonists ( SECU and IXE). The doses of biologics and the timing of their administration were determined according to the respective biologics protocols as follows – : ADA, 80 mg at the beginning, 40 mg after one week and 40 mg every two weeks. For USTE, we prescribed 45 mg followed by 45 mg at fourth week and 45 mg every 12 weeks .We gave 90 mg for the patients whose weight was more than 100 kg. We prescribed 300 mg of SECU at the beginning of treatment, weeks 1, 2, 3, 4, and every 4 weeks. For young (6–18 years old) and less than 50 kg patients, we gave 150 mg for every injection. We administered 100 mg of GUSE at week 0, week 4 and every 8 weeks .For IXE, we gave 160 mg at week 0 and 80 mg every four weeks .The dosage was reduced to half for kids and teens .

Considering the large number of psoriatic patients who are being treated in our department, we preferred to use Cochran’s sample size calculation formula, which is useful for large or unknown populations , . This formula combines the level of precision, confidence level and variability as follows: n = Z 2 ∗ p∗ q/e 2 , where n is the sample size, Z is the Z score (Z = 1.96 for the 95% confidence interval), p is the proportion ( p = .5), q equals 1-p and e is the level of precision (we use e = 5%).

Then, we determined that a minimum sample size of 385 participants was needed. This sample size was considered a sufficient representative sample of the psoriatic population treated with systemic biologic treatment.

This study included all patients aged no more than 70 years of both sexes who were diagnosed with psoriasis vulgaris and who fulfilled the criteria for treatment with biologics. Psoriatic patients who had received biologic treatment before this study or who changed biologics during follow-up were excluded. Psoriatic patients who were treated by biologics in our department but who began it before the beginning of our study, patients who fulfilled the criteria to be treated by biologics but were unable to afford treatment financially, and patients who were unable to comply with the planned cohort monitoring or whose follow-up was expected to be difficult were also excluded from the study.

For each patient, the baseline patient and disease characteristics were recorded. These included sex, age, weight, height, date of initial diagnosis, disease duration, history of comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidemia), previous therapeutic history (topical treatment, phototherapy, biologic treatments, systemic non-biologic treatments), and area of psoriasis involvement (nails, joints, scalp, palmoplantar, and genital area). BMI was calculated according to the following formula , : weight (kg)/[height (m)] 2 .

The severity of the disease and treatment response were evaluated by the PASI, BSA and DLQI at baseline and after 4, 12 and 24 weeks of follow-up. These three parameters were used for the evaluation of clinical efficacy.

After clinical evaluation by a physician, dermoscopy or histopathology was conducted by different dermatologists to confirm the diagnosis if needed. After the diagnosis and evaluation of disease severity, patients were categorized into 3 groups: mild, moderate or severe. Patients were categorized as mild if they had a PASI ≤ 3 and a BSA ≤ 3% or a DLQI < 5, moderate if they had a PASI 3–10 and a BSA 3–10% or a DLQI 5–10 and severe if they had a PASI ≥ 10 and a BSA ≥ 10% or a DLQI > 10. For the assessment of clinical efficacy, we also evaluated and compared the PASI 100 score for different biologics at week 4, week 12 and week 24 of follow-up. PASI 100 indicates complete resolution of the patient’s basal lesions, which is commonly known as complete skin clearance (CSC).

From the beginning, we paid attention to the influence of biologics on metabolic parameters, including triglycerides (TGs), total cholesterol (TC), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), non-HDL-C, glucose (GLU) and uric acid (UA), as well as inflammatory indicators, including the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), TNF-α, IL-6 and ferritin, from psoriatic patients. In this study, the reference standards for major lipid indicators are from the 2023 Chinese guidelines for lipid management as follows : TC < 5.2 mmol/L, LDL < 3.4 mmol/L, TG < 1.7 mmol/L, non-HDL < 4.1 mmol/L and HDL ≥ 0.9 mmol/L. Hyperglycemia was defined as a fasting blood glucose (FBG) level greater than 6.1 mmol/L, and an FBG level greater than 7 mmol/L was considered to indicate DM according to the World Health Organization (WHO) definition . The reference values are the normal range used in our laboratory fixed as follows: UA (202–416 µmol/L), ESR < 15 mm/h, ferritin (30–400 ng/mL), TNF-α ≤ 8.5 pg/mL, hs-CRP (0–5 mg/L) and IL-6 (0–7 pg/ml) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

After initial screening, which included screening for infectious diseases such as HIV, viral hepatitis B and C, tuberculosis (TB) and malignancies, a final decision about biologic choice was made. Patients with hepatitis B virus were treated with entecavir, and biologics were started after a negative test. Those with positive T-SPOT results but without TB symptoms were administered an anti-TB regimen for three months and then started biologics after screening.

After TP1, we conducted follow-ups for the patients at week 4 (TP2), week 12 (TP3), and week 24 (TP4). At each time point, the PASI, BSA, DLQI, and blood levels of metabolic and inflammatory markers were assessed. At the same time, any treatment side effects or any clinical complaints from patients were recorded.

Each patient’s required details were recorded in Microsoft Excel 2016. After the data collection, we transferred the Excel file to SPSS software version 25.0 for analysis. We used the ANOVA test to determine if there was a statistically significant difference between the means of different groups. The chi-square test, t test, and one-way ANOVA test were used where needed to compare the scores of the indicators. We considered a two-sided p value less than 5% ( p < .05) to indicate statistical significance.

The research protocol of this study was approved by the Shenzhen Hospital of Southern Medical University Ethical Committee (Reference number: NYSZYYEC20210001). The patients were informed of the objectives and conduct of the research (or, if applicable, their legal guardians were informed on their behalf) and signed a written informed consent to participate. This study was conducted in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration.
sections.methods:
This study is a monocentric, prospective, randomized cohort that includes patients receiving systemic biological treatment for moderate to severe psoriasis.

The study included patients who received biological treatment in the Department of Dermatology, Cosmetology and Venereology, Shenzhen Hospital of Southern Medical University. The department has set the psoriasis clinic as one of the national psoriasis programs in the hospital.
sections.results:
This study included 385 participants; among them, 274 were males (71.2%), and 111 were females (28.8%). The age of the participants ranged from 6 to 70 years, with a mean age of 39.26 ± 12.52 years (SD). Only 6 patients less than 18 years old were treated with biologics: five patients were treated with SECU (aged 6, 7, 9, and 17 years old respectively) and one patient was treated with USTE. The mean BMI of our study population was 24.95 ± 4.84 kg/m 2 . The age of psoriasis onset in our study population was 28.88 ± 13.62 years (SD), and the mean disease duration was 10.17 ± 9.08 years (SD). Five biologics were given to our study cohort: IXE (42.86%), SECU (36.10%), GUSE (16.10%), ADA (2.86%), and USTE (2.08%) (Table ).

Overall, there was clinical improvement from baseline to week 24, with a statistically significant difference ( p < .001) among the different time points.

The DLQI score was 12.99 ± 6.55 (SD) at TP1 and 0.58 ± 1.92 (SD) at TP4. The same decreasing trend was also observed for the PASI score: the PASI score was 21.81 ± 13.52 (SD) at TP1 and 0.62 ± 2.14 (SD) at TP4. The mean BSA decreased from 40.66 ± 21.87 (SD) at TP1 to 0.80 ± 3.08 (SD) at TP4 (Table ).

For all three parameters, the trend decreased rapidly from baseline to week 24 (Fig. ).

Overall, 35 patients (9.09%), 145 (37.14%) and 335 (86.75%) achieved CSC at TP2, TP3, and TP4, respectively, during follow-up. The proportion of patients who achieved a PASI of 100 was IXE 12.12% at TP2 and 87.27% at TP4 for IXE and 7.79% at TP2 and 89.92% at TP4 for SECU. Compared with other biologics, IXE and SECU showed better performance. At TP3, the proportion of patients who obtained PASI 100 was 38.71% for those using GUSE and 40.28% for those using SECU. When all biologics were compared, few patients achieved CSC after treatment with ADA or USTE (Table ).

For all biologics, there was a statistically significant difference (p < .001) in the PASI score, DLQI score, and BSA from baseline to week 24. However, no significant difference was found in the DLQI among biologics for the same time point ( p > .05 at all time points). A statistically significant difference was observed for the PASI at TP2 and TP3 ( p < .001) and for the BSA at TP2 ( p = .001), indicating further cutaneous improvements in the IXE and SECU compared with the other biologics (Table ).

For all the metabolic markers tested, there was systemic efficacy, as the number of abnormal markers (markers with increased values) decreased from TP1 through TP4. This was also reflected by the sum of the values within the normal range and the decreasing values of the markers, which increased from TP1 to TP4, with a statistically significant difference for all metabolic markers (Table ).

We compared the mean values of metabolic markers for different biologic therapies at the same time point. For all 5 biologics used in this study, a statistically significant difference in the efficacy of biologics was observed for GUSE at TP3 ( p = .041), with low values of TC (mean = 4.35 mmol/L). Compared with other biologics, GUSE also showed significantly greater efficacy ( p = .046) in decreasing non-HDL-C (mean = 3.16 mmol/L) at TP3. SECU and ADA, respectively, had greater effects on GLU (TP3, mean value = 5.75 mmol/L, p = .037) and UA (TP4, mean = 320.15 µmol/L, p = .033) (Table ).

For all the included inflammatory markers, there was biological efficacy, as the number of abnormal markers decreased from TP1 to TP4. The sum of the values within the normal range and the decreased values of the markers also increased from TP1 to TP4, with a statistically significant difference except for TNF-α ( p = .352) (Table ).

For all 5 biologics tested in this study, a statistically significant difference ( p = .024) was observed in the efficacy of biologics at TP4, where GUSE showed greater efficacy in decreasing TNF-α than the other biologics did, as indicated by the mean values (Table ).
sections.discussion:
Biological treatment is a rapidly expanding type of treatment that is now widely used to manage psoriasis and its comorbidities. It has become one of the main medical options for psoriasis patients. It has played an active and effective role in treating moderate to severe and special types of psoriasis. As the use of biological therapy to treat psoriasis is recent and fast-growing in China, there is a great need for real-world studies to evaluate its clinical and systemic efficacy and to guide clinicians and patients in the selection of biologics. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of biological treatment and compare different biologics in the Chinese psoriatic population. It included 385 participants. Among them, 274 were males (71.2%), and 111 were females (28.8%). A slight male predominance was also reported by Jiang et al. in China. The findings of the present study may be due to sex differences in the Chinese population, which is predominantly male . Psoriasis is a multifactor disease that is equally prevalent in both sexes, although the results from a recent study have shown that, on average, men have more severe forms of the disease than women do .

To assess clinical efficacy in treating skin lesions, we evaluated three parameters, namely, the PASI score, DLQI score, and BSA, from baseline to week 24. For all three parameters, the trend decreased rapidly from baseline to week 24. The mean values of these parameters gradually decreased from baseline to week 24. Five biologics were given to our study cohort: IXE, SECU, GUSE, ADA, and USTE. For all biologics, there was a statistically significant difference in the PASI, DLQI, and BSA from baseline to week 24. However, no significant difference in the DLQI among different biologics at the same time point was observed. A statistically significant difference was observed for the PASI at weeks 4 and 12 ( p < .001) and for the BSA at week 4 ( p = .001), indicating that the clinical efficacy of IXE and SECU was greater than that of other biologics. The same findings were revealed in a meta-analysis conducted in 2020, which revealed that all biologics were more efficacious than placebo or methotrexate at 10–16 weeks . IXE is a highly tolerated biologic agent with minimal side effects . Studies have shown that IXE is the fastest-acting biologic agent. A comparative study revealed a more rapid onset of action for IXE than for GUSE during the treatment of plaque psoriasis . Compared with ADA in the treatment of PsA, both IXE and ADA were found to have similar abilities to control symptoms . Another study revealed that infliximab and ixekizumab combined and had high short-term efficacy but relatively lower tolerability than the other agents did . SECU has excellent efficacy for the management of several psoriasis domains, such as the scalp, nail, and palmoplantar psoriasis and PsA . According to Bajel et al. Compared with several other subcutaneous biologic agents, such as etanercept and USTE, SECU has high efficacy. Our results are similar to the findings of other studies that confirmed better performance of the SECU than the USTE in PsA management , . GUSE is approved for different indications, including moderate–to-severe plaque psoriasis and PsA. Compared with ADA, it has shown superior efficacy in the management of plaque psoriasis, palmoplantar psoriasis and scalp psoriasis . Our results are comparable to the findings of Reich et al. where GUSE and IXE showed the same efficacy at week 24 of follow-up .

We also evaluated how biologics can contribute to clearing skin lesions from baseline. Overall, 9.09%, 37.14%, and 86.75% achieved PASI 100 at week 4, 12, and 24, respectively. Compared with other biologics, the two IL-17 A antagonists (IXE and SECU) performed better. At week 12, a high percentage of patients who achieved PASI 100 were positive for GUSE (38.71%) and SECU (40.28%). A low percentage of the PASI 100 was continuously observed for ADA and USTE. The achievement of CSC is a very important goal in daily dermatology practice, especially given patients’ expectations. With the era of biologic therapy for psoriasis treatment, the clearance of skin lesions has become a realistic target in clinical settings , . Our results were similar to the findings of different clinical trials where PASI 100 response rates were higher with IXE and SECU than with USTE ,– . Some real-world studies confirmed that the efficacy of GUSE was significantly better than that of ADA ,, . A systematic literature review aimed at analyzing PASI 100 response during psoriasis treatment revealed that PASI 100 response rates ranged from 3.7 to 11.1% at week 12 and 44.3–57.2% at week 24 for TNF-α .

To evaluate systemic efficacy, we tested different metabolic and inflammatory markers at baseline and at each time point. For all metabolic and inflammatory markers tested, there was systemic efficacy, as the number of abnormal markers can decreased from baseline to week 24. The sum of values within the normal range and the decreasing values of the markers increased from baseline to week 24, with a statistically significant difference, except for TNF-α ( p = .352). We also compared the mean values of metabolic and inflammatory markers from the study participants for each biologic therapy at the same time point. For all 5 biologics used in this study, a statistically significant difference in biologics’ efficacy was observed for GUSE at TP3 and TP4 for TNF-α compared with other biologics. SECU and ADA had greater effects on GLU and UA, respectively. The same results were reported by Timis et al. who confirmed that biologic treatment significantly improved CRP, HDL-C, and ESR levels at the 6th month. On the other hand, the level of ADA, which is a TNF-α antagonist, did not significantly differ from that of TNF-α in this study. This may be due to the small number of participants who were treated with the TNF-α antagonist. Psoriasis is an inflammatory autoimmune disease that is accompanied by inflammatory and metabolic disorders such as metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease. The biologics used to treat psoriasis act by targeting different cytokines involved in its pathogenesis . For example, ADA targets TNF-α, whereas IXE and SECU specifically target IL-17 A, resulting in blockade of the activation of immune and inflammatory responses. Various studies have confirmed the ability of biologics to positively affect the metabolic status of psoriatic patients , . Sichun et al. in China recently showed how biologics can affect glycophospholipid metabolism and facilitate the transition from metabolic status to an anti-inflammatory phenotype in psoriasis vulgaris patients.

As any other treatment, the biologics may cause side effects. The commonly attributed to biologics are the injection site reactions, infections, allergic reactions, and reactivation of latent TB .We monitored at every TP the occurrence of clinical situations which may be related to the use of biologics. We also found these conditions in this study but at a low prevalence. For example, 0.77% of this study’ participants presented active TB at week 4 against 0.25% at week 24. A study conducted on psoriatic patients with latent TB treated showed that active TB occurred in 0.1–0.2% of the patients who received biological treatment .This prevalence is lower compared to our results. This difference may be due to the prevalence of TB in Chinese population which is relatively elevated.

To our knowledge, this study is the first to compare five different biologics at the same time and in real-world settings. Moreover, very few studies have tested the impact of biologic treatment during psoriasis management by evaluating systemic efficacy, which adds more considerations for choosing biologics.

A lower number of participants who used ADA and USTE constituted a limitation of this study. A comparative study with a large number of participants for every biologic treatment conducted in many research centers may help support our findings.

This study confirmed the clinical efficacy of biologics and their contribution to achieving CSC, an important indicator of quality of life for psoriatic patients. We found that biologics have different effects on metabolic markers, such as GUSE on non-HDL and SECU on glucose. We also discovered that all biologics can reduce inflammation not only in the skin but also in the whole body. This will help the busy practicing dermatologist make a fast choice of biologic treatment for use according to the desired clinical or systemic therapeutic effects. The biologics used in this study have been shown to be safe, even though some side effects of the drugs, like TB re - activation, have been encountered. Our study ultimately validated psoriasis as a systemic disease.

title: Bimekizumab Efficacy in Psoriasis by Subgroups: Post Hoc Analysis of Phase 3/3b Clinical Trials.
abstract: Introduction Patient demographics, disease characteristics, and treatment history can impact the efficacy of biologic treatments in patients with psoriasis. Understanding the efficacy of biologics, such as bimekizumab, across diverse patient subgroups is important for optimising treatment outcomes. Here, we assess whether high overall clinical responses observed in bimekizumab-treated patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis are consistent across subgroups, both versus comparators and with long-term treatment. Methods Data were analysed post hoc from the BE SURE, BE VIVID, and BE READY phase 3 trials, their open-label extension (OLE) BE BRIGHT, and the BE RADIANT phase 3b trial. Patients received either bimekizumab or adalimumab to week 24 (BE SURE), bimekizumab or ustekinumab to week 52 (BE VIVID), and bimekizumab or secukinumab to week 48 (BE RADIANT). In the 3-year pooled analysis (all trials), included patients received bimekizumab continuously from baseline into the OLE. Subgroups of patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis were defined by age, sex, weight, disease duration, disease severity, nail involvement (modified Nail Psoriasis Severity Index > 0), and prior biologic exposure, at baseline. The proportions of patients achieving complete skin clearance (PASI 100; 100% improvement from baseline in Psoriasis Area and Severity Index) in each subgroup are reported alongside 95% confidence intervals (CI). Modified non-responder imputation (mNRI) was used for missing data. Results Following comparator-controlled periods, the proportion of bimekizumab-treated patients who achieved PASI 100 was consistent across subgroups and numerically greater versus patients who received adalimumab (to week 24), ustekinumab (to week 52), and secukinumab (to week 48) in all subgroups. Among patients who received bimekizumab continuously for 3 years (N = 1107), PASI 100 response rates remained consistent across age (68.6% [40 to 20 years]), disease severity (67.7% [PASI 12 to Conclusion Bimekizumab demonstrated consistently high long-term efficacy in patients with psoriasis across diverse subgroups. Higher rates of PASI 100 were achieved with bimekizumab versus adalimumab, ustekinumab, and secukinumab, across all subgroups. These results highlight bimekizumab as an effective treatment for a broad range of people living with psoriasis. Trial registration NCT03412747, NCT03370133, NCT03410992, NCT03598790, NCT03536884.

sections.other:
Psoriasis is a common, chronic, immune-related disease of the skin, estimated to affect 56 million adults globally [], approximately 20–30% of whom have moderate to severe disease []. According to the Global Burden of Disease study in 2019, there were 4.6 million incident cases of psoriasis worldwide [, ]. Given the significant physical, mental, and social impacts associated with the disease, psoriasis represents a large global health burden [].

A multitude of different systemic treatment options are available for psoriasis, including conventional non-biologics, biologics, and small molecule therapies []. The introduction of novel biologic interleukin (IL) inhibitors has made complete skin clearance an achievable treatment goal for patients with psoriasis, greatly increasing the potential for improved quality of life []. However, there is significant diversity among the global patient population living with psoriasis and it is important to understand the relationship between patient characteristics and the efficacy of biologic therapies to optimise treatment outcomes.

Patients with moderate to severe psoriasis are in a state of chronic systemic inflammation [], and therefore often have increased rates of comorbidities such as obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and cardiovascular disease caused by increased insulin resistance [–]. Several post hoc subgroup analyses have identified obesity and T2DM as factors which significantly impact response to biologic therapies [–]. Additionally, while switching between biologic therapies can improve clinical outcomes for some patients, previous exposure to biologics has been linked with an impaired response to subsequent biologic therapies [–]. Given the chronic nature of psoriasis and the range of different therapies available, discontinuing and switching treatments is common and patients often receive more than one biologic therapy [–]. Furthermore, patient age, and duration and severity of disease, may also be associated with numerical differences in clinical outcomes following biologic treatment [, ]. There is therefore still a need for treatments that consistently provide high rates of clinical responses across a variety of patients, regardless of patient and disease characteristics [].

Bimekizumab is a monoclonal IgG1 antibody that selectively inhibits IL-17F in addition to IL-17A, both of which are pivotal drivers of psoriasis pathogenesis [–]. Bimekizumab has demonstrated rapid onset of response and superior efficacy versus adalimumab, ustekinumab, and secukinumab in multiple phase 3/3b studies in patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, with durable clinical responses in the long term [–]. Whilst post hoc analyses in patient subgroups stratified according to patient demographics, disease characteristics, and treatment histories have been performed for several other biologics [–, ], such analyses for bimekizumab have not yet been reported. It is important to establish whether the efficacy of bimekizumab is consistent across heterogeneous subgroups of patients with psoriasis, particularly those with higher prevalence of the disease and increased rates of treatment failure, as these groups are most relevant for dermatologists to aid clinical decision-making.

The purpose of this post hoc analysis was to evaluate the consistency of clinical responses to bimekizumab across diverse subgroups based on baseline demographics, disease characteristics, and treatment histories. To achieve this, we investigated the long-term efficacy of bimekizumab over 3 years in these patient subgroups, and also compared response rates with adalimumab, ustekinumab, and secukinumab, over periods of up to 1 year.
sections.methods:
Data were analysed post hoc from the BE SURE ( NCT03412747 ), BE VIVID ( NCT03370133 ), and BE READY ( NCT03410992 ) phase 3 trials, their open-label extension (OLE) BE BRIGHT ( NCT03598790 ), and the BE RADIANT phase 3b trial ( NCT03536884 ). Study designs and eligibility criteria have been published previously for all trials [–]. Study protocols, amendments, and patient informed consent were reviewed by a national, regional, or independent ethics committee or institutional review board. All studies were conducted in accordance with current version of the applicable regulatory and International Conference on Harmonization Good Clinical Practice requirements, the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki [], and the local laws of the countries involved. All participants provided informed written consent documented in accordance with local regulations.

In BE SURE, patients were randomised 1:1:1 to bimekizumab 320 mg every 4 weeks (Q4W) for 56 weeks; bimekizumab 320 mg Q4W to week 16, then every 8 weeks (Q8W) to week 56; or adalimumab 80 mg at baseline, followed by 40 mg at week 1 then every 2 weeks (Q2W), then bimekizumab 320 mg Q4W from weeks 24 to 56 [].

In BE VIVID, patients were randomised 4:2:1 to bimekizumab, ustekinumab, or placebo. Bimekizumab 320 mg was administered Q4W to week 52. Ustekinumab 45 mg or 90 mg (in patients weighing ≤ 100 kg or > 100 kg, respectively) [] was administered at baseline and week 4, then every 12 weeks (Q12W) thereafter [].

In BE RADIANT, patients were randomised 1:1 to bimekizumab or secukinumab. Bimekizumab 320 mg was administered Q4W to week 16, then patients were re-randomised 1:2 to bimekizumab Q4W or Q8W to week 48. Secukinumab was administered 300 mg weekly to week 4, then Q4W to week 48 [].

In BE READY, patients were randomised 4:1 to bimekizumab 320 mg Q4W or placebo. Bimekizumab-treated patients achieving 90% improvement from baseline in Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI 90) at week 16 were re-randomised (1:1:1) to receive bimekizumab 320 mg Q4W, bimekizumab 320 mg Q8W, or placebo to week 56 [].

Patients who completed the BE VIVID, BE SURE, and BE READY trials were eligible to enter BE BRIGHT; patients who completed the 48-week double-blinded period of BE RADIANT were eligible to enter its OLE [, ]. On OLE entry, patients received bimekizumab 320 mg Q4W or Q8W for up to 3 years (BE RADIANT OLE week 96) or 4 years (BE BRIGHT OLE week 144) of total treatment. All remaining bimekizumab Q4W patients were switched to bimekizumab Q8W at OLE week 16/48 (BE RADIANT/BE BRIGHT) or their next scheduled clinic visit.

Efficacy responses were evaluated across patient subgroups defined according to baseline demographics, disease characteristics, and treatment history. These included age (< 40, 40 to < 65, ≥ 65 years), sex (male, female), weight (quartiles), body mass index (BMI; < 25 kg/m 2 , 25 to < 30 kg/m 2 , 30 to < 35 kg/m 2 , and ≥ 35 kg/m 2 ), disease duration (≤ 5 years, > 5 to 10 years, > 10 to 20 years, and > 20 years), disease severity (PASI 12 to < 15, 15 to < 20, and ≥ 20; Investigator’s Global Assessment [IGA] 3, IGA 4), nail involvement (modified nail psoriasis severity index [mNAPSI] > 0; yes, no), scalp involvement (scalp IGA > 0; yes, no), medical history of psoriatic arthritis (PsA; yes, no) or T2DM (yes, no), prior biologic treatment exposure (yes, no), anti-tumour necrosis factor (TNF) exposure (yes, no), anti-IL-17 exposure (yes, no), anti-IL-23 exposure (yes, no), and number of prior biologics (1, ≥ 2). Weight quartiles were calculated on the basis of the overall distribution in each study population for all treatment arms combined. Categories of disease severity were based on PASI ranges considered to be clinically informative for increasing severity.

The primary outcome was the proportion of patients who achieved 100% improvement from baseline in PASI (PASI 100) in each subgroup. Proportions who achieved PASI 90 in each subgroup are reported in the Supplementary Material.

This analysis included all randomised patients who received bimekizumab or adalimumab, ustekinumab, or secukinumab from baseline in the BE SURE, BE VIVID, and BE RADIANT trials, respectively, and all patients pooled across BE VIVID, BE SURE, BE READY, and BE RADIANT who received bimekizumab continuously from baseline and entered their respective OLEs.

Responses are reported at week 24 in BE SURE, week 52 in BE VIVID, week 48 in BE RADIANT (end of the comparator-controlled periods), and OLE week 96 (year 3; pooled analysis). All patients who received bimekizumab were analysed regardless of dosing regimen (bimekizumab Total). The patient subset who received bimekizumab 320 mg Q4W to week 16 and then Q8W thereafter (bimekizumab Q4W/Q8W; the approved dosing regimen for most patients with psoriasis) [, ] were analysed separately for the pooled analysis.

Differences in response rates between subgroups and treatment arms were indicated by non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals (CI), with overlapping CIs indicating no robust difference. Modified non-responder imputation (mNRI) was used for missing data: patients who discontinued treatment due to lack of efficacy or treatment-related adverse events were considered non-responders, and multiple imputation was used for other missing data. Observed cases (OC) are also reported in Supplementary Table .

Below is the link to the electronic supplementary material.
sections.results:
In BE SURE, 319 and 159 patients were randomised to bimekizumab and adalimumab, respectively. In BE VIVID, 321 and 163 patients were randomised to bimekizumab and ustekinumab, respectively. In BE RADIANT, 373 and 370 patients were randomised to bimekizumab and secukinumab, respectively.

The 3-year pooled analysis included 1107 patients who received bimekizumab continuously and entered the OLEs (bimekizumab Total), of whom 374 received the approved dosing regimen (bimekizumab Q4W/Q8W). Baseline demographics and disease characteristics were generally similar between patient groups (Table ).

The overall proportion of patients with complete skin clearance (PASI 100) after 24 weeks of treatment was 68.5% in patients receiving bimekizumab and 31.6% in patients receiving adalimumab. In patients treated with bimekizumab, PASI 100 rates were consistent across all analysed subgroups, with overlapping 95% CIs indicating no meaningful differences in responses (Fig. ). Compared with adalimumab, the proportions of PASI 100 responders with bimekizumab were consistently numerically higher across all subgroups at week 24; 95% CIs were non-overlapping between bimekizumab and adalimumab in almost all subgroups, indicating meaningful differences between the two treatments (Fig. ).

The proportion of PASI 100 responders with bimekizumab was consistent across further subgroups, including IGA score (67.1% [3]/71.3% [4]), medical history of PsA (67.3% [yes]/68.7% [no]), medical history of T2DM (83.6% [yes]/67.4% [no]), scalp involvement (68.3% [yes]/73.3% [no]), and previous exposure to anti-IL-17 (76.5% [yes]/66.3% [no]) and anti-IL-23 inhibitors (60.0% [yes]/68.6% [no]), at week 24.

After 52 weeks of treatment, 67.5% of bimekizumab-treated patients compared with 41.0% of ustekinumab-treated patients achieved PASI 100. The proportion of PASI 100 responders was consistent across all analysed subgroups of bimekizumab-treated patients, as demonstrated by overlapping 95% CIs (Fig. ). Compared with ustekinumab (dose adjusted per label according to weight), the proportions of PASI 100 responders with bimekizumab were numerically higher across all subgroups at week 52, with non-overlapping 95% CIs between the treatments in the majority of subgroups (Fig. ).

With bimekizumab, the rate of PASI 100 achievement at week 52 was consistent across further subgroups, including IGA score (69.8% [3]/64.3% [4]), medical history of PsA (63.1% [yes]/68.5% [no]), medical history of T2DM (75.1% [yes]/66.9% [no]), scalp involvement (66.8% [yes]/78.4% [no]), and previous exposure to anti-IL-17 (69.9% [yes]/66.8% [no]) and anti-IL-23 inhibitors (50.0% [yes]/68.4% [no]), at week 52.

At week 48, 70.0% of patients treated with bimekizumab achieved PASI 100 versus 49.9% of patients treated with secukinumab. Among patients receiving bimekizumab, PASI 100 rates were consistent across all subgroups analysed, with overlapping 95% CIs indicating uniform efficacy and no robust differences (Fig. ). Bimekizumab treatment led to numerically higher PASI 100 rates than secukinumab across all subgroups at week 48 and 95% CIs did not overlap in the majority of subgroups, suggesting meaningful differences between the two treatments (Fig. ).

The proportion of PASI 100 responders with bimekizumab was consistent across further subgroups, including IGA score (69.8% [3]/70.1% [4]) medical history of PsA (63.3% [yes]/71.4% [no]), medical history of T2DM (66.6% [yes]/70.3% [no]), scalp involvement (70.1% [yes]/69.6% [no]), and previous exposure to anti-IL-17 (74.9% [yes]/69.5% [no]) and anti-IL-23 inhibitors (81.0% [yes]/69.3% [no]), at week 48.

After 3 years of treatment, the overall proportion of patients with PASI 100 was 70.1% among all bimekizumab-treated patients who entered the BE RADIANT and BE BRIGHT OLEs, and 74.2% in the bimekizumab Q4W/Q8W subset. The uniformity in PASI 100 response rates observed at the end of comparator-controlled periods in bimekizumab-treated patients was mirrored in the long-term to year 3, across all subgroups analysed (Fig. ). 95% CIs generally overlapped among all subgroups of bimekizumab-treated patients, indicating no robust differences in PASI 100 responses (Fig. ).

The proportion of PASI 100 responders with bimekizumab at year 3 was consistent across further subgroups, including IGA score (71.4% [3]/67.5% [4]), medical history of PsA (66.8% [yes]/70.8% [no]), medical history of T2DM (71.6% [yes]/70.0% [no]), scalp involvement (70.4% [yes]/64.6% [no]), number of prior biologics (73.3% [1]/67.6% [≥ 2]), and previous exposure to anti-IL-17 (73.3% [yes]/69.3% [no]) and anti-IL-23 inhibitors (70.3% [yes]/70.1% [no]). PASI 100 response rates at year 3 in the subset of patients receiving BKZ Q4W/Q8W were consistent with the overall group of bimekizumab-treated patients across all subgroups (Fig. ).

Equivalent trends were seen in these analyses when using PASI 90 as the endpoint (Supplementary Fig. –).
sections.discussion:
This post hoc analysis is the first to evaluate bimekizumab’s efficacy across diverse patient subgroups, incorporating both head-to head phase 3/3b trial data and long-term outcomes. Consistently high proportions of patients achieved complete skin clearance (PASI 100) for up to 3 years of continuous bimekizumab treatment across all the diverse patient subgroups analysed. Moreover, in all subgroups, proportions of patients with complete skin clearance were higher for bimekizumab versus adalimumab, ustekinumab, and secukinumab during the comparator-controlled periods. These findings reinforce bimekizumab’s potential as an effective treatment option across patients with heterogeneous baseline characteristics, comorbidities, and treatment histories.

Our results also demonstrate bimekizumab’s efficacy in patient subgroups that have historically proven difficult to treat. Higher body weight and obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ) are well-established factors associated with reduced efficacy for biologics and previous studies have demonstrated a negative impact on clinical responses to biologic treatment for psoriasis [, , ]. For example, in two phase 3 clinical trials, PASI 75 response rates in patients receiving ustekinumab 45 mg were 76.9% in patients ≤ 100 kg vs 54.6% in patients > 100 kg after 28 weeks of treatment [], leading to the recommendation of an increased dose (90 mg) for patients > 100 kg []. Dose optimisation for other biologics like secukinumab has also been evaluated in patients with obesity because of inconsistent efficacy []. In our analysis, bimekizumab was consistently more effective than comparators across all weight quartiles. In the highest weight quartile, bimekizumab treatment had higher rates of complete skin clearance compared with adalimumab (≥ 104.3 kg: 61.0% vs 20.2%), ustekinumab (≥ 102.6 kg: 66.9% vs 35.6%), and secukinumab (≥ 102.0 kg: 68.7% vs 36.3%). Notably, for comparator treatment arms, the lowest PASI 100 rate was always observed in the highest weight quartile, whilst for bimekizumab treatment arms this was only true in the 3-year pooled analysis. This pattern may reflect pharmacokinetic challenges in heavier patients, such as increased drug clearance or altered distribution, which could impact long-term outcomes. Nevertheless, findings from this analysis suggest that high efficacy is maintained with bimekizumab in patients with higher body weights, making it a valuable treatment option for these patients without the need for dosing adjustments, except in exceptional circumstances (e.g., body weight ≥ 120 kg: it is recommended to consider increasing dosing frequency at week 16 if PASI 100 is not achieved) [, ]. As highlighted by these results, it is important to closely monitor treatment response in patients with higher body weight and to utilise individualised dosing strategies when appropriate.

Prior biologic exposure has also been associated with reduced responses to subsequent biologic treatments [, , ]. While biologics have shown impressive efficacy in treating moderate to severe psoriasis, only an estimated 53% of patients remain on their first course of biological therapy after 3 years []. This suggests that patients often switch biologic treatment to potentially improve their chances of achieving and maintaining long-term efficacy [, ]. In this analysis, it seems that prior exposure to biologics may not impact subsequent efficacy with bimekizumab, with the proportion of bimekizumab-treated PASI 100 responders with prior biologic experience being consistent with biologic-naive patients through 3 years (71.7% vs 69.1%). Moreover, greater proportions of biologic-experienced patients treated with bimekizumab achieved PASI 100 at the end of comparator-controlled periods compared with adalimumab, ustekinumab, and secukinumab.

Comorbidities are common in patients with psoriasis and T2DM is another factor that has been shown to negatively impact the efficacy of biologics; increased biologic clearance and reduced clinical responses have been reported in patients with psoriasis and concomitant T2DM, an effect likely compounded by its association with obesity [, , ]. For example, an analysis of guselkumab-treated patients revealed that the absence of a T2DM diagnosis was significantly associated with complete skin clearance []. In contrast, we found that the rate of PASI 100 achievement was consistent among bimekizumab-treated patients regardless of a T2DM diagnosis through 3 years (T2DM diagnosis: 71.6% [ n = 86]; no T2DM diagnosis: 70.0% [ n = 1021]). However, the number of patients with both psoriasis and T2DM was low across the studies included here, limiting the ability to draw reliable conclusions about the relative efficacy of bimekizumab in these patients.

Previous post hoc subgroup analyses involving the IL-23 inhibitors guselkumab and risankizumab have also focused on patient subgroups which historically exhibit lower responses to biologic treatments, such as patients with higher body weights and prior biologic exposure [, ]. At 24 weeks, guselkumab treatment resulted in completely clear skin (IGA 0) in 48.0% ( n = 225) and 44.0% ( n = 207) of patients weighing 86.4 to < 100 kg and ≥ 100 kg, respectively, and 47.7% ( n = 172) of biologic-experienced patients []. In our analysis, 24 weeks of bimekizumab treatment resulted in complete skin clearance rates of 63.7% (patients weighing 87.0 to < 104.3 kg), 61.0% (patients weighing ≥ 104.3 kg), and 75.0% (biologic-experienced patients) for these groups. Meanwhile, long-term data show that after approximately 3 years (160 weeks) of risankizumab treatment, 61.1% ( n = 262) of patients > 86.6 kg achieved PASI 100 []; in our analysis, 66.5% of bimekizumab-treated patients ≥ 87.3 kg achieved PASI 100 after 3 years. While results from different studies and clinical programmes are not directly comparable, considering bimekizumab’s consistently high efficacy in the context of published literature on IL-23 inhibitors, such as guselkumab and risankizumab, may provide insights into the impact of dual IL-17F and IL-17A inhibition on efficacy across subgroups. Further studies exploring these differences directly could be valuable.

Results across patient subgroups of different disease durations can also help to optimise treatment choices and clinical decision-making regarding the appropriate timing for biologic use. In this analysis, bimekizumab treatment displayed high rates of complete skin clearance regardless of patients’ disease duration. The consistent efficacy of bimekizumab across different disease duration subgroups supports its use for patients early in their disease as well as those with long-term disease. Furthermore, if used as a first-line treatment, bimekizumab’s consistently high efficacy in diverse patient subgroups may help to reduce unnecessary switching between biologic therapies as a result of inadequate responses in patients. However, patients with shorter disease duration ≤ 2 years were not analysed here because of the small number of patients in this subgroup. Data in this subgroup would provide valuable insights into how early treatment may impact patients with psoriasis in the short and long term.

Strengths of this study include the granularity of subgroups adding clinical relevance to the results, and the randomisation of patients likely balancing the numbers receiving background study medications between subgroups. Limitations include the post hoc nature of this analysis and the lack of adjustment for multiple comparisons increasing the risk of a false positive, inter-study variation in treatment duration, the small patient numbers in some subgroups, and the lack of long-term comparator data which is limited to up to 1 year in these trials. However, the impact of the lack of an OLE comparator group is minimised for this analysis as it focuses on the variation within subgroups of the bimekizumab treatment arm.

Overall, these results demonstrate bimekizumab’s consistently high efficacy, up to 3 years, across diverse patient subgroups. Moreover, bimekizumab achieved higher rates of complete skin clearance compared with adalimumab, ustekinumab, and secukinumab across all subgroups analysed. These findings reinforce the value of bimekizumab for patients, clinicians, and payers as a treatment option which provides effective and durable disease control across a broad spectrum of patients with moderate to severe psoriasis.

title: Meaningful Change Thresholds for the Psoriasis Symptoms and Signs Diary: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Importance Change from baseline score on the validated Psoriasis Symptoms and Signs Diary (PSSD) is a widely used, patient-reported end point in clinical trials for psoriasis. Meaningful score change thresholds anchored to patient-reported assessments have not been established in a clinical trial setting. Objective To evaluate meaningful within-patient score change thresholds for the PSSD using data from the phase 3 Program to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Deucravacitinib, a Selective TYK2 Inhibitor (POETYK), PSO-1 clinical trial, which compared the efficacy and safety of deucravacitinib vs placebo and apremilast among adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis. Design, setting, and participants In this predefined analysis using data from the POETYK PSO-1 multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 clinical trial, conducted from August 7, 2018, to September 2, 2020, 666 adults with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis completed the PSSD daily throughout the trial. Meaningful change thresholds were derived by anchoring mean PSSD score change from baseline to week 16 to category improvements on the Patient Global Impression of Change (PGI-C) and the Patient Global Impression of Severity (PGI-S). Interventions Deucravacitinib, 6 mg, once daily; placebo; or apremilast, 30 mg, twice daily. Main outcome and measures The main outcome was score change from baseline to week 16 on the PSSD, anchored to the PGI-C and PGI-S. Results The trial included 666 patients (mean [SD] age, 46.1 [13.4] years; 453 men [68.0%]). Three thresholds were identified using an analysis set of 609 patients. Score improvement of at least 15 points from baseline reflected meaningful within-patient change anchored to the PGI-C. Score improvements of 25 points were supported by both the PGI-C and the PGI-S, while a 30-point score change identified patients with greater improvements in their psoriasis symptoms and signs. Conclusions and relevance This analysis suggests that PSSD score improvements of 15, 25, or 30 points represent increasing improvements in disease burden that are meaningful to patients with psoriasis.

sections.other: The Psoriasis Symptoms and Signs Diary (PSSD) is a validated patient-reported outcome instrument that assesses patient-perceived psoriasis sign and symptom severity. ,, A PSSD score change of −40 points from baseline, derived with reference to clinician-assessed anchors, has been proposed as a threshold reflecting clinically meaningful improvement. However, regulatory guidelines, including recent draft guidance issued by the US Food and Drug Administration, recommend that thresholds defining responders on patient-reported outcome instruments be derived using patient-reported, rather than clinician-rated, anchor-based methods , and suggest the Patient Global Impression of Change (PGI-C) and the Patient Global Impression of Severity (PGI-S) as suitable anchors. A meaningful within-patient change threshold (MWPCT) for the PSSD using patient-reported anchors has not been identified in clinical trials, to our knowledge. We describe the determination of MWPCTs for the PSSD incorporating patient perspectives using pooled, treatment-blinded PSSD, PGI-S, and PGI-C data from baseline to week 16 in the Program to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Deucravacitinib, a Selective TYK2 Inhibitor (POETYK), PSO-1, a recent phase 3 clinical trial in plaque psoriasis.
sections.methods:
POETYK PSO-1 was conducted from August 7, 2018, to September 2, 2020, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Independent institutional review board approval was obtained from all 154 sites, and all participants provided written informed consent ( NCT03624127 ) (trial protocols and statistical analysis plans in ), which applies to this analysis. The clinical trial collected patients’ baseline demographics, including race and ethnicity (patients were categorized as Asian, Black, White, or other). The secondary analysis presented here did not stratify patients by race or ethnicity. Patients (N = 666; eFigure 1 in ) completed the PSSD daily throughout the trial, rating 5 skin symptoms (itch, pain, stinging, burning, and tightness) and 6 skin signs (dryness, cracking, scaling, shedding or flaking, redness, and bleeding) associated with psoriasis on an 11-point scale from 0 (absent) to 10 (worst imaginable). If more than 3 items were missing, the domain score was considered missing. To obtain symptom and sign scores, responses within each domain were averaged and multiplied by 10. Domain summary scores were averaged to derive total scores ranging from 0 to 100; higher scores indicated greater disease burden. , Weekly scores were calculated by averaging daily scores for each 7-day period; baseline PSSD scores were calculated from daily diary data collected during screening. If more than 3 days of the weekly period were missing, that week’s score was set to missing.

Any patient who completed at least 1 PSSD item at baseline and a postbaseline visit was included in the derivation analysis (n = 609; deucravacitinib, n = 303; placebo, n = 150; apremilast, n = 156). At week 16, patients responded to the PGI-C question, “Since you started taking the study medication, how would you rate the overall impact of psoriasis on your life currently?” on a 7-point scale ranging from very much better to very much worse. At baseline and week 16, patients responded to the PGI-S question, “How severe are your psoriasis symptoms currently?” using a scale from 0 (absent) to 3 (severe).

With all treatment groups combined, patients were grouped according to their responses on the anchors. Polyserial correlations were calculated between category changes on the anchors and change from baseline in the PSSD domain and total scores at week 16; a coefficient of at least 0.4 was considered suitable for use. Within each anchor group, the mean (SD) PSSD score change from baseline, the 95% CI, and the standardized effect size (SES) were calculated. The smallest improvement category on each anchor with an SES of at least 0.5 and a significant P value was identified ( P ≤ .05 [2-sided] from a paired [within-samples] t test). The lowest point outside the overlap in the 95% CI between the anchor group with no change and the improved group constituted the preliminary estimate. All analyses were performed using SAS, version 9.4 or higher (SAS Institute Inc).

Anchor-based and distribution-based estimates (0.5 SDs and standard error of measurement [SEM]) were triangulated. Distribution-based approaches yield the lowest score change exceeding that expected to occur by chance; they cannot determine patient-perceived meaningfulness. Thus, anchor-based analysis formed the primary approach, while distribution-based methods were supportive. This process was repeated for the change from baseline in each individual PSSD item.

Cumulative distribution functions were generated for each anchor category. Any given point on the continuous line indicated the cumulative proportion of patients who reported that degree of score change from baseline or lower. Derived MWPCTs were applied to unblinded data from POETYK PSO-1 after database lock to compare the cumulative distribution of patients achieving meaningful PSSD responses at week 16 by treatment group. These cumulative distribution functions permit visualization of between-group differences in within-patient PSSD score changes from baseline.
sections.results:
The trial included 666 patients (mean [SD] age, 46.1 [13.4] years; 453 men [68.0%]). Of the 601 patients who completed the PGI-S and PSSD at baseline, 481 patients completed the PGI-S and PSSD at week 16, and 486 patients completed the PGI-C and PSSD at week 16. Of the 666 included patients, 121 (18.2%) were Asian, 6 (0.9%) were Black, 534 (80.2%) were White, and 5 (0.8%) identified their race as “other.” The secondary analysis did not collect data on race or ethnicity. Correlation coefficients between week 16 change from baseline in each PSSD domain, and each anchor (0.541-0.606) indicated suitability for MWPCT derivation (eTable 1 in ). The “a little better” PGI-C category (mean [SD] change from baseline: PSSD symptom score, –18.7 [19.9] [95% CI, –32.5 to 23.7]; P < .001; PSSD sign score, –19.1 [18.2] [95% CI, –22.8 to –15.5]; P < .001; PSSD total score, –18.9 [18.6] [95% CI, –22.7 to –15.2]; P < .001) and the 1-point improvement PGI-S category (mean [SD] change from baseline: PSSD symptom score, –26.5 [19.6] [95% CI, –29.3 to –23.6]; P < .001; PSSD sign score, –27.7 [18.5] [95% CI, –30.4 to –25.0]; P < .001; PSSD total score, –27.1 [18.6] [95% CI, –29.8 to –24.4]; P < .001) each showed significant within-group improvements in week 16 PSSD score, with medium to large SES (). Changes from baseline from −14.7 to −15.5 points were the lowest levels of change falling outside the 95% CI for the no-change group and within that of the improved group on the PGI-C; changes from baseline from −23.6 to −25.0 points were the lowest levels of change falling outside the 95% CI for the no-change group and within that of the improved group on the PGI-S (). Cumulative distribution function curves for change from baseline in PSSD total score, using each anchor, showed clear separation between the no-change groups and each improvement category, indicating that the response categories on the anchor scale adequately discerned the difference in scores (). eFigures 2 and 3 in show similar cumulative distribution function curves for PSSD domain scores.

Patient Global Impression of Change anchor-based analysis supports an MWPCT for improvement of 15 points for domain and total scores. A higher MWPCT of 25 points represents improvements on both the PGI-C and PGI-S anchors, including SES for within-group changes that exceeded 1.0. An MWPCT of 30 points identified patients who improved higher than “a little” on the PGI-C. These anchor-based estimates were all higher than the distribution-based estimates represented by 0.5 SDs, which ranged from 11.1 to 12.8, and the SEM, which ranged from 4.1 to 5.8 (eTable 2 in ). Owing to small sample sizes and nonsignificant effect sizes within worsened disease anchor groups, no MWPCTs for deterioration were identified.

eTables 3 and 4 in report the anchored change for individual PSSD items. The meaningfulness of a score improvement of 2 points on individual PSSD items is supported by the PGI-C and 0.5 SDs (eTable 5 in ).

depicts cumulative distribution function curves for the PSSD total score change from baseline at week 16 by treatment group, with the deucravacitinib group consistently above both comparators at each MWPCT. eFigures 4 and 5 in show similar cumulative distribution functions for week 16 change from baseline in symptom and sign scores. These curves indicate that, at any of the 3 thresholds, greater proportions of patients receiving deucravacitinib experienced meaningful improvement in their psoriasis burden at week 16 than those receiving apremilast or placebo.
sections.discussion:
The interpretability of patient-reported outcome end points is best established with reference to MWPCTs derived from patient-reported anchors rather than clinician assessments. Armstrong et al recommended a −40-point change from baseline threshold on the PSSD to indicate a minimum clinically meaningful improvement, derived from clinician-rated anchors; however, smaller changes in score may be meaningful to patients themselves. The use of the PGI-C and PGI-S as anchors for determining patient-relevant change measured by the PSSD therefore constitutes an important advance in interpreting changes in PSSD scores. Moreover, this anchored analysis conforms to published credibility criteria and regulatory guidelines for determining MWPCTs.

This study has some limitations. The lowest MWPCT identified, −15 points, corresponds to a rating of change rather than the rating of concept recommended by some researchers to overcome present-state bias. ,,, In addition, the applicability of MWPCTs for improvement to worsening psoriasis symptoms or signs has not been examined.

In this analysis, data from the POETYK PSO-1 trial anchored to responses on the PGI-C established PSSD domain and total score decreases of 15 points as meaningful to patients with psoriasis. The patient-perceived meaningfulness of a −25-point change from baseline is supported by both the PGI-C and the PGI-S, while a −30-point MWPCT identified patients who reported higher improvement on the PGI-C. The determination of MWPCTs allows for responder analyses of the PSSD score change from baseline, enhancing the patient-relevant interpretation of this widely used instrument in clinical trials of psoriasis.

title: Deucravacitinib in the treatment of psoriasis.
abstract: Purpose of the article Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated, skin disease with a significantly negative impact on patients' quality of life. Moderate-to-severe disease often requires systemic therapies and currently available ones still have numerous disadvantages or limitations. Tyrosine kinase 2 (TYK2) mediates immune signaling of IL-12, IL-23, and type I interferons, without interfering with other critical systemic functions. This article aims to review the current knowledge on deucravacitinib, a new oral drug which selectively inhibits TYK2, granting it a low risk of off-target effects. Materials and methods A review of the published literature was conducted using the PubMed database, published abstracts and virtual presentations from scientific meetings, data from industry press releases, and results published on ClinicalTrials.gov regarding the deucravacitinib for the treatment of psoriasis. Manuscripts with trial results, case series, clinical trial data from ClinicalTrials.gov, and articles highlighting expert perspectives on the topic of the article were selected. Results Two phase 3, 52-week trials evaluated deucravacitinib 6 mg against placebo and apremilast - POETYK PSO-1 and PSO-2, enrolling 1688 patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis. At week 16, over 50% of patients treated with deucravacitinib reached PASI75, significantly superior to placebo and apremilast. Symptomatic improvement was also reported, with greater impact on itch. Deucravacitinib was well tolerated and safe. There were no reports of serious infections, thromboembolic events, or laboratory abnormalities. Persistent efficacy and consistent safety profiles were reported for up to 2 years. Conclusions Deucravacitinib has the potential to become a safe, effective, and well-tolerated treatment for patients with moderate-to-severe disease. Future studies will be important to determine the exact role of this drug in the treatment of psoriasis.

title: Employing zero-inflated beta distribution in an exposure-response analysis of TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor brepocitinib in patients with plaque psoriasis.
abstract: Brepocitinib is an oral selective dual TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor and based on its cytokine inhibition profile is expected to provide therapeutic benefit in the treatment of plaque psoriasis. Efficacy data from a completed Phase 2a study in patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis were utilized to develop a population exposure-response model that can be employed to inform dose selection decisions for further clinical development. A modeling approach that employs the zero-inflated beta distribution was used to account for the bounded nature and distributional characteristics of the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) score data. The developed exposure-response model provided an adequate description of the observed PASI scores across all the treatment arms tested and across both the induction and maintenance dosing periods of the study. In addition, the developed model exhibited a good predictive capacity with regard to the derived responder metrics (e.g., 75%/90%/100% improvement in PASI score [PASI75/90/100]). Clinical trial simulations indicated that the induction/maintenance dosing paradigm explored in this study does not offer any advantages from an efficacy perspective and that doses of 10, 30, and 60 mg once-daily may be suitable candidates for clinical evaluation in subsequent Phase 2b studies.

sections.other:
Psoriasis is estimated to affect more than 8 million people in the United States, and approximately 125 million people worldwide (2–3% of the global population) []. Although psoriasis primarily affects the skin and is not a life-threatening disease, it can profoundly impact the quality of life resulting in impairment analogous to other major diseases such as type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, and arthritis []. The most common variant of psoriasis, plaque psoriasis, is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by red, scaly, raised plaques. Increased levels of several pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-a), interleukin (IL)-6, IL-9, IL-12, IL-17, IL-22, and IL-23 and interferon gamma (IFN-γ) have been implicated in the pathophysiology of chronic plaque psoriasis [, , ].

Brepocitinib (PF-06700841) is an oral selective dual TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor targeting signaling of multiple cytokines (IFN, IL-6, IL-12, IL-21, IL-22, and IL-23) and based on its cytokine inhibition profile is expected to provide therapeutic benefit in the treatment of plaque psoriasis [, ]. In the first-in-human clinical trial, brepocitinib was well tolerated by healthy participants and patients with plaque psoriasis. Additionally, psoriasis patients receiving active treatment in this study (30 or 100 mg once daily for 28 days) had clinically meaningful decreases in disease activity []. Based on these data, a Phase 2a multicenter study was subsequently designed to assess efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetics (PK) of oral brepocitinib in patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, and test various doses and dosing regimens for induction and maintenance of brepocitinib (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02969018 ). This study has been now completed, and overall results showed a promising efficacy and a favorable safety profile in patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis [].

One of the most commonly used efficacy assessments in psoriasis clinical trials is the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI). PASI score is a clinical tool that reflects both the extent (area) and severity of the disease and it can range from 0 (no evidence of the disease) to 72 (worst possible outcome) in 0.1 increments []. In addition, the PASI-derived responder metrics (e.g., PASI75 and PASI90 referring respectively to the proportion of patients achieving at least 75% or at least 90% improvement from baseline PASI scores) are commonly used primary endpoints. Due to their dichotomous nature and the fact that they omit the granularity of the raw PASI scores, the derived responder metrics may not be optimal for exposure-response assessment especially in small sample size early clinical development trials. Therefore, exposure-response analysis in the domain of the raw PASI scores is often desirable, especially if this can be also accompanied with satisfactory predictions of the derived responder metrics. However, modeling the PASI scores directly presents particular challenges as they are bounded between 0 and 72 and their distribution is often skewed. In addition, the obtained PASI datasets may often contain observations at the lower bound (0), particularly in the presence of a strong drug effect.

The primary aim of this work is to utilize the data derived from the completed Phase 2a study of brepocitinib in psoriasis patients to develop a population exposure-response model that can be employed to inform dose selection decisions for further clinical development. In parallel, this work aims to assess the utility of an approach that employs the zero-inflated beta distribution to overcome the challenges involved in PASI score modeling.

Below is the link to the electronic supplementary material.
sections.methods:
Model development was performed using data from a Phase 2a, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group, multicenter study in subjects with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02969018 ). A schematic of study design is shown in Fig. . The first part of the study, following a screening period (up to 6 weeks), was a 4-week induction period with double-blind daily treatment. At the end of week 4, all subjects switched to their predefined double-blind maintenance treatment regimen for week 5 through week 12.

Approximately 200 subjects were planned to be randomized into the study, to allow for approximately 160 evaluable subjects (20 completers per arm). The randomization ratio was 7:1, active: placebo. During the first 4 weeks of the treatment period, subjects received orally either 30 mg once-daily (QD), or 60 mg QD of brepocitinib, or matching placebo. During the 8-week maintenance portion of the treatment period (weeks 5 through 12), subjects received orally either 10 mg QD, or 30 mg QD, or a 100 mg once weekly (QW) regimen of brepocitinib, or matching placebo. Maintenance dose level and regimen were assigned at the initial time of randomization into the study. All subjects, regardless of assigned regimen (i.e., QD or QW) received blinded QD tablets throughout the study treatment period to maintain the study blind.

The duration of study subject participation was approximately 26 weeks, including screening (up to 6 weeks), 12-week treatment period, and 8-week follow up period. For further details on the study design, the reader is referred to the associated publication [].

Female and male patients between 18 and 75 years of age with a diagnosis of plaque psoriasis for at least 6 months before the start of the study, PASI score of ≥ 12, physician’s global assessment (PGA) score of 3 or 4, and psoriasis covering ≥ 10% of total body surface area were eligible to participate in the study. Key exclusion criteria were non-plaque psoriasis, other skin conditions that would affect the assessment of psoriasis, drug-induced psoriasis, use of corticosteroids, and psychiatric conditions including suicidal ideation or behavior.

The study was conducted in compliance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines established by the International Council on Harmonisation. The final protocol, amendments, and informed consent documentation were reviewed and approved by the institutional review boards and independent ethics committees of the investigational centers.

PASI scoring, which quantifies body surface area and lesion severity into a single score, was used to assess brepocitinib efficacy in this study. PASI score is calculated by combining the percentage of body areas (head and neck, upper limbs, trunk, and lower limbs) covered, with the severity of erythema, thickness/induration, and desquamation/scaling, for a score between 0 and 72 []. PASI scores were assessed: at screening; on week 0 (baseline); on weeks 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12; and during follow-up (weeks 14 and 16). Only data collected during the 12-week active treatment period of the study were included in the analysis. Any data collected during screening and the follow-up period were not included in the analysis.

Blood samples for PK analysis of brepocitinib were collected pre-dose on week 0 (baseline) and week 1; pre-dose and 30 min post-dose on weeks 2, 6, 8, and 10; and pre-dose, 30 min, 1, 2, and 4 h post-dose on weeks 4 and 12. The samples were analyzed using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. The lower limit of quantification for brepocitinib was 0.2 ng/mL.

For additional details and study assessments not related to the current analysis, the reader is referred to the associated publication [].

A population pharmacokinetic (PK) model has been previously developed for brepocitinib using data from five clinical trials, consisting of three Phase 1 and two Phase 2 studies (including the Phase 2a study in psoriasis patients described in this manuscript) []. Briefly, brepocitinib PK were described with a one-compartment model with first-order oral absorption and an absorption lag for the tablet formulation (apparent clearance (CL/F) of 18.7 L/h, apparent volume of distribution (V/F) of 136 L, first-order absorption rate constant (k a ) of 3.46 h −1 and a lag time (A lag ) of 0.24 h). The effect of body weight on CL/F and V/F was included with an allometric relationship (referenced to 70 kg) and the associated coefficients were fixed to 0.75 and 1, respectively. Random inter-individual variability was accounted in the CL/F and V/F parameters using a full variance-covariance matrix (coefficient of variation (CV) of 78% and 60.5% for CL/F and V/F, respectively, and a correlation coefficient of 0.76).

The empirical Bayes estimates (EBEs) of CL/F for all study participants (η-shrinkage < 0.1%) were extracted from the population PK model output and were used to calculate the average concentration ( \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$${C}_{ave}$$\end{document} C ave ) of each individual across the induction and maintenance periods of the study, using Eq. , where \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$\tau$$\end{document} τ refers to the dosing interval (24 h for QD dosing and 168 h for QW dosing) and \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$$Dose$$\end{document} Dose refers to the administered brepocitinib dose either during the induction or the maintenance period of the study.

In addition to evaluating the relative standard errors derived from the NONMEM ® covariance step, the parameter uncertainty of the final model was also assessed using sampling importance resampling (SIR) [, ]. SIR was performed by subjecting the final model covariance step output to five iterations of sampling, resampling, and multivariate Box-Cox transformation. Samples for the sampling and resampling steps used 1000, 1000, 1500, 2000, 2000 and 200, 250, 500, 1000, 1000 samples, respectively. The median and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for each parameter were calculated from the SIR resamples of the final iteration.

The model’s performance to adequately describe the observed PASI scores was assessed via a visual predictive check (VPC) based on 1000 simulations using the design of the index dataset. Additionally, although the model was developed using the raw PASI scores, it is of particular importance to be also able to describe derived responder metrics, as the latter are important endpoints for future studies. Therefore, the model performance was also evaluated with respect to its capacity to predict the following responder metrics: proportion of participants achieving at least 50%, 75%, 90%, and 100% improvement from baseline PASI (PASI50, PASI75, PASI90, and PASI100, respectively). For this evaluation these responder metrics were derived from the raw simulated PASI scores in each of the 1000 simulated datasets, and associated 95% CIs were generated. The latter were then compared to the responder metrics that were observed in the current study.

The developed population exposure-response model was used to perform clinical trial simulations to aid dose selection for subsequent trials.
